The supreme Shinto deity and solar goddess — born from Izanagi's left eye. When Susanoo's violence drove her into the cave (Ama-no-Iwato), the world fell into darkness. The other gods danced and laughed until she emerged, restoring light.
Great Spirit of the Cherokee — the supreme creator. Pervades all things. Beyond gender and form. The earth itself was made from mud brought up by Water Beetle from beneath the primordial waters.

Corn Mother of the Cherokee — produced corn from her own body. When her sons discovered the secret and were horrified, she instructed them to kill her and drag her body in seven circles — corn grew from the bloodied earth. The Cherokee dying-and-rising vegetation goddess.
The Hunter — Cherokee culture hero. Husband of Selu. Father of the Twin Thunders. Knew all animals before they roamed free; his sons released them out of curiosity, creating the hunting world.
The Apache Life-Giver — supreme deity who is the source of all life and breath. Not actively interventional but the underlying source of all existence. Withdrawn but always present.
primary_sources: Goodwin, The Social Organization of the Western Apache

deities.summary: The Mountain Spirits — supernatural beings who taught humanity how to live. They dance in the Crown Dance (Gaan Dance) and protect Apache people. They are the source of healing power.

The elder of the Navajo Hero Twins — son of Changing Woman and the Sun. With his brother Born-for-Water, slays the monsters that plagued the Earth, making it safe for the Diné. Their journey is recounted in the Blessingway.
The younger Navajo Hero Twin — son of Changing Woman. Born for Water complements his brother Monster Slayer through cunning and spiritual practice rather than violence.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Waters, Book of the Hopi (1963)
deities.summary: The Hopi supreme being — the Creator. In the beginning was Taiowa alone, then he created Sotuknang to make the universe. Taiowa is the source from which all emerges.
The nephew (or first creation) of Taiowa — the one who shaped the universe according to Taiowa's plan. He created the Spider Grandmother and the first humans.

The Spirit of Death and Earth — guardian of this Fourth World (the current age). He greeted the emerging Hopi when they came up from the Third World and taught them how to live in this world. He alone can step between worlds.

The ancestral spirits and nature-spirits of the Hopi — hundreds of named kachinas. They visit the villages from the San Francisco Peaks for half the year. Each represents an aspect of creation: rain, corn, animals, ancestors. Children receive kachina dolls (tihu) as both toys and teaching.

The Spider — Lakota trickster and culture hero who created the world but is also the source of foolishness and trouble. His tricks teach as often as they harm. Inventor of language and the first to deceive humans.
The supernatural thunder beings — they bring rain and lightning. Their wings make thunder; their flashing eyes are lightning. They protect humans but are too powerful to look upon directly.
The Great Spirit of the Anishinaabe peoples — supreme creator and source of all spiritual power. Not a personal god but the cosmic spiritual force.

The cannibal ice spirit — embodies the destructive force of greed and starvation. A human who eats human flesh becomes a Windigo. Stands as a moral warning against selfishness in a survival-marginal climate.
The trickster-hero-creator of the Anishinaabe — the Great Hare. Brought fire, taught medicines, recreated the world after the great flood. Same figure as Nanabozho in different transliteration.

The supreme being of the Mapuche people — the lord/maker of people. Quadripartite: old man, old woman, young man, young woman — the cosmic four-fold unity. The most articulated quadripartite supreme deity in South America.
Ancestral spirits and volcanic-thunder beings of the Mapuche — they inhabit volcanoes and govern weather. The thunderous voices of the ancestors.
The Muisca Great Mother — emerged from Lake Iguaque with a three-year-old boy. When he grew up they married and populated the world. After teaching the people, both returned to the lake as serpents.
primary_sources: Spanish colonial accounts of Muisca religion

deities.summary: The Muisca supreme creator — pure light contained within himself. He released the light from his interior, creating black birds that flew over the world bringing dawn.

The Akkadian goddess of love, war, sex, and political power — successor to Sumerian Inanna with distinct Akkadian emphases. Her descent to the underworld in the Akkadian version differs from Inanna's. Patron of Nineveh.
primary_sources: Descent of Ishtar to the Underworld (Akkadian)

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1900 BCE (city); supreme deity from c. 1300 BCE
deities.summary: The Assyrian state god — supreme deity of the Assyrian Empire. Originally a city deity of Ashur (the city), elevated to imperial chief deity. Identified with Anshar (heaven), and given Marduk's attributes during Assyrian conquest of Babylon.
God of writing, wisdom, scribes, and the planet Mercury. Son of Marduk. His cult flourished in Babylon and especially Borsippa. Akkadian Thoth/Hermes — the divine scribe.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2000 BCE (Sumerian lilītu); developed in Talmud, Zohar
deities.summary: The night-demon — wind-demoness in Sumerian, the disobedient first wife of Adam in later Jewish tradition (refusing to lie beneath him), queen of demons in the Zohar. She steals infants and seduces sleeping men. The most theologically developed female demon in Western tradition.
primary_sources: Alphabet of Ben Sira c. 700-1000 CE

deities.summary: The wrathful protective goddess — the only female deity among the eight Dharmapala (Dharma protectors). Rides a mule across a sea of blood. Holds a skull cup. Her wrath protects the Dharma.
The first patriarch of Chan/Zen Buddhism — the Indian monk who brought meditation tradition to China. Reportedly sat facing a wall for 9 years at Shaolin. Founder of the lineage that became Zen.
The Sixth Patriarch of Chan — illiterate woodcutter who became enlightened upon hearing the Diamond Sutra. Author of the Platform Sutra. Founded the Southern School of sudden enlightenment.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1500 BCE (Zhou dynasty); central in Confucian thought
deities.summary: Heaven — not a personal god but the cosmic moral order. Tian Ming (Mandate of Heaven) gives rulers legitimacy and removes it when they fail. The impersonal supreme principle of Chinese imperial cosmology.

Confucius as the supreme sage of Chinese civilization — progressively elevated to divine status, with state cult and temple offerings. The most successful philosopher-to-deity transformation in human history.

The Supreme Being of Caodaism — combines Buddha, Lao Tzu, Confucius, Jesus, and Muhammad with Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen, and Joan of Arc as saints. The most explicit modern syncretism of world religions into one tradition.
alternate_names: Đại Đạo Tam Kỳ Phổ Độ

deities.summary: The Birth Grandmother — Korean shamanic deity of childbirth, infants, and child-rearing. Three goddesses or one triple goddess. Mothers pray to her for safe birth and healthy children.
The Seven Stars — Korean shamanic deities of the Big Dipper. They govern longevity, fortune, and human destiny. Their cult predates Buddhism in Korea and was absorbed into Korean Buddhism.
The ancestor spirits of Mongolian shamanism — spirits of deceased shamans and significant ancestors that protect and guide the living. Embodied in small images kept in the home (also called ongon).

The supreme deity of the Buryat — the bald-headed father god. Rules the 99 Tenger (sky beings): 55 western (good) and 44 eastern (evil). The cosmic dualism of Buryat shamanic theology runs through the entire pantheon.
The Great Mother of Buryat shamanism — feminine cosmic source. Various local manifestations across the Buryat region.

deities.earliest_attestation: pre-Christian Magyar; survived in Christian Hungarian
deities.summary: The supreme Magyar deity — Old Hungarian name for God, surviving the conversion to Christianity. Possibly cognate with Turkic Tengri family. Rules the Sky and the celestial Tree of Life.

The Ryukyuan creation goddess — descended from heaven to create the islands. Mother of all life in Okinawa. The Ryukyuan kami system is distinct from mainland Shinto, with strong matriarchal elements.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1800 CE (Cuban transformation of Yoruba Shango)
deities.summary: The Santeria transformation of Yoruba Shango — fully fused with the Catholic saint Santa Bárbara. The red and white colors, thunder, and royal power persist. The most fully-realized syncretism in the Afro-Caribbean tradition.

The rebellious first creation of Amma — impatient, he tore himself from the cosmic egg before time, taking only part of his placenta (which became the earth in fragmented form). His sin contaminated creation. He became the Pale Fox (Vulpes pallida), wandering the earth as the source of disorder and divination.
primary_sources: Griaule and Dieterlen, The Pale Fox

deities.summary: The Two Men — ancestor beings of the Western Desert peoples who traveled across the desert in the Dreamtime, creating waterholes, plants, and sacred sites. They are the most widespread Western Desert ancestor figures.

The most iconic figure of Minoan religion — bare-breasted woman holding snakes, sometimes with a cat on her head. Her exact identity and theology are unknown (Linear A is undeciphered), but the iconography suggests a powerful goddess of life, death, and rebirth.

The supreme Armenian deity — derived from Persian Ahura Mazda but assimilated with Greek Zeus during the Hellenistic period. Father of the gods, creator of heaven and earth. His chief temple was at Ani-Kamakh.

Armenian goddess of fertility, healing, and wisdom — descended from Iranian Anahita. Mother and protector goddess. Her major shrine at Eriza had a famous golden statue (destroyed by Antony, restored by Tiridates III).

deities.earliest_attestation: pre-Christian; preserved in Georgian Christian period
deities.summary: The supreme Georgian deity — pre-Christian sky god whose name became the Georgian word for God after Christianization. Lives in the highest heaven, removed from direct intervention. Lower deities and mountain spirits serve as mediators.
primary_sources: Charachidze, Le système religieux de la Géorgie païenne

deities.summary: The supreme deity of the Luba — beyond comprehension, beyond image. Worshipped indirectly through ancestor spirits and the sacred kingship. The Luba sacred kingship is one of the most institutionally articulated divine kingships in Africa.
primary_sources: Luba oral tradition; Reefe, The Rainbow and the Kings

deities.summary: The female ancestral medium of the Luba kingdom — when the king died, his sacred essence was transferred to a female medium (Mwadi) who held the kingship's spiritual power. A rare example of explicit female mediation of male royal divinity.
primary_sources: Reefe; de Heusch, The Drunken King

deities.summary: The Good Twin (Teharonhiawako) — son of Sky Woman's daughter. Created beneficial things: human beings, edible plants, gentle animals, the sun. Defeated his evil twin in cosmic combat. The Iroquois Christ-figure.

The Evil Twin (Tawiskaron) — created harmful things: thorns, predators, disease, monsters, winter. Born by tearing through his mother's side (killing her). Defeated by Sapling but his creations remain.

The hummingbird god of war and sun — patron of the Mexica/Aztec. Born from Coatlicue when a ball of feathers fell into her clothes. Killed his sister Coyolxauhqui (the moon) the moment he was born, defending his mother. The Aztec sun who needs human hearts to continue rising.

The Moon — daughter of Coatlicue, sister of Huitzilopochtli. She led her 400 siblings (the stars) to kill their pregnant mother but was decapitated and dismembered by the newborn Huitzilopochtli, who threw her body down Coatepec mountain. The famous Coyolxauhqui Stone shows her dismembered form.

Obsidian Butterfly — the fierce skeletal deity with jaguar claws and butterfly wings of obsidian knives. A tzitzimitl (star-demon) of the Cihuateteo (warrior-women who died in childbirth). Patron of fertility and warfare in their inverse forms.

The Moche/Chimu moon deity — the most powerful celestial body in coastal Andean religion (more important than the sun, contrary to the highland Inca tradition). Si governed fishing, crops, and storms.

The Olmec proto-deity — a composite creature combining crocodile, serpent, and bird features. The earliest documented divine image in Mesoamerica. Possibly the prototype of all later Mesoamerican feathered serpents.
primary_sources: Olmec stone sculpture (San Lorenzo, La Venta)

deities.summary: Fish avatar — saved Manu and the Vedas from the cosmic flood. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
Tortoise avatar — supported Mount Mandara during the churning of the cosmic ocean. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
Boar avatar — lifted the earth from the cosmic ocean where it had been dragged by the demon Hiranyaksha. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.

Man-lion avatar — killed the demon Hiranyakashipu to protect the devotee Prahlada. Neither man nor animal, neither inside nor outside, neither day nor night. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
Dwarf avatar — defeated the demon-king Bali by asking for three paces of land then expanding to cosmic size. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
Axe-wielding warrior — destroyed corrupt Kshatriya rulers 21 times. The wrathful Brahmin avatar. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
The hero of the Ramayana — virtuous king of Ayodhya, perfect husband, restorer of dharma. Killed the demon-king Ravana. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
In Vaishnava tradition, the Buddha is the 9th avatar — sent to lead unworthy beings away from the Vedas. The Hindu absorption of the Buddha. One of the ten avatars (Dasavatara) of Vishnu.
Goddess of fortune, wealth, beauty, and abundance. Consort of Vishnu. Born from the churning of the cosmic ocean. She blesses whomever she chooses; she is fickle but never absent from the divine.
Goddess of wisdom, music, arts, and rivers. Consort of Brahma. The Saraswati river in Vedic times was sacred; she is identified with its life-giving flow.

The supreme goddess in her gentle, married form — daughter of the mountain (Himavat), wife of Shiva, mother of Ganesha and Kartikeya. She is the same divine feminine as Kali and Durga but in domesticated form. Parvati = Kali = Durga as Tridevi.

God of war, victory, and youthful divine power. Son of Shiva and Parvati. Major Tamil deity (Murugan). Leads the divine army against demons. His six faces correspond to the six attributes of perfection.
The monkey god — devoted servant of Rama, the embodiment of bhakti (devotion). Son of the wind god Vayu. Possesses immense strength and yogic powers. The model of perfect service to the divine.
God of the wind, breath, life-force. Father of Hanuman and Bhima. The breath in living beings is his presence. Cognate with Avestan Vayu.
The cosmic feminine energy — the active principle without which Shiva is inert. "Shiva without Shakti is shava (corpse)." All goddesses are manifestations of Shakti.

Preserver of the trimurti. The cosmic principle that maintains dharma across the yuga cycles. Descends as a series of avatars (traditionally ten: Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana, Parashurama, Rama, Krishna, Buddha, and the future Kalki) whenever dharma declines. In Vaishnava theology, the supreme Source itself, with Brahma and Shiva as his expressions.
iconography: reclining on Shesha the cosmic serpent on the ocean of milk

deities.summary: The creator — first of the Trimurti. Has four faces looking in all directions. Born from the lotus growing from Vishnu's navel. Rarely worshipped despite being the creator — only two temples in all of India.

The historical Buddha — Siddhartha Gautama, prince of the Shakya clan who renounced his kingdom, achieved enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, and taught the Dharma for 45 years before his parinirvana. The founder of Buddhism.
The Diamond Being — embodiment of the purification of all karmic obscurations. His 100-syllable mantra is the most important Vajrayana purification practice.
The Destroyer of Death — the wrathful form of Manjushri. Buffalo-headed, with multiple faces and arms, surrounded by skulls and flames. He defeated Yama (death) to liberate beings from samsara.
The female bodhisattva of compassion and longevity. Seven eyes (one on forehead, palms, soles of feet) see suffering in all directions. Particularly invoked for healing and long life.
The Great Black One — protector of the Dharma, fierce defender of practitioners. Originally a Hindu form of Shiva, adopted into Vajrayana as a protector. Multiple forms (2-arm, 4-arm, 6-arm).
The Buddha in tantric union with his consort Nairatmya. Eight heads, 16 arms. Central deity of the Hevajra Tantra — one of the most important Anuttarayoga Tantras. His name means "Joyful Vajra."

God of the sea, wealth, and seafaring. Chief of the Vanir before peace with the Aesir. Father of Freyr and Freya. His marriage to the mountain-giantess Skadi failed because she hated the sea and he hated the mountains.

The original Germanic war god — likely the original sky-father (PIE *Tiwaz, cognate with Zeus). His role diminished as Odin rose. Lost his hand to Fenrir to bind the wolf, becoming the god of oaths and lawful combat.
deities.etymology: PG *Tiwaz = PIE *Dyeus

deities.summary: Keeper of the golden apples that maintain the gods' youth. When Loki delivered her to the giant Thiazi, the gods began to age — proving that even gods need her gift.

Three female beings who weave the fate of all beings, including the gods: Urd (Was/Fate), Verdandi (Becoming), Skuld (Shall-Be). They tend Yggdrasil with water from the Well of Urd. Their decrees cannot be undone, not even by Odin.

Jackal-headed god of mummification and the journey of the dead. Conducts the Weighing of the Heart against the feather of Ma'at. The earliest Egyptian death deity, later displaced by Osiris but retaining the judgment role.
Lord of the dead, dying-and-rising god. Murdered and dismembered by Set, gathered and revived by Isis enough to conceive Horus. Then ruled the underworld. Every dead Pharaoh became Osiris.
deities.tradition_claim: Osiris was once a living king who civilized Egypt — who taught agriculture, law, and worship. Set tricked him into a beautifully crafted sarcophagus, sealed it, and cast it into the Nile. Isis searched every corner of Egypt, reassembled the body, fashioned a golden phallus to replace the piece eaten by fish, and breathed life into him long enough to conceive Horus. Osiris descended to become eternal king of the underworld — judge of every soul. Those whose heart is lighter than Ma'at's feather receive eternal paradise. Those heavy with wrongdoing are devoured by Ammit and cease to exist.
deities.russell_connection: Osiris's 14-piece dismemberment and reassembly maps to Russell's 14-note two-octave system. The death of integration and resurrection of reintegration is the cosmic wave pattern at the scale of divine narrative.

deities.summary: The cosmic serpent of chaos — every night attacks Ra's solar barque trying to prevent the sun's rebirth. He is the absolute adversary, the principle of non-being. Defeated by Set (and Ra's magic) each night, but eternal in his enmity.

Goddess and concept of cosmic order, truth, justice, and balance. The feather of Ma'at is weighed against the heart of the dead. She is both a goddess and the cosmic principle she embodies — the most important abstract concept in Egyptian theology.
Queen of the Olympian gods — wife and sister of Zeus. Goddess of marriage, women, and family. Her jealousy is famous; she persecutes Zeus's mortal lovers and their children (especially Heracles).
Lord of the underworld and the dead. Brother of Zeus and Poseidon. Drew the underworld in the lots-drawing among the three brothers. Not evil — just the impersonal lord of an irreversible domain.
God of wine, ecstasy, theatre, ritual madness, and resurrection. Born twice (from Semele and Zeus's thigh). His maenads tear apart whoever opposes him. The god who dissolves boundaries of self.

The legendary singer-shaman whose music could move stones and tame beasts. Descended to the underworld to retrieve his wife Eurydice — almost succeeded but lost her by looking back. Founder of the Orphic mystery tradition.
The Three Fates — Clotho spins the thread of life, Lachesis measures it, Atropos cuts it. Even Zeus is subject to Fate. The Greek parallel of the Norns, Norse Norns, and Mokosh.

The divine champion — son of Zeus and Alcmene. Performed the 12 Labors. Eventually ascended to Olympus, deified after death. The paradigmatic divine hero — half-mortal, suffering, achieving godhood through trial.

The primordial cosmic being — emerged from the cosmic egg. As he grew (10 feet per day for 18,000 years), his body separated yin and yang, sky and earth. When he died, his body became the world: eyes = sun and moon, breath = wind, hair = stars, flesh = earth.
iconography: gigantic figure between sky and earth

deities.summary: Mother of the ten suns — she gives birth to suns and bathes them. The original Chinese cosmology had ten suns rising in rotation until Houyi shot down nine of them.
The divine archer who shot down nine of the ten suns when their simultaneous appearance scorched the earth. His wife Chang'e took his elixir of immortality and fled to the moon.

Wife of Houyi — drank his elixir of immortality and ascended to the moon, where she lives with a jade rabbit. The mid-Autumn festival celebrates her. The most beloved Chinese mythological figure for ordinary people.

deities.earliest_attestation: Yuan dynasty (1271-1368 CE); older folk origins
deities.summary: The eight legendary immortals of Taoist tradition: Lu Dongbin, He Xiangu, Zhang Guolao, Han Xiangzi, Tieguai Li, Cao Guojiu, Lan Caihe, Han Zhongli. Each represents a path to immortality and carries a unique magical implement.

The Nine-Tailed Fox — both auspicious omen (in Tang dynasty) and shapeshifting seductress demon (in popular tradition). Becomes more powerful with each century of life. In some traditions, a benevolent goddess; in others, a man-eating demon.

deities.earliest_attestation: Journey to the West (Wu Cheng'en, 16th c.); older folk origin
deities.summary: The Monkey King — born from a stone egg, learned the 72 transformations, defeated the gods of heaven, was imprisoned under a mountain by Buddha for 500 years, then accompanied Tang Sanzang to retrieve the Buddhist sutras from India. Bridge between Hindu Hanuman and East Asian trickster traditions.

The legendary controller of the floods — tamed the rivers of China by digging channels rather than building dams. Founded the Xia dynasty. The cultural hero whose taming of nature founded Chinese civilization.
Vedic dawn goddess — the most beautiful in the Rigveda. Her appearance is celebrated with 20+ hymns. The most direct surviving PIE *h₂éwsōs.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit Ushas = PIE *h₂éwsōs = Greek Eos, Latin Aurora, Lithuanian Auszra, English Eostre

deities.summary: The first man — survived the flood by Matsya's warning. Father of humanity. Author of the Manusmriti (Laws of Manu). The Vedic equivalent of Adam — the first human and the first patriarch.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit Manu = PIE *manus (man) = English man, German Mann

deities.summary: All-Father of the Norse pantheon. Restless wisdom-seeker who sacrifices himself to himself on Yggdrasil. Wanderer in disguise. Carries knowledge of his own doom at Ragnarök.
deities.tradition_claim: Odin hungered for what no god had: knowledge of what was hidden, what was coming, what lay beneath. He gave his right eye to Mimir's well without hesitation — one eye for wisdom. Still not enough. He speared himself and hung on Yggdrasil for nine days and nine nights — wounded, fasting, alone — staring into the void below until the runes rose up to meet him. The runes are not an alphabet. They are cosmic forces — each rune a principle of reality, a living pattern in the structure of existence. He gathers the fallen warriors into Valhalla not from cruelty but because he needs them for Ragnarok — the final battle he knows is coming and cannot prevent. He will die. He knows it. And still he prepares, and still he learns. That is what makes him a model of what it means to face the inevitable with wisdom and will.
deities.russell_connection: Odin hanging on Yggdrasil (the axis of the universe) and receiving universal knowledge maps to Russell's description of accessing the zero-point — the axis around which all motion rotates — where universal knowledge is available.

deities.summary: Greatest Irish hero, son of Lugh. His battle-frenzy (riastrad) transforms him into a monstrous figure. Defended Ulster alone against Connacht.
First king of the Tuatha De Danann — lost his arm in battle, replaced with a silver prosthetic by Dian Cecht. King must be physically perfect; he abdicated and was restored.
Physician of the gods — healed the wounded Tuatha De by throwing them in the Well of Slaine. Crafted Nuada's silver arm. Killed his own son Miach when Miach's healing surpassed his.
The master magician of the Welsh gods — shapeshifter, trickster, creator of the flower-bride Blodeuwedd. Uncle and guardian of Lleu Llaw Gyffes.

Witch-goddess and keeper of the Cauldron of Inspiration (Awen). Brewed the potion for a year; it was accidentally tasted by the servant Gwion, who fled through shapeshifting transformations before being swallowed and reborn as the bard Taliesin.
God of fertility, sunshine, and rain — chief of the Vanir alongside his sister Freya. Gave away his sword to win Gerd; it fights giants on its own. At Ragnarok, dies fighting Surt without his sword.
The watchman of the gods — stands at Bifrost to guard Asgard. His senses are so acute he can hear grass grow. Will sound the Gjallarhorn at Ragnarok.

The World Tree — the immense ash tree connecting the nine worlds. At its roots: the Well of Urd (Norns), Mimir's Well of Wisdom (Odin's eye price), and Niflheim. Its branches reach to Asgard. Nidhogg gnaws its roots; the eagle perches at its crown.
The Midgard Serpent — child of Loki, encircles all the earth and bites its own tail. Thor's cosmic enemy. At Ragnarok, Thor kills Jormungandr but dies from its venom.

The great wolf — child of Loki. Was bound by the magical ribbon Gleipnir (made from impossible things). Tyr sacrificed his hand as pledge of good faith when Fenrir submitted to be bound. Will break free at Ragnarok and kill Odin.
The first Imam in Shia Islam — cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad. His authority was divinely ordained at Ghadir Khumm. Embodies divine knowledge (ilm) and is the gate of the Prophet's knowledge.

The martyred Imam — grandson of Muhammad, killed at Karbala on Ashura. His martyrdom is the foundational tragedy of Shia Islam — the cosmic sacrifice that illuminates the nature of justice and injustice.
The daughter of Muhammad and wife of Imam Ali — "the radiant." In Shia theology she holds a unique cosmic status; her intercession is sought. The Infallible Lady.

In Nizari Ismaili Islam, the Imam is always present — a living, walking divine guide descended from Ali. Currently His Highness the Aga Khan IV. The Imam is the speaking Quran (natiq) to the written Quran's silence.
The cosmic Christ in Revelation — slain yet standing, with seven eyes and seven horns, worthy to open the seven seals. The sacrificial lamb who becomes the sovereign of the cosmos.

The great harlot — rides the scarlet beast, drunk on the blood of saints. In Protestant tradition identified with Rome; in critical scholarship, likely refers to Rome itself. The anti-divine feminine of Revelation's cosmic drama.
The Bride of Christ descending from heaven — the new creation, 12,000 stadia on each side, walls of jasper, streets of gold. The eschatological city-paradise.

Amida as the object of nembutsu practice — calling the name with sincerity guarantees rebirth in the Pure Land. Shinran (1173-1263) made this even more radical: the call itself is Amida's gift, not human effort.
Founder of Jodo Shinshu — the most radical Pure Land school: salvation is entirely Amida's work. The nembutsu is not a practice to earn merit but a response of gratitude to already-received grace.

The butterfly-dreamer — wrote the most profound of Taoist philosophical texts. A cook cuts a bull by following the grain of nature (Tao). Death is transformation, not loss. The sage flows with Tao like water.
Chaos — the ruler of the Center. Emperors of North and South drilled seven holes in him (to give him senses), and he died. The Taoist parable: intervention destroys what it intends to improve.

Supreme deity of the Mother Tantra — in union with his consort Vajravarahi. Subdued Shiva's 24 power-sites. Blue, with four faces and twelve arms. At the center of the Kagyu and Gelug meditation practices.

The supreme female deity of Vajrayana — naked, red, holding a skull cup of blood and a curved knife. The embodiment of bliss-emptiness. Her practice is considered the highest and most secret in Tibetan Buddhism.
The Secret Assembly — one of the oldest Vajrayana tantras. Three-faced, six-armed, in union with his consort Sparshavajra. Lord of body, speech, and mind. The foundational tantra of Gelug practice.

The supreme being of the Igbo — "the great chi." Omnipresent, all-powerful, unknowable directly. The sun (Anyanwu) is his messenger. He is approached through chi (personal spirit) and lesser deities (alusi).
Earth goddess of the Igbo — the most important deity in daily life. Governs morality, fertility, and the dead (who rest in her womb). Her laws (nso ala) are the foundation of Igbo ethics.
God of thunder and lightning — speaks through thunder, brings justice through lightning strike. In Igbo tradition, a lightning death is a divine judgment.
God of yams and agriculture — the Igbo staple crop deity. The new yam festival (Iwa Ji) is the most important Igbo ceremony.
The Earth Mother of the Akan — the consort of Nyame. Thursday is her day (farmers do not work the earth on Thursday). She receives the dead into her body. More approached than Nyame in daily life.
primary_sources: Rattray, Religion and Art in Ashanti

deities.summary: The great Ashanti priest-magician — called the Golden Stool from the sky, legitimizing Osei Tutu's kingdom. The Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) became the sacred repository of Ashanti collective soul.
The Zapotec rain and lightning god — the Zapotec parallel of Tlaloc/Chaac. His glyph is a jaguar combined with a serpent-lightning bolt. He controlled rain, agriculture, and time.
The Zapotec corn god — lord of the sustaining food, parallel to the Maya Corn God.

The historical Quetzalcoatl Ce Acatl Topiltzin — the Toltec priest-king of Tula who embodied the god. He was driven out by Tezcatlipoca's trickery and fled east, promising to return. His return was awaited in 1519.
The Maker Above — supreme creator of the Crow people. He created the first people from mud. Benevolent and relatively distant; the Crow approach him through vision quest and the Medicine Wheel.
primary_sources: Frey, The World of the Crow Indians

deities.summary: The Crow trickster-transformer — the one who remade the world from a duck's dive into the primordial waters. Simultaneously creator, teacher, and fool.
The supreme orixa of Candomble — Brazilian transformation of Yoruba Obatala. He creates human bodies at the moment of birth. Wears white, associated with Jesus Christ (syncretically).
primary_sources: Bastide, The African Religions of Brazil

deities.summary: Brazilian sea goddess — transformation of Yoruba Yemoja. Queen of the sea, mother of the orixas. Her festival (February 2) on Brazilian beaches is the most widely attended religious ceremony in Brazil.

Brazilian goddess of fresh water, fertility, love, and wealth — transformation of Yoruba Oshun. Gold, honey, mirrors, and the river. Syncretically identified with Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception.

The Khakass sky god — Father Sky (Cher-Ezi) paired with Mother Earth (Cher-Ezi). The shamanic cosmos of the Yenisei Turks has 16 heavens above and 16 underworld realms below, with our world in between.
The Yakut supreme deity — the White Creator Lord who dwells in the highest eastern heaven. The most benevolent deity; all good things descend from him.

The Real — Ibn Arabi's central divine name. Reality itself is the divine self-disclosure. All existence is Al-Haqq making itself known through its own attributes. The cosmos is the dream of God knowing itself.

The First Intellect emanating from the One — Al-Farabi's Islamic Neoplatonism maps Plotinus's Nous onto the Islamic divine order. The intellect of the First Intellect generates the ten intellects of the planetary spheres.
Founder of Shugendo — the Japanese mountain asceticism that combines Shinto, Buddhist, and Taoist elements. Said to command demons and fly through the air.
The Avatar Buddhas of the mountains — in shinbutsu-shugo (Shinto-Buddhist syncretism), Japanese mountain kami are avatars (gongen) of specific Buddhas. Zao Gongen is the most famous.
The Mordvin/Erzya supreme deity — the great god (Ine-Pas = Great God). Creator of the world. The Mordvin pantheon includes Sky God, Earth Mother, Water Mother, and a host of lesser pas (gods).

The lwa of love, luxury, and feminine power — the Haitian Venus. She loves beautiful things, weeps for humanity's suffering and her own unfulfillment, and wears three wedding rings (for three husbands: Damballa, Ogou, Agwe).

The great snake lwa — the oldest and most venerable. He is the cosmic serpent, the rainbow serpent, the creator who lives in trees and springs. White, pure, ancient beyond words. He and his wife Ayida Wedo are the serpent couple that supports the sky.
The warrior lwa of iron and revolution — the Haitian transformation of Yoruba Ogun. He carries a machete and wears red. Patron of soldiers and revolution; the spirit of Haitian independence.
The cosmic anaconda of Shipibo-Conibo cosmology — the great serpent whose body generates the geometric patterns (kene) that structure reality. Shamanic (ayahuasca) contact reveals her patterns.
The spirit of the Jurema tree (Mimosa hostilis) — the sacred plant deity of the Brazilian Jurema religion. The tree contains the divine drink that allows shamanic journeys.
The Santeria transformation of Yoruba Orunmila — master of Ifa divination. He knows every person's destiny because he witnessed creation. Syncretically identified with Saint Francis of Assisi.
The Santeria Obatala — creator of human bodies, lord of white and purity. Syncretically identified with Our Lady of Mercy (Las Mercedes). The supreme creative principle in Lucumi theology.
Sister of Isis and Osiris — the shadow twin of Isis. While Isis represents the visible, Nephthys represents the hidden. She mourns with Isis at Osiris's death. Lady of the House.
The crocodile god — lord of the Nile, fertility, and military power. Associated with the pharaoh's might. His major temple at Kom Ombo shares space with Horus the Elder.
The ram-headed potter god — shapes human bodies and their ka (spiritual double) on his potter's wheel. His temple at Elephantine, at the source of the Nile.
Falcon-headed war god of Thebes — the original patron of the pharaoh's military might before Amun rose to prominence. His fierce power was the epitome of royal military valor.
Moon goddess — the moon itself, driving her chariot across the night sky. She fell in love with Endymion and put him in eternal sleep so she could kiss him each night.
The sun itself — drives his chariot across the sky each day. His son Phaethon borrowed it, lost control, and Zeus had to destroy him with a thunderbolt to save the world.
Goddess of victory — stands beside Zeus, carries a palm branch and wreath. Her winged form was one of the most reproduced images in the ancient world.

God of medicine and healing — son of Apollo, killed by Zeus for raising the dead. His snake-staff (Rod of Asclepius) is still the symbol of medicine. His temples (Asclepia) combined healing, dream-incubation, and religious practice.
The goddess of dawn — the rosy-fingered dawn who opens the gates of heaven for the sun. The most directly surviving PIE *h2ewsos in Greek. She loved mortal men (Tithonus) who aged while she did not.
Necessity — the primordial goddess of inevitability, compulsion, and fate. Even the Moirai are instruments of Ananke. Plato's Spindle of Ananke holds the eight spheres of the cosmos.
Queen of the Roman gods — guardian of the state, women, and marriage. Her anger at Troy persisted through the Aeneid. The Capitoline Triad: Jupiter, Juno, Minerva.
Goddess of wisdom, crafts, and strategic warfare — uniquely Roman; born from Jupiter's head. Patron of teachers, artisans, and doctors. Part of the Capitoline Triad.

deities.earliest_attestation: Republican period; mystery cult from c. 200 BCE
deities.summary: The Roman Dionysus — god of wine and ecstatic release. His mystery cult (Bacchanalia) was suppressed by the Senate in 186 BCE for alleged immorality, then rehabilitated. His mysteries promised afterlife.
The Roman lord of the underworld — Hades in his wealth aspect (Pluto = the wealthy one, for underground riches). His cult was more positive than the Greek Hades — he was a generous patron.
God of the sea and fresh water — not exactly Poseidon's Roman equivalent; he had domain over all water sources, not just the sea. Horse deity as well (Equestrian Neptune).
God of merchants, travelers, communication, and the underworld — Roman Hermes. The most syncretically absorbed deity in the Roman Empire (identified with Celtic Lugus, Germanic Wotan, etc.).
Roman goddess of grain and harvest — her name gives us cereal. Mother of Proserpina. The Aventine triad (Ceres, Liber, Libera) was the plebeian parallel to the Capitoline triad.

The Gorgon whose gaze turns to stone — once a beautiful priestess of Athena, transformed as punishment. Killed by Perseus. Her blood generated Pegasus and the origin of snakes in Libya. Her severed head became Athena's shield.
The identity of the individual soul (Atman) with the cosmic soul (Brahman) — "Tat tvam asi" (That art thou). The central insight of Vedanta.
The emptiness of inherent existence — all phenomena lack a fixed, independent self. Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka philosophy made this the foundation of Mahayana.
The teaching, the truth, the cosmic law — in Buddhism, the second of the Three Jewels. The Buddha's teaching as a living cosmic principle.
The Spirit of God that hovers over the primordial waters before creation — the divine breath/wind as cosmic principle.
The great prophet who was taken to heaven in a fiery chariot without dying — expected to return before the Day of the LORD.
The household gods of Rome — Lares are ancestral protective spirits, Penates are guardians of the pantry. Every Roman household maintained their domestic cult.

The ten-headed demon-king who abducted Sita — the great antagonist of the Ramayana. Also the greatest devotee of Shiva, whose hymn (Shiva Tandava Stotra) he composed. The most theologically complex adversary in Indian religion.
The Buddhist tempter — tempted Siddhartha the night of his enlightenment with desire (daughters), fear (army), and doubt. Lord of the realm of samsara that keeps beings trapped.
The PIE cosmic truth/order — Avestan Asha (opposed by Druj/Lie), Sanskrit Rita (cosmic order). The moral order built into the structure of reality.
Goddess of sin and purification — she eats filth (sexual transgression) from dying confessors. Both causes and cleanses erotic sin.
Seven Serpent — Aztec goddess of corn and sustenance. Seven represents harvest abundance.
She of the Jade Skirt — goddess of rivers and storms, wife of Tlaloc. Destroyed the fourth world with a great flood.
Snake Woman — earth mother and war goddess. She appears carrying an empty cradle, wailing — an omen of war and sacrifice.
Cloud Serpent — god of the hunt and the Milky Way. Father of Quetzalcoatl in some Toltec traditions.
The corn god — the male divine corn, paired with Chicomecóatl. Son of Tlazolteotl in some accounts.
God of death and ruler of Metnal (the lowest underworld) — depicted as a skeletal figure wearing bells. The most feared Mayan deity.
The younger Hero Twin — becomes the moon after defeating the lords of Xibalba alongside his brother Hunahpu.
The elder Hero Twin — becomes the sun after victory in the underworld. Father of the Maize God.
The Earthquake Maker — son of Seven Macaw, boasted he could shake mountains. Defeated by the Hero Twins.
Thor's wife — her golden hair was cut off by Loki, then replaced by the dwarves with magical gold. Possibly an earth goddess whose hair is the grain.
The Silent God — son of Odin, second strongest of all gods. Will survive Ragnarok and avenge Odin by killing Fenrir.
Born for revenge — Odin begot him specifically to avenge Baldur's death. Killed Hod the day after his birth. Survives Ragnarok.
God of poetry and eloquence — the skald of the gods, husband of Idun. He who greets the slain at Valhalla.
Son of Baldur — god of justice and reconciliation. The best judge among gods and men, settles all disputes.
God of skiing, hunting, and single combat — invoked on oaths alongside Odin. One of the most ancient Norse deities.
Guardian of the Well of Wisdom at Yggdrasil's root — Odin sacrificed his eye to drink from it. After Mimir's death, Odin preserved his head and consulted it for counsel.
The wisest being ever — created from the saliva of all gods. Killed by dwarves who brewed the Mead of Poetry from his blood.
Sea goddess who collects the drowned in her net — wife of Aegir, mother of the nine wave-daughters. To drown is to be taken by Ran.
Lord of the sea — brews ale for the gods in an enormous cauldron. His nine daughters are the waves.
The goddess of righteous retribution — punishes hubris and undeserved good fortune. The cosmic balancer of excess.
Goddess of fortune and luck — spins the wheel of fate, her gifts are unpredictable. Roman equivalent: Fortuna.
God of the wild, shepherds, and rustic music — half-man, half-goat, son of Hermes. His sudden appearance caused panic.
Goddess of the rainbow — divine messenger before Hermes took that role, connecting heaven and earth with her rainbow bridge.
Personification of gentle death — twin of Hypnos (Sleep), son of Nyx. The process of dying as divine presence.
God of sleep — twin of Thanatos, lives in the underworld where sun never shines. Even Zeus feared Hypnos.
The shape-shifting sea god who knows all things — must be caught and held through all his transformations to force him to tell the truth.
The deified Romulus — third member of the archaic Roman triad (Jupiter, Mars, Quirinus). The founder of Rome made divine.
Goddess of fruit trees and orchards — uniquely Roman with no Greek equivalent. Won by Vertumnus after his many disguises.
God of seasons, change, and gardens — shapeshifted through many forms to win Pomona's love.
Goddess of flowers and spring — her festival Floralia (April 28) was a raucous celebration of spring's return.
Roman lord of the underworld and underground wealth — equated with Pluto/Hades. Connected to the Gauls through Caesar.
God of fertility and the eastern desert — depicted ithyphallically, associated with lettuce (considered aphrodisiac). One of the oldest Egyptian deities.
Cat goddess — originally lioness, later domesticated into the gentle cat. Goddess of home, cats, music, and dancing. Her annual festival involved enormous numbers of pilgrims.
Lord of the Memphite necropolis — god of the funerary realm specifically at Memphis. Later merged with Osiris and Ptah as Ptah-Sokar-Osiris.
She Who Loves Silence — the cobra goddess of the Valley of the Kings, protecting the royal tombs.
Cobra goddess of harvest and nourishment — she decided each person's ren (name and fate) at birth. Lady of the granary.
Wife of the Moon God Nanna — mother of Inanna and Utu/Shamash. She pleaded with the divine assembly to spare Ur from destruction; they refused.
primary_sources: Lament for the Destruction of Ur

deities.summary: Goddess of grain, writing, and scribal arts — the original Sumerian divine scribe, patron of all scribes before Nabu took the role.
God of war and agriculture — slays the cosmic serpent Asag and the Anzu bird. The archetype of the champion-hero dragon-slayer in Mesopotamia.
King of the wind-demons — terrifying in appearance but used apotropaically against Lamashtu. His image on amulets warded off the child-killing demon.
Sumerian storm god — the Sumerian parallel of Akkadian Adad. Lord of rain and thunder, son of Enlil.
The divine horsemen twins — physicians of the gods, they rescue the drowning, restore youth, bring light at dawn. The Vedic parallel of the Dioscuri.
The storm troop of Indra — 27 or 49 shining warriors who ride with Indra in battle, wielding lightning. Sons of Rudra.
The howling storm god — dangerous, wild, both the source of disease and its healer. Father of the Maruts. Shiva's direct predecessor in the Vedic tradition.
Lord of wealth and king of the Yakshas — guardian of the north quarter and keeper of all divine treasure. Lives on Mount Kailash near Shiva.
God of erotic love — shoots five flower-tipped arrows that cause specific types of longing. Burned to ash by Shiva's third eye; revived through Parvati's love.
Goddess of the night — sister of Ushas (Dawn). One of the most beautiful hymns in the Rigveda addresses her: she illuminates the night with stars.
The divine craftsman of the gods — fashioned the vajra for Indra, made the first soma cup. The divine smith who shapes the implements of cosmic order.
The divine architect — built Lanka for Ravana, the city of Dwaraka for Krishna, and the vehicles and weapons of all the devas.
The Immovable King — wrathful protector of practice, cannot be moved from truth. Blue, with sword and lasso. Most important of the Five Wisdom Kings in Japanese Shingon Buddhism.
The enlightened layman — the bodhisattva in ordinary life. His thunderous silence in response to Manjushri's question about non-duality is the most celebrated moment in Mahayana literature.
The swift-acting Tara — her right foot is extended, ready to spring into action. Faster to answer prayers than any other deity. Specifically for protection from eight fears.
The People of the Goddess Danu — the divine race of Ireland who defeated the Fomorians, were then defeated by the Milesians, and retreated into the sidhe (fairy mounds).
The Silver Wheel — daughter of Don, mother of the twins Lleu and Dylan (the sons she tried to deny). Her name means "silver wheel" — a moon and fate goddess.
The patient craftsman — Welsh equivalent of Manannán Mac Lir. After losing his kingdom, mastered three crafts to sustain his companions.
The Slavic sky-smith — the divine fire of heaven, smith of the gods. Father of Dazbog (the sun) and Svarozhich (the hearth fire).
The Slavic sun god — giver of wealth and prosperity, son of Svarog. The Slavic solar deity.
The midsummer deity — bonfires, water, ferns, and fertility. His festival (Ivan Kupala) is one of the most widely preserved Slavic pre-Christian celebrations.
Goddess of winter and death — her effigy is drowned or burned at the end of winter to welcome spring and the green god Jarilo.
Gaulish thunder god — the wheel is his sacred symbol. Lucan lists him among the three Gaulish gods who received human sacrifice.
Tribal deity — "god of the tribe/people." Equated by Romans with Mars or Mercury. Required sacrifice by drowning in a cauldron.
The Good Striker — mallet god of the Gauls. His mallet could both kill and revive. Associated with forests and Celtic underworld.
God of war and humanity — the red fierce deity who refused to hide from the primal parents' children. Humans are his food.
God of cultivated food and peace — Rongo and Tu are the twin poles of Maori theology: peace and war.
The moon goddess of Polynesia — weaves tapa cloth on the moon, governs lunar cycles, associated with women's crafts.
The good creator of Vanuatu mythology — opposed by the evil Suqe. Together they made the imperfect world.
The Samoan supreme being — Tagaloa created the sky, then the earth, then sent birds to see if the earth was ready.
The great mountain kami — father of Konohanasakuya-hime (the ancestor of emperors). Lord of all mountains.
Princess of Blossoming Trees — wife of Ninigi (Amaterasu's grandson), divine ancestor of the Japanese imperial line. She proved her fidelity by giving birth in a burning hut.
God of thunder and lightning — depicted as a fearsome figure beating drums made of clouds. Twin of Fujin.
God of wind — carries a large bag of winds. Twin of Raijin. Together they guard the gates of shrines.
Dragon King of the Sea — rules the ocean from his undersea palace Ryugu-jo, controls the tides with magical tide jewels.
The divine ghost-catcher — a scholar who failed the imperial exams and killed himself; appointed King of the Ghosts by the Jade Emperor to compensate.
The Earth God — the most local of all deities. Every neighborhood, field, and building has its own Tu Di Gong who reports annually to the Jade Emperor.
The Kitchen God — watches the family all year and reports to the Jade Emperor before the New Year. His picture is burned to send him to heaven.
Duke of Thunder — strikes those who commit hidden crimes that escape earthly justice. His weapon exposes evil.
Mother of Lightning — the female counterpart of Lei Gong, uses mirrors to create the flashes of lightning that illuminate evil.
The Two Door Gods — divine generals who guard the doors of homes and temples against evil spirits. Based on generals of Tang Emperor Taizong.
Judge Bao — the historical incorruptible Song dynasty judge deified as a divine arbiter, accessible to common people seeking justice.

The Korean Maitreya — the future Buddha who will establish a perfect world. In a primordial contest, Mireuk lost the present world to Shakyamuni through Shakyamuni's trickery, explaining the world's imperfection.
The Birth Grandmother — triple goddess who presides over childbirth, child-rearing, and early childhood. Approached with prayer and rice offerings for health and fertility.
The lwa of the sea — admiral and master of the ocean, husband of Erzulie Freda. He accepts offerings of tiny boats sent out to sea.
Lwa of fresh water, crossroads, and magic — patron of sorcerers and diviners. He lives at the boundary of fresh and salt water.
The first mambo (Vodou priestess) — Ayizan initiates all Vodou priests and priestesses, presides over the beginnings of sacred ceremony.
The great trickster of the American Southwest — steals fire, disrupts creation, teaches through chaos and failure. Simultaneously creator and destroyer.
primary_sources: Southwest oral traditions (Navajo, Apache, Paiute, Shoshone)
alternate_names: Old Man Coyote (separate figure in Crow)

deities.summary: Thought Woman (Kokyangwuti) — she thinks things and they come into being. The Hopi first creator who thought the world into existence and helps those in trouble.
The divine mother of corn — the sustainer of life across the Eastern Woodlands. She sacrificed herself so the people could eat.
Mother Earth — Maka is the earth herself. All life comes from her and returns to her womb at death.
The Sun — Grandfather Wi, source of all light, warmth, and life. His strength and endurance are the divine qualities the Lakota admire.
Chief of the Thunderbirds — commands the storms that battle the water serpents (Horned Serpents) lurking in the deep. The cosmic conflict between sky and water.
The prophet-apostle of light — claimed to be the Paraclete promised by Jesus and the successor of Zoroaster, Buddha, and Christ. Executed by the Zoroastrian establishment.
The divine being who descended to fight Darkness — partially defeated, his scattered light-elements became the particles of divine light trapped in matter that constitute human souls.
The Lord of the World in Theosophical teaching — an Ancient of Days who has guided Earth's spiritual evolution for 18.5 million years from his retreat at Shambhala.
primary_sources: Alice Bailey, A Treatise on Cosmic Fire

deities.summary: The great Kushan mother goddess — a synthesis of Anahita, Mesopotamian Nana, and local Central Asian goddesses, widely worshipped from Bactria to Tang China on Silk Road routes.
God of forests and uncultivated land — the liminal deity of the boundary between civilized and wild. Worshipped by slaves and freedmen.

The Great Mother officially adopted by Rome in 204 BCE to win the Second Punic War. Her ecstatic cult with castrated priests (Galli) was the most foreign element ever officially incorporated into Roman religion.
Goddess of Night — mother of Sleep, Death, the Fates, Strife. Even Zeus feared her.
The primordial sky — castrated by Kronos on Gaia's instruction. Aphrodite born from sea foam around his severed genitals.
God of fire and the forge — the Roman Hephaestus, divine blacksmith.
One-handed god of oaths — sacrificed his hand binding Fenrir.
The Irish sea god — his four children were transformed into swans for 900 years by their jealous stepmother.
primary_sources: The Fate of the Children of Lir

deities.summary: Prince of Dyfed who traded places with Arawn, lord of the Otherworld for a year. The mortal who becomes divine through otherworldly encounter.
The Fon trickster-messenger — the youngest of the vodun, who speaks all languages and opens all roads.
The Bounteous/Holy Spirit — the divine emanation through which Ahura Mazda acts in the world. The spirit of good.
Good Mind — the first and greatest Amesha Spenta. He received the Gathas from Zarathustra.
Infinite Light — the three negatives of Kabbalistic theology: Ain (Nothing), Ain Soph (Infinite Nothing), Ain Soph Aur (Infinite Light).
deities.tradition_claim: Before creation, there was only Ain Soph — Without Limit. Not the God who speaks or commands — but the absolute ground of all being, so complete it had nothing to create for and no reason to create. Then Tzimtzum: the Infinite contracted into itself, made a space within itself, a void. Into that space it sent a ray of divine light. The light organized itself through ten Sefirot: Keter (Crown), Chokhmah (Wisdom), Binah (Understanding), Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferet, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, and Malkhut (Kingdom — the material world). The Tree of Life is not a diagram. It is the actual structure of reality from the divine source to the material world, each level transparent to the one above it.
deities.russell_connection: Ain Soph's Tzimtzum (divine contraction creating space for creation) followed by the ray of light organizing through ten Sefirot maps precisely to Russell's zero-point (stillness) from which wave motion emanates, organizing matter through seven harmonic tones.

deities.summary: The cosmic breath/consciousness — Sila is the air, the weather, and the intelligence permeating all things.
primary_sources: Inuit oral tradition (Rasmussen, Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos)

deities.summary: The third being from Chaos — cosmic attraction that enables creation.
The final monster who challenged Zeus for the cosmos.
God of boundaries and property limits — even Jupiter must yield to him.
The Roman Kronos — god of the Golden Age.
Goddess of abundance and harvest — wife of Saturn.
Goddess of prophecy and childbirth.
Goddess of doorposts and hinges — Janus gave her power to repel evil from thresholds.
The self-created — the first to emerge from Nun.
The scarab who pushes the morning sun.
Akkadian storm god — the Akkadian Ishkur.
Grain god of the Philistines and Canaanites — father of Baal in some traditions.
Lord of beginnings — elephant head, remover of obstacles.
War god of youthful divine power, commander of the divine army.
Lord of death in Buddhist iconography — the judge of karma.
The trickster demigod who fished up islands and slowed the sun.
The trickster who speaks all languages and must be propitiated first.
First-born of Kronos and Rhea — the eldest Olympian who tends the eternal hearth flame. She gave up her throne for Dionysus to avoid conflict.
Goddess of strife — threw the Apple of Discord that caused the Trojan War. In Hesiod, she has two forms: the evil strife (war) and the good strife (competition that drives excellence).
God of dreams — takes human forms within dreams. Son of Hypnos, brother of Thanatos. He who shapes the dream.
Triple goddess of magic, crossroads, and the moon.

deities.earliest_attestation: Rabbinic period; developed in Kabbalah (Zohar, 13th c.)
deities.summary: The indwelling divine presence — the immanent, feminine aspect of God in Jewish tradition. In Kabbalah, the Shekhinah is the tenth Sefirah (Malkhut), the divine presence that dwells with Israel, goes into exile with the people, and is reunited with the transcendent masculine divine through righteous action.

deities.etymology: Hebrew śāṭān, 'adversary, accuser, one who obstructs'; verb śṭn 'to oppose, accuse'.
deities.summary: The satan is a member of the heavenly court, one of the bene ha-elohim who present themselves before YHWH. He roams the earth and tests the righteousness of Job with God's permission, stands at the right hand of the high priest Joshua to accuse him, and in Chronicles rises against Israel and moves David to take a census. He has no power of his own: every trial he brings is licensed by the Lord.

deities.etymology: Hebrew mî-kā-ʾēl, 'Who is like God?'
deities.summary: Michael is "one of the chief princes", the great prince who stands guard over Israel. He comes to the aid of the angel sent to Daniel against the prince of Persia, and at the end of days he will arise in a time of trouble when the people are delivered and the dead awake.

deities.etymology: Hebrew gavrî-ʾēl, 'God is my strength' or 'man of God'.
deities.summary: Gabriel is the angel who comes "in swift flight" to make Daniel understand his visions, explaining the vision of the ram and the goat and revealing the seventy weeks. In Enoch he is one of the four great angels who bring the cry of the earth before God.

The Angel of the LORD speaks as God and in God's name: he finds Hagar in the wilderness, stays Abraham's hand at Moriah, appears in the burning bush, and goes before Israel, for "my Name is in him". Those who see him fear they have seen God.

deities.etymology: Hebrew liwyātān, from lwy 'to coil, twist'; cognate with Ugaritic ltn (Litan/Lotan).
deities.summary: Leviathan is the many-headed sea dragon whom God crushed at the beginning, giving its flesh as food to the wilderness people, and whom God will punish "on that day" with his great sword. In Job he is the untameable beast no human can hook; in the Psalms God formed him to play in the sea. Later tradition reserves his flesh for the banquet of the righteous in the world to come.

alternate_names: First of the Ways of God
deities.etymology: Hebrew bəhēmôt, intensive plural of bəhēmâ 'beast' — 'the Beast par excellence'.
deities.summary: Behemoth is the first of God's works, a land-beast of immense strength whose bones are tubes of bronze; only his maker can approach him with a sword. Enoch makes him the male monster of the desert Dendain, paired with Leviathan, the female monster of the deep.

deities.etymology: Hebrew rahav, 'storming, arrogance'; unrelated to Rahab of Jericho (rāḥāb, different spelling).
deities.summary: Rahab is the raging sea power whom God cut to pieces and pierced at creation; her helpers bowed beneath him. The prophets turn her name into a byword for Egypt, the proud power God humbled at the Sea.

deities.etymology: Hebrew hêlēl 'shining one' (root hll 'to shine'); šaḥar 'dawn', also the name of the Ugaritic dawn god.
deities.summary: "How you have fallen from heaven, Shining One, son of Dawn!" The taunt over the king of Babylon tells of one who said in his heart: I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above the stars of El, sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of Zaphon, and make myself like the Most High — and who was brought down to Sheol, to the depths of the pit.

deities.etymology: Ugaritic ltn, vocalisation uncertain (Litan / Lôtan); from lwy 'to coil'.
deities.summary: Litan is the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the tyrant with seven heads. Mot reminds Baal that he struck down Litan, and Anat boasts that she too crushed the twisting dragon, the mighty one of seven heads, among the allies of Prince Yam.

deities.etymology: Hebrew Baʿal Zəvûv 'lord of flies'; probably a pun on Ugaritic/Canaanite zbl bʿl 'Baal the Prince / Exalted Lord'.
deities.summary: Baal Zebub is the god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whose oracle King Ahaziah of Israel sent to consult when he lay injured. He is a lord who answers those who seek him about sickness and recovery.

deities.etymology: Hebrew mōlek: consonants of melek 'king', probably vocalised with the vowels of bōšet 'shame'.
deities.summary: Molech is the king to whom children were "passed through the fire" at the Topheth in the Valley of Hinnom. The Law forbids giving one's offspring to him, and Josiah defiled the Topheth so that none could make a son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech.

primary_sources: KTU 1.23 (The Birth of the Gracious Gods)
deities.etymology: Ugaritic šḥr 'dawn' (Hebrew šaḥar).
deities.summary: Shahar, Dawn, is born to El together with his twin Shalim, Dusk, the gracious and beautiful gods whose mouths reach from earth to heaven. He is the light that opens each day.

deities.etymology: Semitic ʿṯtr, cognate with Akkadian Ištar and Phoenician ʿAštart (Astarte), here a male deity.
deities.summary: When Baal lay dead, El and Athirat set Athtar the Terrible on Baal's throne on the heights of Zaphon. But his feet did not reach the footstool and his head did not reach the top; he declared "I cannot be king on the heights of Zaphon," came down from the throne, and ruled over the earth below instead.

alternate_names: Prince of the Dominion of Wickedness
deities.etymology: Hebrew bəliyyaʿal 'worthlessness' (bəlî 'without' + yaʿal 'worth'), used of scoundrels before it became a proper name.
deities.summary: Belial is the angel of hostility, created by God for the pit, who leads the Sons of Darkness and the spirits of his lot. In this age of wickedness he is let loose against Israel with three nets — fornication, wealth and defilement of the sanctuary — but at the final war God and the Sons of Light will destroy his dominion forever.

deities.etymology: Hebrew maśṭēmâ 'hostility', from the same root śṭm/śṭn as śāṭān.
deities.summary: When Noah prayed for the evil spirits to be bound, Mastema, chief of the spirits, begged God to leave him a tenth of them to do his will, and God granted it. Mastema provoked God to test Abraham with Isaac, sought to kill Moses on his way to Egypt, and strengthened Pharaoh's magicians — but always within the bounds God allows.

deities.etymology: Hebrew rəfāʾ-ʾēl, 'God heals'.
deities.summary: Raphael is one of the seven holy angels who stand before the glory of the Lord. Disguised as the kinsman Azarias he guides young Tobias, binds the demon Asmodeus and heals Tobit's blindness; in Enoch God sends him to bind Azazel hand and foot in the desert and to heal the earth the Watchers corrupted.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 3rd c. BCE (Astronomical Book of Enoch)
deities.etymology: Hebrew ʾûrî-ʾēl, 'God is my light'.
deities.summary: Uriel is set over the luminaries of heaven and over Tartarus. He shows Enoch the laws of the sun, moon and stars and the reckoning of the year, guides him through the prisons of the fallen, and in 4 Ezra answers the seer's questions about the justice of God.

deities.etymology: Generally derived from Avestan aēšma-daēva, 'demon of wrath' (Middle Persian Xešm).
deities.summary: Asmodeus, the evil demon, loved Sarah and killed each of her seven husbands on the wedding night, until Raphael taught Tobias to drive him off with the smoke of a fish's heart and liver; the demon fled to Upper Egypt where Raphael bound him. The rabbis remember Ashmedai as king of demons, captured by Solomon to help build the Temple.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2nd c. CE (Ascension of Isaiah); rabbinic texts 3rd–9th c. CE
primary_sources: Treatise on the Left Emanation (R. Isaac ha-Kohen)
deities.etymology: Commonly read as sam-ʾēl 'poison of God'; the Gnostic Hypostasis of the Archons glosses it 'god of the blind' (Aramaic samya 'blind').
deities.summary: Samael was the great prince in heaven, with twelve wings. When God made Adam, Samael took his band, came down, and chose the serpent as his mount to lead Eve astray. He is the wicked one, chief of all the satans, and the angel of death who waits to take each soul. In the Kabbalah he is lord of the Other Side, and Lilith is his mate.

deities.etymology: Greek synadelphos 'co-brother', i.e. the brother of Metatron.
deities.summary: Sandalphon stands on the earth while his head reaches the living creatures of the Chariot; he is taller than his fellows by a journey of five hundred years. He stands behind the Chariot binding crowns for his Creator out of the prayers of Israel.

deities.etymology: Greek Satanas from Hebrew/Aramaic śāṭān 'adversary'; 'devil' from Greek diabolos 'slanderer', the Septuagint rendering of śāṭān.
deities.summary: Satan is the Devil, a murderer from the beginning and the father of lies, who tempted Christ in the wilderness and prowls like a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour. Once a glorious angel, he fell through pride and drew a third of the stars of heaven with him. He is the god of this age, disguising himself as an angel of light, but Christ has disarmed him on the cross; he will be bound and finally cast into the lake of fire.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 382–405 CE (Vulgate, Isaiah 14:12); applied to Satan from the 3rd c. CE
deities.etymology: Latin lux 'light' + ferre 'to bear', rendering Greek Heōsphoros and Hebrew hêlēl.
deities.summary: Lucifer is the name of Satan before his fall: the brightest of the angels, the light-bearer and son of the morning, who said in his heart "I will be like the Most High" and was cast down from heaven to the depths of the pit. The fathers read Isaiah's fallen Day Star and Ezekiel's anointed cherub of Eden as his story.

deities.etymology: From Baal Zebub of Ekron (2 Kings 1) and/or zbl bʿl 'Baal the Prince'; Gospel manuscripts vary between Beelzeboul and Beelzebub.
deities.summary: Beelzebul is the prince of demons. When Jesus cast out demons his opponents said he did it by Beelzebul; Jesus answered that if Satan casts out Satan his kingdom cannot stand, and that he binds the strong man and plunders his house.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1st c. CE (New Testament); creedal definition 381 CE
deities.etymology: Greek pneuma hagion and Latin spiritus sanctus, translating Hebrew rûaḥ ha-qōdeš; rûaḥ means wind, breath and spirit.
deities.summary: The Holy Spirit is the third person of the Holy Trinity, the Lord and Giver of Life, who proceeds from the Father and with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, and who spoke through the prophets. He descended on Christ at the Jordan as a dove and on the apostles at Pentecost as tongues of fire; he is the Paraclete who abides with the faithful and leads them into all truth.

deities.etymology: Hebrew mî-kā-ʾēl 'Who is like God?'
deities.summary: Michael is the prince of the heavenly host who waged war in heaven against the dragon and cast him and his angels down to earth. He disputed with the Devil over the body of Moses, defends the Church in battle, and weighs souls and leads them to judgment.

Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God, announced to Zechariah the birth of John and to the Virgin Mary that she would conceive the Son of the Most High: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you."

Before the end the man of lawlessness will be revealed, who exalts himself above every so-called god and takes his seat in God's temple. The beast rising from the sea with ten horns and seven heads receives his power from the dragon and is worshipped by the nations, while the beast from the earth works signs on his behalf and marks his followers with his number, 666 — until Christ destroys him with the breath of his mouth.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1st c. CE (Revelation); as a place, Hebrew Bible
deities.etymology: Hebrew ʾăbaddôn 'destruction' (root ʾbd 'to perish'); Greek Apollyōn 'destroyer'.
deities.summary: When the fifth trumpet sounds, the shaft of the abyss is opened and locusts like war-horses come out to torment those without the seal of God. Their king is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in Hebrew is Abaddon and in Greek Apollyon, the Destroyer.

deities.earliest_attestation: 2nd c. CE (Basilides as reported by Irenaeus); magical gems 2nd–4th c. CE
primary_sources: Gospel of the Egyptians (NHC III,2; IV,2)
deities.etymology: Unknown; the isopsephic value Α-Β-Ρ-Α-Σ-Α-Ξ = 1+2+100+1+200+1+60 = 365.
deities.summary: Abrasax is the ruler of the three hundred and sixty-five heavens, for the letters of his name add up to 365, the days of the year. He holds the whole cycle of the heavens together and is invoked as a mighty name of power.

alternate_names: Rūḥ al-Qudus (the Holy Spirit, per most exegetes)
deities.etymology: Arabic form of Hebrew Gavriʾel.
iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Jibrīl is the noblest of the angels, the Trustworthy Spirit who brought the Qurʾān down upon the heart of the Prophet Muḥammad by God's permission. He appeared to the Prophet on the horizon, came to teach the believers their religion — islām, īmān and iḥsān — and accompanied him on the Night Journey.

deities.etymology: Arabic form of Hebrew Mikhaʾel.
iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Mīkāʾīl is one of the angels brought near, named in the Qurʾān beside Jibrīl: whoever is an enemy to God, His angels, His messengers, Jibrīl and Mīkāl, God is an enemy to the disbelievers. He is entrusted with the rain and the sustenance of creation.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th–9th c. CE (named in ḥadīth; the Trumpet in the Qurʾān)
deities.etymology: Uncertain; sometimes connected with Hebrew śərāfîm (seraphim) or Raphael — both conjectural.
iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Isrāfīl holds the Trumpet to his lips, waiting for the command. At the first blast all in the heavens and the earth will swoon; at the second they will rise, standing and looking on, for the Day of Resurrection.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th c. CE (Angel of Death in the Qurʾān); name later
iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Say: the Angel of Death who is set over you will take your souls, then to your Lord you will be returned. ʿAzrāʾīl takes each soul at its appointed time, gently from the believer and harshly from the wrongdoer, acting only by the command of God.

iconography: Not depicted in devotional practice; folklore imagines smoke and flame
deities.summary: God created humankind from clay and the jinn from smokeless fire. Like humans they have free will, are male and female, marry, and will be judged; some heard the Qurʾān and believed, while others follow Iblīs, who was one of the jinn. They were made, like humans, only to worship God.

iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Muḥammad is the Messenger of God and the Seal of the Prophets, sent as a mercy to the worlds, to whom the Qurʾān was revealed. He is not divine and is not worshipped; believers send blessings upon him, follow his example, and hope for his intercession on the Day of Judgment. Sufis honour the Muḥammadan Light, created first of all things, through which the cosmos came to be.
deities.tradition_claim: Venerated, not worshipped: Islam regards Muḥammad as wholly human; listed here as a figure of veneration.

iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: Two angels, Hārūt and Mārūt, were sent down at Babylon and taught people sorcery, but never without warning: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." Exegetes tell that they mocked human weakness, were sent to earth with human desires, fell into sin with a woman named Zuhara, and now hang in a pit at Babylon until the Day of Judgment.

deities.etymology: Arabic mālik 'owner, master'.
iconography: Not depicted: Sunni and most Islamic practice is aniconic for prophets and angels; represented by calligraphy of the name
deities.summary: The damned will cry: "O Mālik, let your Lord make an end of us!" He will answer: "You will remain." Mālik is chief of the stern angels set over the Fire, who do not disobey what God commands them.

deities.etymology: Mandaic hiia rbia 'the Great Life'.
deities.summary: In the name of the Great Life! Hayyi Rabbi is the first, the King of Light, from whom all the uthras (beings of light) proceed. The Life dwells in the World of Light, beyond all darkness, and every Mandaean prayer opens in its name.

deities.etymology: Mandaic manda 'knowledge' (cf. Greek gnōsis) d-hiia 'of Life'.
deities.summary: Manda d-Hayyi is the Knowledge of Life, the saviour sent down from the World of Light. He descended to the world of darkness, defeated its powers, brought the soul to Adam, and teaches the elect the way of ascent; Mandaeans take their very name from him.

deities.etymology: Often explained as Egyptian Ptah + -il ('god'); the derivation is proposed, not certain.
deities.summary: Ptahil is the uthra who fashioned the material world, Tibil, and the body of Adam with the help of Ruha and the seven planets. But he could not give life to his creature; the soul had to be brought from the World of Light. For his fault he is barred from the Light until the end, when he will be baptised and restored.

deities.etymology: Aramaic rûḥā 'spirit'; her title Ruha d-Qudsha means 'the Holy Spirit', inverted into a power of darkness.
deities.summary: Ruha is the queen of the world of darkness, mother of Ur and of the seven planets and twelve signs of the zodiac. She helped Ptahil fashion Adam and works to keep souls bound in the body through lust, music and drunkenness, though she sometimes laments her own fallen state.

Abathur sits at the scales at the boundary of the World of Light and weighs every departing soul. From his gaze into the black waters Ptahil came into being. Souls pass through the purgatory houses (matarata) before they are weighed and admitted to the Light.

deities.etymology: Mandaic Hibil = Abel; ziwa 'radiance'.
deities.summary: Hibil Ziwa, the radiant one, descended through the worlds of darkness, overcame their kings, learned their secrets, and brought back Ruha, by whose captivity the powers of darkness were subdued. He returns victorious to the Light as the model of the soul's descent and ascent.
Ur is the gigantic dragon-king of the world of darkness, son of Ruha, who rages against the Light. Hibil Ziwa and the uthras subdue him, and the dead soul must pass him on its way to the scales.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1st c. CE (as a figure); Book of John later
deities.summary: Yahya Yuhana is the great teacher and priest of the Mandaeans, who baptised in the Jordan (yardna) by the power of the Life. He is not the founder of the religion but its greatest prophet, the model of the priest who performs masbuta, living-water baptism.
deities.tradition_claim: Venerated as prophet and priest, not as a god.

primary_sources: Hymn of the Creation (Qewlê Afirîna Dinyayê)
deities.etymology: Kurdish/Persian xwadê 'lord, God'.
deities.summary: Xwedê is the one God who created the world from a pearl and then entrusted its care to the Seven Angels whom he brought forth from his own light. He is beyond the world and is approached through his angels and holy beings.

deities.etymology: Kurdish tawûs 'peacock' + Arabic malik 'king/angel' (malak).
deities.summary: Tawûsî Melek, the Peacock Angel, is the first and chief of the Seven Angels, to whom God gave rule over the world. When God commanded the angels to bow before Adam he refused, for he would bow only to God — and God approved his faithfulness and made him lord of the earth. Yazidis pray facing the sun and honour him with the sacred peacock standard (sancaq).

Sheikh ʿAdī ibn Musāfir came to Lalish and renewed the faith; his tomb at Lalish is the holiest place of the Yazidis, the goal of pilgrimage at the autumn Feast of the Assembly. Yazidis honour him as a manifestation of Tawûsî Melek in human form.

God created seven angels from his light and placed the world in their care; each was later manifest in one of the holy figures of the faith. Tawûsî Melek is first among them, and the seven are honoured as the mysteries through which God governs creation.

Al-Ḥākim, the sixth Fatimid caliph, was the final and complete locus (maqām) in which the One God manifested his unity to humankind. In 1021 he withdrew from sight to test the faithful; at the end of time he will return to establish justice.
deities.tradition_claim: Druze doctrine (secret in its full form); details held by the initiated ʿuqqāl are not public.

deities.summary: Ḥamza ibn ʿAlī is the Imam of the Unitarians and the earthly embodiment of the Universal Intellect, the first being emanated from the One. He proclaimed the Daʿwa in 1017 and wrote many of the Epistles of Wisdom; he too will return with al-Ḥākim at the end.

primary_sources: Gleanings from the Writings of Bahá'u'lláh
deities.summary: God is one, an unknowable essence exalted above every human attribute and comprehension. He reveals himself through a succession of Manifestations — Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, Buddha, Jesus, Muḥammad, the Báb and Bahá'u'lláh — each reflecting his light like a perfect mirror, according to the capacity of the age.

alternate_names: Him Whom God Shall Make Manifest
iconography: Bahá'ís do not display his image publicly; a photograph is viewed only on rare occasions
deities.summary: Bahá'u'lláh is the Manifestation of God for this age, the Promised One of all religions, who declared his mission in the Garden of Riḍván in Baghdad in 1863. He revealed the laws of the Most Holy Book and taught the oneness of God, of religion and of humankind.

The Báb, "the Gate", was the Manifestation of God who declared his mission in Shiraz in 1844, proclaimed himself the promised Qá'im of Islam, and heralded "Him Whom God shall make manifest". He was executed by firing squad in Tabriz in 1850; his shrine stands on Mount Carmel.

ʿAbdu'l-Bahá, eldest son of Bahá'u'lláh, is the Centre of the Covenant, the authorised interpreter of his father's writings and the perfect exemplar of the Bahá'í life. He is not a Manifestation of God, but his servitude is the model for all believers.
deities.tradition_claim: Explicitly not a Manifestation of God in Bahá'í doctrine; listed as a figure of veneration.
