deities.summary: The God of Israel is one, the creator who chose Mount Gerizim as the place where his Name dwells (Deuteronomy as preserved by the Samaritans). His Name is not pronounced; it is read as Shema, "the Name".

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th c. CE (Memar Marqah) with earlier roots
deities.etymology: Aramaic tāʾēb 'he who returns / restores'.
deities.summary: The Taheb is the prophet like Moses whom God will raise up. He will restore the Divine Favour (Rahuta) that withdrew in the Era of Disfavour (Fanuta), recover the hidden sacred vessels of the Tabernacle on Mount Gerizim, and renew true worship.

alternate_names: Son of the House of God
deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th c. CE (Memar Marqah) with earlier roots
deities.summary: Moses is the unique prophet, the only one to whom God spoke face to face, the light of the world and the faithful one of God's house. The Samaritan creed confesses one God, Moses his prophet, the Torah, Mount Gerizim and the Day of Vengeance and Recompense.
deities.tradition_claim: Venerated as the unique prophet, not as a god.

deities.etymology: From Hebrew yāh, short form of YHWH, as printed 'JAH' in the King James Version, Psalm 68:4.
deities.summary: Jah is the Most High, the living God, who is present in every person ("I and I") and who revealed himself in the flesh as Haile Selassie I. Rastafari praise Jah through reasoning, Nyabinghi drumming and the chanting down of Babylon.

alternate_names: Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah
deities.summary: Haile Selassie I, King of Kings, Lord of Lords, Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah, of the line of Solomon and Sheba, is the returned Messiah and the living God revealed. His coronation in 1930 fulfilled prophecy; his visit to Jamaica on 21 April 1966 is celebrated as Grounation Day.

primary_sources: Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey (1923–25)
deities.summary: Marcus Mosiah Garvey is honoured as the prophet who taught Africans at home and abroad to look to Africa and to God in their own image. His call for repatriation and Black self-reliance prepared the way for the recognition of Haile Selassie.
deities.tradition_claim: Venerated as prophet, not as a god.

primary_sources: The Eleven Satanic Rules of the Earth (1967)
iconography: Sigil of Baphomet (goat head in an inverted pentagram)
deities.summary: Satan is not a being to be worshipped but a symbol: the carnal, proud, self-determining nature of the human animal that religion has condemned. Satan represents indulgence instead of abstinence, vital existence instead of spiritual pipe dreams, and vengeance instead of turning the other cheek. The Satanist is his or her own god; the Infernal Names — Satan, Lucifer, Belial, Leviathan — are invoked in ritual as psychodrama.
deities.tradition_claim: Atheistic: the Church of Satan holds that Satan does not exist as a personal being.

primary_sources: Diverse group-specific texts; no common canon
deities.summary: Satan is a real spiritual being, the liberator who gave humanity knowledge and freedom and who was slandered by the religions of submission. Theistic Satanists honour him through prayer, ritual and devotion as patron, teacher and source of personal power and self-realisation.

Lucifer is the bringer of light, the spirit of illumination, enlightenment and self-deification. Like Prometheus he gave humanity the fire of reason and independent will; the Luciferian walks the path of becoming a self-made light, not a servant.

alternate_names: Satan (as corrupted name, per the Temple)
primary_sources: The Book of Coming Forth by Night (Michael Aquino, 1975)
deities.summary: Set is the Prince of Darkness, the oldest of gods, a real metaphysical being who stands apart from the natural order. He gave humanity the Black Flame — the isolate, self-aware intelligence that sets each mind apart from the universe. Setians do not worship Set but honour him as a friend and model, following the path of Xeper, "to come into being", toward self-created immortality. The Hebrew "Satan" is a later distortion of his name.

primary_sources: The Seven Tenets of The Satanic Temple
Anatole France, The Revolt of the Angels (1914, as literary source)
deities.summary: Satan is a literary symbol, not a deity: the eternal rebel against arbitrary authority, the champion of reason, bodily autonomy, compassion and the pursuit of knowledge. Satanists embrace the name of the Adversary as a declaration of independence from tyranny and superstition.
deities.tradition_claim: Non-theistic: The Satanic Temple does not believe in a supernatural Satan.

deities.summary: Baphomet, winged and goat-headed, sits enthroned with two children gazing up at him: the reconciliation of opposites, of animal and human, male and female, and a symbol of pluralism and open inquiry. The Temple sets him beside monuments to other faiths in public squares to defend religious liberty.

primary_sources: Éliphas Lévi, Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie (1854–56), frontispiece "Baphomet du Temple"
Records of the Trial of the Templars (1307–1312)
deities.summary: Baphomet is the hieroglyph of the Great Magical Agent, the astral light: a winged, goat-headed androgyne with a torch of intelligence between the horns, a pentagram on the brow, one arm raised (SOLVE) and one lowered (COAGULA), sitting on the globe. It is the synthesis of all opposites — male and female, light and darkness, good and evil — balanced in the hand of the magus.

primary_sources: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), 1904
Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu, Cairo)
deities.summary: "I am Infinite Space, and the Infinite Stars thereof." Nuit is the boundless circumference, the night-sky goddess arched over all things, who calls every man and every woman to her: "Every man and every woman is a star." She gives unimaginable joys on earth and certainty, not faith, in death.

primary_sources: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), 1904
Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu, Cairo)
deities.summary: "I am the flame that burns in every heart of man, and in the core of every star. I am Life, and the giver of Life." Hadit is the infinitely small point at the centre of Nuit's infinite circle, the hidden self and true will within every being; he is complement and lover of Nuit.

primary_sources: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), 1904
Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu, Cairo)
iconography: hawk-headed god enthroned with the solar disk (as on the Stele of Revealing)
deities.summary: Ra-Hoor-Khuit is the crowned and conquering child, the god of war and of vengeance who rules the new Aeon of Horus that began in 1904. He displaces the Aeon of Osiris, the age of the dying god, with the age of the self-realised child whose law is "Do what thou wilt".

primary_sources: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), 1904
Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu, Cairo)
deities.summary: Hoor-paar-kraat is the silent, passive twin of Ra-Hoor-Khuit; together they form the double god Heru-ra-ha. He is the Lord of Silence, the babe in the egg of spirit, whom Aiwass serves as minister.

deities.etymology: Crowley's spelling of Babylon, taken from the angelic communications he worked through in 1909.
deities.summary: Babalon is the Great Mother, the Scarlet Woman who rides the Beast and holds the cup filled with the blood of the saints: the ecstatic, liberated feminine who receives all things into herself. The adept who pours every drop of his blood into her cup crosses the Abyss and becomes a Master of the Temple in the City of the Pyramids.

primary_sources: Liber AL vel Legis (The Book of the Law), 1904
Stele of Revealing (Stele of Ankh-ef-en-Khonsu, Cairo)
deities.summary: Aiwass is the praeterhuman intelligence who dictated The Book of the Law to Aleister Crowley in Cairo on 8, 9 and 10 April 1904, speaking as the "minister of Hoor-paar-kraat". Crowley later identified him as his own Holy Guardian Angel.
To Mega Therion, the Great Beast, is the title of Aleister Crowley as the prophet of the Aeon of Horus, chosen to receive the Law and to proclaim it to the world with his consort the Scarlet Woman.
deities.tradition_claim: Thelemites regard Crowley as prophet, not god.

primary_sources: The Charge of the Goddess (Doreen Valiente, from Gardnerian Book of Shadows)
Aradia, or the Gospel of the Witches (Charles Godfrey Leland, 1899)
deities.summary: "I who am the beauty of the green earth and the white moon among the stars." The Goddess is the Great Mother of all life, known by countless names — Artemis, Astarte, Diana, Melusine, Aphrodite, Cerridwen, Arianrhod, Isis, Bride. She is Maiden, Mother and Crone, the moon in its phases; "all acts of love and pleasure are my rituals."

alternate_names: the Oak King and Holly King
deities.summary: The Horned God is the Lord of the wild, of animals, the hunt, death and rebirth, consort and son of the Goddess. He is born at Yule, weds the Goddess at Beltane, dies at harvest and rules the summerland of the dead until he is born again: the turning of the Wheel of the Year.

"What is God? God is the supreme intelligence, the first cause of all things." God is eternal, immutable, immaterial, unique, all-powerful, sovereignly just and good. He created spirits simple and ignorant, to progress through many incarnations toward perfection.

primary_sources: The Gospel According to Spiritism (1864), ch. 6
deities.summary: The Consoler promised by Jesus has come as the Spirit of Truth: the collective revelation of the higher spirits who teach the meaning of Christ's words in plain terms. Spiritism itself is the fulfilment of that promise, and messages signed "The Spirit of Truth" guide the work.

primary_sources: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures (Mary Baker Eddy, 1875), esp. p. 465
deities.summary: God is incorporeal, divine, supreme, infinite Mind, Spirit, Soul, Principle, Life, Truth, Love. God is All-in-all, and since God is good and God is All, matter, sin, sickness and death have no true reality; healing comes from understanding this. God is our Father-Mother.

primary_sources: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures, pp. 332–334
deities.summary: Jesus was the human man; Christ is the divine idea, "the true idea voicing good", the spiritual selfhood that Jesus most fully expressed. The Christ is eternal and still heals today wherever the divine idea is understood.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1870s CE (Bible Students); name of the movement 1931
primary_sources: New World Translation of the Holy Scriptures (1950/1961)
deities.summary: Jehovah is the only true God, one person, not a Trinity, whose name must be known and sanctified. The great issue before the universe is the vindication of his sovereignty, challenged by Satan in Eden; his Kingdom, ruled by Christ since 1914, will soon replace human governments and restore paradise on earth.

Jesus is God's firstborn son and first creation, the Word through whom all other things were made, known in heaven as Michael the Archangel. He gave his perfect life as a ransom, was raised as a spirit, and has ruled as King of God's Kingdom since 1914, when he cast Satan out of heaven.

God is one person, the Father, and not three. Jesus is a human being exalted by God, the teacher and exemplar of the way to God, but not God himself. Later Unitarian Universalism opened this into a non-creedal free search for truth.

alternate_names: Our Lady of the Covenant of Mercy
deities.earliest_attestation: medieval Ethiopia (Taʾammera Maryam, "Miracles of Mary", 15th c. CE)
deities.summary: Kidane Mehret is the Covenant of Mercy that Christ made with his mother Mary: that whoever calls on her name, honours her memory or gives in her name will receive mercy. On the feast of Kidane Mehret the faithful celebrate this covenant and seek her intercession.

Father Sky, the shining heaven. With Mother Earth (Pṛthivī) he is the primeval parent-pair of gods and men, invoked together as Dyāvāpṛthivī. Father of Uṣas, Agni, Indra and the Aśvins, he is a remote presence whose place in worship has passed to his sons.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit dyaús 'sky, day' + pitṛ 'father', from PIE *dyēus ph2tēr 'sky-father'

deities.summary: The broad Earth, mother of all beings. With Dyaus she forms the cosmic parents; the Atharvaveda's great Earth Hymn praises her as the bearer of mountains, plants, waters and every people, who is asked to forgive the wounds of the plough.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit pṛthivī 'the broad one', from PIE *pleth2-wih2 'broad (earth)'

deities.summary: The golden Impeller who rouses all beings to motion at dawn and lays them to rest at dusk. The Gāyatrī mantra, the most recited verse of the Veda, is addressed to him: 'May we meditate on the excellent radiance of the god Savitṛ; may he stimulate our thoughts.'
deities.etymology: From root sū/sav 'to impel, vivify'

deities.summary: Guardian of roads, herds and journeys; finder of lost cattle and lost things. Drawn by goats and eating gruel because he is toothless, he guides the traveller on earth and the dead on the path to the fathers.
deities.etymology: From root puṣ 'to nourish, thrive'

deities.summary: An Āditya, companion of Mitra and Varuṇa, guardian of hospitality, the bonds of the Ārya community, marriage and the road. In later tradition he is chief of the Pitṛs (ancestors).
The Āditya who apportions each person's share of wealth and fortune, invoked at dawn for prosperity and marital happiness.
deities.etymology: From root bhaj 'to apportion, share'

deities.summary: The thundering rain-cloud, a bull who impregnates the earth with rain; at his coming the winds blow, lightning flies and plants spring up.

Lord of creatures, the creator who in the beginning was alone, desired to be many, heated himself in tapas and emitted the worlds, gods and beings. Exhausted and fallen apart after creation, he is reassembled in the Vedic fire-altar — every sacrifice restores the creator.

The Golden Embryo arising in the beginning on the cosmic waters, sole lord of all that is born, who holds earth and sky. In the Purāṇas the world-egg floats on the waters and Brahmā is born within it.
deities.etymology: Sanskrit hiraṇya 'gold' + garbha 'womb, embryo'
iconography: golden egg on the cosmic waters

deities.summary: Trita the Third, son of the waters, who with Indra's aid slays the three-headed, six-eyed Viśvarūpa son of Tvaṣṭṛ and frees the cattle; a hero cast into a well who calls on the gods from its depths.
The Child of the Waters: fire that shines within the waters without fuel, golden, surrounded by the maternal waters who nourish him. He is the hidden fire of lightning and of the depths.
The rock-cave enclosure in which the Paṇis hid the stolen cows of dawn. Indra and Bṛhaspati with the Aṅgiras singers split Vala by the power of the chant and released the cattle and the light.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–6th c. CE (Devī Māhātmya); earlier Mahiṣa in epic
deities.summary: The buffalo-asura who, by a boon that no man or god could kill him, conquered heaven and drove out the devas. From the gods' combined fury the Goddess arose, and on the tenth day she cut off his head as he emerged from the buffalo's body. Navarātri and Durgā Pūjā celebrate his defeat.

Daitya king, son of Kaśyapa and Diti, who won a boon that he could be killed neither by man nor beast, by day nor night, indoors nor out, on earth nor in the sky, by no weapon. He tormented his son Prahlāda for worshipping Viṣṇu, until Narasiṃha burst from a pillar at dusk and slew him on his lap at the threshold.
Brother of Hiraṇyakaśipu who dragged the Earth down into the cosmic ocean; Viṣṇu as the boar Varāha dived, slew him and lifted the Earth on his tusks.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium BCE (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.5 three-steps motif); epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: The generous asura king, grandson of Prahlāda, under whom all lived in equality and plenty. When the dwarf Vāmana begged three paces of land, Bali kept his word, and Viṣṇu in cosmic form covered earth and sky and placed the third step on Bali's head, sending him to rule Sutala. Each year at Onam he returns to visit his people.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th–2nd c. BCE (Saṅkarṣaṇa-Vāsudeva coins of Agathocles, c. 180 BCE)
deities.summary: Elder brother of Kṛṣṇa, the plough-bearing strongman, avatāra of the serpent Śeṣa (and in some lists the eighth avatar of Viṣṇu). He diverted the Yamunā with his plough and taught both Bhīma and Duryodhana the mace.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th c. CE (Puri temple by Anantavarman Chodaganga); earlier local cult
deities.summary: The Lord of the Universe at Puri, worshipped with his brother Balabhadra and sister Subhadrā in wooden forms with great round eyes. Every year the three ride in towering chariots in the Ratha Yātrā; every 12–19 years the images are renewed (Nabakalebara) as the divine essence passes into new wood.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 13th c. CE (Pandharpur inscriptions; Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev)
deities.summary: Viṭhoba of Pandharpur, a form of Kṛṣṇa who stands on a brick with hands on his hips, waiting for his devotees. He came to see the devotee Puṇḍalīka, who, busy serving his parents, tossed him a brick to stand on; he has stood there ever since. The Vārkarī pilgrims walk to him every Āṣāḍhī Ekādaśī.

deities.earliest_attestation: Inscriptions at Tirumala from c. 9th c. CE; Āḻvār hymns (6th–9th c. CE)
deities.summary: Viṣṇu as Lord of the Venkaṭa hill at Tirumala, who came to earth in the Kali age and borrowed from Kubera to fund his wedding to Padmāvatī; devotees offer their hair and wealth to help repay the debt. His temple is among the most visited shrines on earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Sabarimala tradition; Sastha worship attested in Kerala inscriptions from c. 9th–10th c. CE
deities.summary: Ayyappan, son of Śiva and Viṣṇu in the form of Mohinī, born to destroy the buffalo-demoness Mahiṣī. Raised as prince Maṇikaṇṭhan of Pandalam, he took his seat as a celibate yogi on the Sabarimala hill, where pilgrims who keep a 41-day vow climb the eighteen holy steps.

Khaṇḍobā of Jejuri, a warrior form of Śiva (Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava) who rides a horse with his wife Mhāḷsā, slaying the demons Maṇi and Malla. His devotees shower turmeric (bhandara) until the hill turns gold; dogs are his companions.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1500 BCE (Rigveda); temples c. 5th–13th c. CE (Konark, Modhera)
deities.summary: The Sun, eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, driving his chariot of seven horses with Aruṇa as charioteer; first of the Navagrahas. Saura devotees worshipped him as the supreme god; Chhath and Makara Saṅkrānti still honour him.

The Moon, identified with Soma, married to the twenty-seven Nakṣatras, daughters of Dakṣa. Cursed by Dakṣa to waste away for favouring Rohiṇī, he wanes and is restored by Śiva, who wears him as a crescent.
Mars among the Navagrahas, red son of the Earth (Bhūmi), warrior and commander of the planetary army.
Lord of the sacred word and preceptor (guru) of the gods; with the chant he split the Vala cave. As the planet Jupiter he is the great benefic of the Navagrahas.

deities.earliest_attestation: Vedic (Uśanā Kāvya, RV); epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: Preceptor of the asuras, master of the Mṛtasañjīvanī art that revives the dead; as the planet Venus he grants beauty, wealth and pleasure.

Saturn, son of Sūrya and Chāyā, dark and slow-moving, whose gaze brings hardship as the reward of karma. His seven-and-a-half-year transit (sāḍe sātī) is feared; he is propitiated on Saturdays with oil and black sesame, and devotees of Hanumān are spared his torment.

deities.earliest_attestation: Svarbhānu in Rigveda 5.40; Rāhu in epic and Purāṇas
deities.summary: The severed head of the asura Svarbhānu who stole a sip of amṛta at the churning of the ocean. Sūrya and Candra exposed him; Viṣṇu's discus cut off his head, but the nectar had made it immortal. In revenge Rāhu swallows the sun and moon at eclipse.
The headless body of Svarbhānu, the descending lunar node; a shadow planet of detachment, comets and liberation.
The nine 'seizers' that govern human fate: Sūrya, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śani, Rāhu and Ketu. They are installed in shrines in a 3×3 grid and propitiated in graha-śānti rites.

The heavenly river who descended to earth at the prayer of King Bhagīratha to purify the ashes of his ancestors; Śiva caught her in his hair to break her fall. To bathe in her erases sin, and ashes cast in her waters reach heaven.

The thousand-headed serpent king, 'the Remainder' who survives the dissolution of the worlds. He bears the earth on his hoods and is the couch on which Viṣṇu sleeps on the cosmic ocean; he incarnates as Lakṣmaṇa and Balarāma.
Nāga king who served as the churning rope wound around Mount Mandara when gods and asuras churned the ocean for amṛta; the poison he spewed was swallowed by Śiva. He coils around Śiva's neck.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium BCE (Vedic sarpa; Buddhist and Jain texts); Bharhut reliefs (2nd c. BCE)
deities.summary: Semi-divine serpent beings dwelling in Pātāla, lakes and springs, guardians of waters, rain and treasure. Children of Kaśyapa and Kadrū, enemies of Garuḍa; honoured at Nāga Pañcamī and in serpent groves (sarpa kāvu).

King of birds, son of Kaśyapa and Vinatā, who stole the amṛta from the gods to free his mother from slavery to the serpents, and became Viṣṇu's mount. Enemy of the nāgas, invoked against snake poison.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE–4th c. CE (Rāmāyaṇa); Vedic Sītā (furrow goddess)
deities.summary: Born from a furrow ploughed by King Janaka, wife of Rāma and incarnation of Lakṣmī. Abducted by Rāvaṇa, faithful through captivity and trial by fire, she finally returned into the Earth her mother.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th c. CE (Gīta Govinda); earlier Prakrit verse (Gāthā Saptaśatī)
primary_sources: Writings of the Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana
deities.summary: The cowherd beloved of Kṛṣṇa in Vṛndāvana, supreme among the gopīs. For the Gauḍīya and Nimbārka schools she is Kṛṣṇa's own bliss-energy (hlādinī śakti), the goddess of devotion whose love surpasses all.
The divine sage who wanders the three worlds with his vīṇā singing 'Nārāyaṇa'; messenger of the gods, teacher of bhakti, and a mischief-maker whose quarrels always serve a divine purpose.
Son of the sage Atri and Anasūyā, in whom Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva became one; the wandering avadhūta guru who learned from twenty-four teachers in nature, followed by four dogs and a cow.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 13th c. CE (Bengali Maṅgal-kāvya); earlier serpent cults
deities.summary: Goddess of snakes in Bengal and the east, who protects from snakebite and grants fertility. The merchant Chand Sadagar refused her worship until she killed his sons; his daughter-in-law Behulā floated her husband's corpse downriver to win him back, and Chand at last offered her a flower with his left hand.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval (Skanda Purāṇa); folk cult widespread in North India
deities.summary: The 'Cool One', goddess of smallpox and pustular disease, riding a donkey with broom, winnowing fan and pot of cool water. She both visits the disease and cools it away; she is worshipped with cold food on Śītalā Aṣṭamī.
The physician of the gods who rose from the churning of the ocean bearing the pot of amṛta; an avatāra of Viṣṇu and the founder of Āyurveda, worshipped on Dhanteras.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 6th–8th c. CE (Kāpālika and Purāṇic sources)
deities.summary: The terrifying form of Śiva who sprang from his wrath and cut off Brahmā's fifth head for its arrogance. Bearing the skull stuck to his hand, he wandered as a beggar until it fell at Kāśī, where he is now kotwal, the city's guardian. His mount is a black dog.
The fierce warrior born from a lock of Śiva's hair when Satī immolated herself at Dakṣa's sacrifice; he destroyed the sacrifice and beheaded Dakṣa.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st millennium CE (bull emblem of Śiva earlier, Kushan coins)
deities.summary: The bull who is Śiva's mount, gatekeeper of Kailāsa and chief of the gaṇas; he sits facing the sanctum of every Śiva temple, and devotees whisper their wishes in his ear.

deities.earliest_attestation: Kushan period images (1st–3rd c. CE); Devī Māhātmya (5th–6th c. CE)
deities.summary: The seven Mothers — Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā — the śaktis who emerged from the gods to fight the demon Raktabīja, drinking his blood before each drop could spawn new demons.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 10th–15th c. CE (Śākta Purāṇas and Tantras)
deities.summary: Ten forms of the Great Goddess — Kālī, Tārā, Tripurasundarī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Bhairavī, Chinnamastā, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī and Kamalā — which Satī displayed to Śiva, surrounding him on all ten directions, when he forbade her to attend Dakṣa's sacrifice.

Daughter of Dakṣa and first wife of Śiva, who gave up her body in the fire of her father's sacrifice when Śiva was insulted. Śiva wandered with her corpse until Viṣṇu's discus cut it apart; the places where her body fell became the Śakti Pīṭhas. She was reborn as Pārvatī.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th–8th c. CE (Kāmarūpa inscriptions); Kālikā Purāṇa (c. 10th c. CE)
deities.summary: The Goddess of desire on Nīlācala hill in Assam, worshipped as a yoni-shaped stone where Satī's womb fell. Each year during Ambubācī the goddess menstruates and the temple closes for three days.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th–9th c. CE (Tamil inscriptions of Sāttan/Sāstā)
deities.summary: Guardian god of the Tamil village boundary, riding out each night on a horse or elephant to protect the fields, with his consorts Pūraṇā and Puṣkalā. Villagers dedicate terracotta horses to him, often of enormous size.
iconography: seated with one leg raised by a strap (yogapaṭṭa)

deities.summary: The great mother goddess of Tamil villages, bringer of rain and of pox. The 'pearls' of smallpox are her grace and her anger; at her festivals devotees walk on fire, carry fire-pots and pierce themselves in vow.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval (Saundatti temple, c. 12th–13th c. CE); Renukā in epic
deities.summary: Mother of Paraśurāma, beheaded at her husband Jamadagni's order and restored to life. Worshipped at Saundatti in Karnataka and across the Deccan as Yellammā, 'mother of all', with her headless and head-only forms; her devotees include the jogappa and jogati.
A fierce Tamil guardian deity, regarded as a form of Śiva, who protects villages, roads and homes against evil spirits and thieves; he receives offerings of meat, toddy and cigars.
The black guardian god, chief of the kaval deivam, armed with a sickle (aruval), riding a horse; he upholds justice, punishes oath-breakers and protects the villages of southern Tamil Nadu.

Vaikuṇḍar, the incarnation of Nārāyaṇa born of the sea at Tiruchendur in 1833, the final avatāra who destroys Kali (the evil of the age). He gathered the oppressed of Travancore, abolished caste distinctions at the well and the temple, and established the Dharma Yukam.

The primordial evil born at the beginning of creation, a monstrous being of mountainous size. Cut into fragments by Nārāyaṇa, each fragment was reborn as an enemy of righteousness in each age — Ravana, Duryodhana — and last as Kaliyan, the spirit of the Kali Yuga.

primary_sources: Vachanas of Basava, Allama Prabhu, Akka Mahadevi
deities.summary: Śiva the formless Lord worn by each devotee on the body as the personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga). The Lingayat needs no temple or priest: 'the body is the temple'. The vachana poets call him by personal names — Kūḍalasaṅgama, Cennamallikārjuna, Guhēśvara.

Statesman-saint of Kalyāṇa who founded the Anubhava Maṇṭapa, a hall of spiritual dialogue open to all castes and to women. Lingayats revere him as the founder of their faith, regarded by many as an incarnation of Nandī.
The formless supreme creator of the Tai-Ahom, who existed alone in the void and created the world, the gods and humankind.

King of heaven in Ahom religion, god of thunder and rain, who sent his grandsons Khunlung and Khunlai down to earth by a golden ladder to rule; from them descend the Ahom kings (Swargadeos, 'lords of heaven').

The two divine brothers sent down from heaven by Lengdon, who descended at Mong-Ri-Mong-Ram and founded the Tai kingdoms; ancestors of the Ahom royal line and founders of the Me-Dam-Me-Phi ancestor rites.

deities.earliest_attestation: Gandharan reliefs (1st–3rd c. CE); Pāli Ambaṭṭha Sutta (as Vajirapāṇi yakkha)
deities.summary: The thunderbolt-bearing bodhisattva, protector and constant companion of the Buddha, who embodies the power of all Buddhas. In the Pāli canon a yakkha with a blazing vajra stands over those who would refuse the Buddha's question; in Vajrayāna he is the wrathful lord of secrets who subdues the obstacle-makers.

Guardian kings of the four quarters dwelling on the slopes of Mount Meru: Dhṛtarāṣṭra (east, gandharvas), Virūḍhaka (south, kumbhāṇḍas), Virūpākṣa (west, nāgas) and Vaiśravaṇa (north, yakṣas). They protect the Dharma and the world, and stand at the gates of temples across Asia.

deities.earliest_attestation: Pāli canon; Gandharan and Central Asian images
deities.summary: Guardian King of the North and lord of the yakṣas, giver of wealth and protector of the Dharma; carrying a banner or stūpa and a mongoose spitting jewels. In Khotan he was royal ancestor; in Japan Bishamonten is a god of war and fortune.

Sakka, lord of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three on the summit of Meru, a devout follower of the Buddha who questions him on the Dharma, protects the virtuous and attained stream-entry. He received the Buddha's hair at the renunciation and attended the descent from Tāvatiṃsa.

The great Brahmā who, when the newly awakened Buddha hesitated to teach, descended and begged him to open the doors of the Deathless for beings with little dust in their eyes. In the Brahmajāla Sutta another Mahābrahmā wrongly believes himself the creator.

deities.earliest_attestation: Gandharan sculpture (2nd–3rd c. CE); Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya
deities.summary: A yakṣiṇī mother of five hundred children who stole and devoured the children of Rājagṛha. The Buddha hid her youngest son Priyaṅkara under his alms-bowl; feeling a mother's grief she converted and became protector of children and childbirth, fed daily from the monks' alms.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Samye); biographies from 12th c. CE
primary_sources: Zangling-ma (terma biography revealed by Nyangral Nyima Özer)
deities.summary: The Lotus-Born master from Oḍḍiyāna, invited to Tibet by King Trisong Detsen, who bound the hostile spirits of Tibet under oath to protect the Dharma, founded Samye monastery and hid treasure-teachings (terma) for future ages. The Nyingma revere him as the Second Buddha.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 8th c. CE (Samye tradition); later Nechung oracle
deities.summary: A powerful worldly spirit-king bound by Padmasambhava to guard the treasury of Samye, later seated at Nechung, where he speaks through the State Oracle of Tibet.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 12th–15th c. CE (epic in oral performance)
primary_sources: Epic of King Gesar (Tibetan oral epic)
deities.summary: The divine warrior-king sent down from heaven to Ling to subdue the demon kings of the four directions, defend the weak and establish the Dharma. Bards (drungpa) receive the epic in visions; he is invoked as a war god and as a coming saviour.

deities.earliest_attestation: Bhaiṣajyaguru Sūtra (Gilgit manuscripts, c. 6th–7th c. CE; Chinese 4th–7th c. CE)
deities.summary: The Medicine Buddha of lapis-lazuli light, lord of the eastern Pure Land Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa, who vowed twelve great vows to heal the sick in body and mind and to cure the poison of ignorance.

deities.earliest_attestation: Aṣṭasāhasrikā (c. 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE); goddess images c. 9th–12th c. CE (Pala)
deities.summary: The Perfection of Wisdom personified as a serene goddess holding a book and a lotus; she is the insight into emptiness from which every Buddha is born.

The five Buddha-families of the vajra maṇḍala — Vairocana (centre), Akṣobhya (east), Ratnasambhava (south), Amitābha (west) and Amoghasiddhi (north) — who embody the five wisdoms that transform the five poisons and the five aggregates.

The nāga king who, during a seven-day storm in the weeks after the Awakening, coiled seven times around the meditating Buddha and spread his hood over his head, then took the form of a young man and bowed.
iconography: seven-headed cobra hood over the seated Buddha

deities.earliest_attestation: Kalpa Sūtra (c. 4th–5th c. CE redaction); Mathura images (Kushan period)
deities.summary: The first Tīrthaṅkara of our cycle, who taught humanity agriculture, writing, crafts and the social order when the wish-fulfilling trees failed, then renounced his kingdom and attained liberation on Mount Aṣṭāpada. His emblem is the bull.

deities.earliest_attestation: Historical figure c. 9th–8th c. BCE (traditional); Kalpa Sūtra
deities.summary: The twenty-third Tīrthaṅkara, prince of Vārāṇasī, who saved a pair of snakes burning in an ascetic's fire. In his final meditation the demon Meghamālin (his enemy through many births, Kamaṭha) assailed him with storms, and the serpent king Dharaṇendra with Padmāvatī spread his hood over him. His fourfold restraint preceded Mahāvīra's teaching.

The twenty-second Tīrthaṅkara, cousin of Kṛṣṇa, who on his wedding day heard the cries of animals penned for the feast and renounced the world at once; his bride Rājīmatī followed him into renunciation. He attained liberation on Mount Girnar.

The twenty-four Ford-Makers of each half time-cycle, from Ṛṣabha to Mahāvīra, who conquered passions, attained omniscience and taught the path across the ocean of rebirth. They neither create nor intervene; they are worshipped as perfect models.

deities.earliest_attestation: Shravanabelagola statue 981 CE; Ādipurāṇa (9th c. CE)
deities.summary: Son of Ṛṣabha who defeated his brother Bharata in combat, then renounced the kingdom on the field and stood in meditation so long that vines grew up his limbs. Dig. Jains hold him the first to attain liberation in this cycle; his 17-metre statue at Shravanabelagola is anointed every twelve years (Mahāmastakābhiṣeka).

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 9th–10th c. CE images; Śvetāmbara and Digambara hymns
deities.summary: The yakṣī (śāsanadevī) of Pārśvanātha, queen of Dharaṇendra, who sheltered the Jina with her husband. Crowned with a serpent hood, she is the most worshipped Jain goddess, granting protection and worldly aid to devotees.

The yakṣī of Neminātha, a mother goddess seated under a mango tree with a child on her lap and a lion as mount. Once a devout wife driven from home, she gave her life with her sons and was reborn as the goddess.
The nāga king (yakṣa of Pārśvanātha), reborn from one of the snakes Pārśva saved from the fire, who spread his hoods over the Jina during Meghamālin's assault.

The enemy of Pārśvanātha across ten lifetimes, born as the ascetic Kamaṭha whose fire Pārśva exposed, and as the demon Meghamālin who hurled storms and floods at the meditating Jina. Defeated by his equanimity, he finally converted.

primary_sources: Guru Granth Sahib (Japji and Nanak's hymns)
deities.summary: The first Guru and founder of the Sikh path, who after three days in the river Vein proclaimed 'there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' and taught the remembrance of the One Name (Nām), honest work and sharing. His light passed to each successive Guru and now dwells in the Guru Granth Sahib.

The tenth Guru, poet and warrior, who created the Khalsa at Anandpur on Vaisakhi 1699 with the initiation of the double-edged sword, and before his death declared the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru.

primary_sources: Ardas (Sikh common prayer, opening 'Pritham Bhagauti simar kai')
deities.summary: The divine power as sword: the Ardās begins 'First remembering Bhagautī, then remember Guru Nānak.' In the Dasam Granth's Chaṇḍī dī Vār the goddess Chaṇḍī battles the demons; in Sikh reading Bhagautī is the Timeless One's power that destroys evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (Bön canon); claimed pre-Buddhist
deities.summary: The primordial Buddha of the Bön Dzogchen teachings, naked and blue like the sky, the dharmakāya from which the Bön teachings flow through Shenlha Ökar to Tönpa Shenrab.
The Great Mother of Bön, embodiment of wisdom and love (also Sherab Jamma), one of the four Transcendent Lords; mother of all enlightened beings.
The god of compassion of Bön, one of the four Transcendent Lords, the sambhogakāya who transmits the teachings from Kuntu Zangpo to Tönpa Shenrab.
The fierce Queen of Existence, chief protector of Bön, riding a mule over a sea of blood, with six arms and three faces; also adopted by some Tibetan Buddhist lineages.
The demon prince who opposed Tönpa Shenrab throughout his life, stealing his horses and seeking to destroy his teaching, until at last he was converted and became a disciple.

deities.earliest_attestation: Dunhuang-era Tibetan (8th–10th c. CE) mountain cult references; later rituals
deities.summary: The great mountain deity of the Nyenchen Thanglha range north of Lhasa, a white god on a white horse, ancestor-protector of central Tibet and lord of the nyen spirits; bound by Padmasambhava as a Dharma protector.

primary_sources: Kalasha oral tradition and festival hymns
deities.summary: The creator god of the Kalasha, distant and supreme, who made the world and the other gods; in the related Nuristani religion he corresponds to Imra (Yamrāy), the creator.
A powerful god of the Kalasha, protector of the valley, of crops and herds, and intercessor with the creator; honoured with goat sacrifice at his altar with carved horse heads.
Goddess of the home, family and marriage, whose clan temple (Jestak Han) holds the community's domestic rites.
The heroic god who rides in on a horse from the land of Tsiyam each winter solstice at the Chaumos festival, counts the people, receives their offerings and returns, carrying their prayers.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 17th–18th c. CE (Malla court institution; earlier kumārī-pūjā)
deities.summary: A prepubescent girl of the Newar Shakya caste chosen by strict signs to embody the goddess Taleju until her first menstruation. The Royal Kumārī of Kathmandu blesses the head of state each year at Indra Jātrā.

The tutelary goddess of the Malla kings, a form of Durgā brought from Simraungadh; her temples tower over each Durbar Square, open to the public only at Dasaiñ. She withdrew from playing dice with the king and promised to dwell in a virgin girl — the Kumārī.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 7th c. CE (legend: Narendradeva); chariot festival records from Licchavi/early Malla
deities.summary: The red rain-giving god of Patan, worshipped by Buddhists as Karuṇāmaya Avalokiteśvara and by Hindus as the yogi Matsyendranāth. When Gorakhnāth sat on the rain-serpents and caused a twelve-year drought, he was brought from Kāmarūpa in the form of a bee, and Gorakhnāth rose to greet his guru, releasing the nāgas. His enormous chariot is pulled through Patan each year.
The Pāṇḍava hero Bhīma deified as patron of Newar traders and craftsmen; merchants keep his image in their shops and he is honoured along the old trade routes to Tibet.

Mother goddess of the Turks, protector of women, childbirth, children and the placenta, wife or consort of Tengri. In the Orkhon inscriptions the khagan's mother is compared to her: 'like Umay my mother the Katun'.
The sacred Earth-and-Water, the homeland as a living divine power, invoked with Tengri and Umay in the Orkhon inscriptions as the protector of the Turkic people.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th c. CE (Plano Carpini, Marco Polo); Mongol ritual
deities.summary: Mother Earth of the Mongols, consort of Tengri (Father Heaven), giver of fertility to herds and people. Marco Polo describes household felt images of the earth-god Natigay with wife and children, fed with meat at meals.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th c. CE (Plano Carpini on fire purification); Mongol fire prayers
primary_sources: Plano Carpini, History of the Mongols
deities.summary: The mother spirit of the hearth fire (golomt), centre of the ger and lineage; purifier through whose flames visitors and goods passed. Fat is offered to her at the winter fire-sacrifice.

deities.earliest_attestation: 13th–16th c. CE (Mongolian Buddhist and shamanic texts)
deities.summary: Chief of the thirty-three tengri (Buryat: of the fifty-five western, benevolent tengri), father of Geser. His name descends, through Sogdian, from Ahura Mazdā, while Mongolian Buddhism identifies him with Indra-Śakra, king of the Thirty-Three.

primary_sources: Buryat shamanic prayers and Geser epic
deities.summary: Leader of the forty-four eastern, malevolent tengri of the Buryats, whose war against the fifty-five western tengri of Khan Khurmas drives the cosmic drama of the Geser epic; demons cast down from his side became earthly evils.
The Bull Lord, a heavenly being who descended as a bull, fathered the Buryat Ekhirit and Bulagat clans and is honoured as their ancestral master spirit of the Baikal region.

deities.earliest_attestation: Turkic folk tradition (widespread; records 19th c. CE)
primary_sources: Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Uzbek and Tatar folk tradition
deities.summary: A female demon with long hair and pendulous breasts, often with backward feet, who attacks women in childbirth and newborns, strangling them or stealing the mother's liver. Iron, onions and a protecting shaman or mullah drive her away.

Patron-spirit of horses among the Kazakhs, one of the four livestock patrons (with Zengi-baba of cattle, Shopan-ata of sheep, Oisyl-kara of camels); horse-breeders call on him at foaling and in danger.

deities.earliest_attestation: Epic in oral performance (written records 19th c. CE); Manas Ordo, Talas
primary_sources: Epic of Manas (Kyrgyz oral epic; recitations of Sagymbai Orozbakov and Sayakbai Karalaev)
deities.summary: The Kyrgyz epic hero who united the forty tribes and fought the Kalmyks and Chinese; manaschi reciters receive the epic in dreams, and pilgrims visit his ordo at Talas.
The Scythian sky-father whom Herodotus calls 'most rightly named' Zeus, husband of Api the Earth, ancestor of the Scythians through their first man Targitaos.

primary_sources: Herodotus 4.5 (mother of Targitaos as daughter of the Borysthenes)
deities.summary: The Scythian Earth goddess, wife of Papaios, whom Herodotus equates with Gē; possibly also the snake-legged mother of the Scythians in the Greek origin legend.
The god Herodotus equates with Apollo; perhaps a solar or herd-protecting god (name possibly 'rich in pastures').

The goddess Herodotus equates with Heavenly Aphrodite; patron of the Enarees, effeminate diviners who received their gift from her. Gold plaques show a goddess enthroned before a horseman with a rhyton.
The god worshipped by the Royal Scythians, equated by Herodotus with Poseidon — likely a god of waters and horses.

The war god of the Scythians, unnamed by Herodotus, worshipped as an ancient iron sword set on a vast platform of brushwood in each district, to which horses, cattle and every hundredth war captive were sacrificed.

The first man of Scythia, son of Zeus (Papaios) and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. His three sons Lipoxais, Arpoxais and Kolaxais saw golden objects fall from the sky — plough and yoke, axe, cup — which burned the elder two but not the youngest, Kolaxais, who became king.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–8th c. CE (Sogdian Buddhist texts; Panjikent murals)
deities.summary: The Sogdian wind-god, 'Vayu who works in the upper region', portrayed in Panjikent with three heads, trident and armour; Sogdian Buddhist translations render the Indian Mahādeva (Śiva) as Weshparkar.
The 'great god' of the Sogdians, used in Sogdian Buddhist translations for Indra-Śakra, king of the gods; probably the Sogdian title of the supreme Mazdean god.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan god shown on coins with four arms, trident, thunderbolt, water-pot, and the bull, in the iconography of Śiva, yet named with the Bactrian descendant of Iranian Vayu, the wind.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1st–3rd c. CE (Kushan coins); Rabatak inscription (Mihir)
primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Bactrian Mithra, shown on Kushan coins as a radiate solar god with a sword, god of contract, light and kingship.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Bactrian form of Verethragna, the Iranian god of victory, depicted on Kushan coins as a warrior with a bird-crowned helmet, spear and sword.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The divine royal glory (Avestan khvarenah) personified, shown on Kushan coins as a youth holding fire or a purse; the glory that chooses and leaves kings.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: Goddess of abundance and fortune, Bactrian form of Avestan Aṣ̌i Vaŋuhī ('Good Reward'), shown on coins holding a cornucopia.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan moon god, shown with a crescent behind his shoulders.

primary_sources: Kushan coinage of Kanishka I and Huvishka
deities.summary: The Kushan fire god, shown with flames rising from his shoulders, the Bactrian form of Avestan Ātar.

primary_sources: Olonkho epics (e.g. Nyurgun Bootur the Swift, recorded by P. A. Oyunsky)
deities.summary: The supreme White Creator Lord dwelling in the ninth heaven, head of the Aiyy, creator of humans and source of light and life; honoured with mare's milk (kumys) at the summer Yhyakh festival.
Goddess of childbirth and fertility who brings the child's soul down from heaven and attends every birth, of humans and of cattle.
The mighty and terrible lord of the western upper-world abaasy, ambivalent master of fate, who gave humanity one of its three souls and fire, and who rules the black shamans.

Lord of the Lower World and chief of the lower abaasy, a monstrous figure with mouth on his forehead who devours souls and sends his demonic sons to wreck the Middle World; enemy of the Olonkho heroes.
The forest spirit and master of game, who gives animals to hunters who respect him; hunters feed the fire for him and never boast of their catch.
The supreme sky-god and creator of the Evenki, who with his rival brother Khargi formed the earth from soil brought up from the primordial waters, and who owns the animals and the upper world.
The evil younger brother of Seveki, master of the lower world, who marred creation with harmful beasts and sends illness through his spirits.
The great hunter-ancestor who chases the cosmic elk Kheglen across the sky (the Milky Way is his ski track) to recover the sun; guardian of the clan's path to the lower world of the dead.
The sky-father of the Mansi and Khanty, dwelling in the highest heaven, who sent down the earth-diver bird to bring up soil and made the earth; father of the World-Surveyor Man and of the bear.

Mother goddess of the Mansi, sister or wife of Num-Torum, who writes each newborn's destiny and length of life in a golden book or on a tree, and attends childbirth; she is linked with the hare and the goose.

The 'World-Watching Man', youngest son of Num-Torum, who rides a white horse round the world watching over humans, carries their prayers to heaven and wins his place by cleverness; also a goose-shaped psychopomp.
The lord of the underworld and of disease-spirits (kul), brother and opponent of Num-Torum, who spoils creation and takes the souls of the dead.
The sky-god and creator of the Nenets, ruler of the upper world and the weather, who sent birds to dive for earth and made the world; reindeer are sacrificed to him at sacred sites.
God of the underworld and of death, who in the creation myth tried to destroy what Num made, and who sends disease; Num had to grant him a share of the world.
Mother Earth of the Nenets, protector of women and childbirth, wife of Num in some accounts; offerings are made to her through the earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ethnographic records 19th–20th c. CE (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
primary_sources: Chukchi myth collections (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Raven, the creator-transformer of the Chukchi, who at the Creator's prompting made the earth with his droppings, freed the sun, moon and stars from a container and brought light; a glutton and trickster as well as creator.

primary_sources: Chukchi shamanic tradition (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Malevolent spirits of the Chukchi who hunt human souls as people hunt animals, causing illness and death; shamans fight them and protective rites deceive them.

primary_sources: Krasheninnikov, Description of the Land of Kamchatka (1755)
Koryak myth collections (Jesup North Pacific Expedition)
deities.summary: Big Raven of the Koryak and Itelmen, first ancestor and creator-trickster who made Kamchatka, lives with his wife Miti and fools and is fooled in endless tales; the ancestor to whom the Koryak trace their way of life.

primary_sources: Sima Zhen, supplement to the Shiji
deities.etymology: Possibly "hidden breath" / "subduer of animals"; also written 庖犧 Paoxi, "sacrificial kitchen".
iconography: serpent lower body entwined with Nüwa
deities.summary: First of the Three Sovereigns. Fuxi looked up at the patterns of heaven and down at the forms of earth and drew the Eight Trigrams; he taught people to knot nets, hunt, fish and marry. With his sister-consort Nüwa he is the serpent-bodied ancestral pair who hold the compass and set-square of cosmic order.

deities.earliest_attestation: 6th–10th c. CE (Chinese Buddhist translation; Scripture on the Ten Kings, c. 9th–10th c.)
primary_sources: Scripture on the Ten Kings (Shiwang jing)
Chinese Buddhist sutra translations of Yama
deities.etymology: Chinese transliteration of Sanskrit Yama-rāja (閻羅王).
deities.summary: Yanluo Wang is the Yama King, ruler of the Fifth Court of Diyu. Every soul stands before him after death; in his mirror of karma it sees its own deeds, and he assigns it to punishment or rebirth. Once ruler of the First Court, he was demoted to the Fifth for being too merciful to the dead.

deities.etymology: 上帝 "the high/supreme Di"; Di may originally have denoted the ancestral sacrifice or a royal ancestor.
deities.summary: Shangdi, the Lord on High, commands wind, rain, thunder and harvest and decides the fate of the kingdom and its wars. Royal ancestors stand in his presence and intercede for their descendants. Under the Zhou he is one with Heaven (Tian), and to the end of the empire the Son of Heaven sacrificed to Huangtian Shangdi at the winter solstice.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song–Yuan period (c. 12th–14th c. CE) Daoist scriptures
primary_sources: Daoist Canon (Daozang) scriptures of the Dipper Mother
iconography: three heads, eight or more arms
deities.summary: Doumu is the Mother of the Dipper, who gave birth to the nine stars of the Northern Dipper that govern every life's length and fate. Many-armed and many-eyed, holding sun and moon, she sits at the pole of heaven; those who recite her scripture can have the records of death erased.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (7th–8th c. CE) as a fixed triad; components 4th–6th c. CE
deities.summary: The Three Pure Ones are the highest emanations of the Dao: Yuanshi Tianzun of the Jade Purity, Lingbao Tianzun of the Upper Purity and Daode Tianzun (the deified Laozi) of the Great Purity. They are the primordial breath divided into three heavens, from which every lower god, scripture and teaching flows.

Yuanshi Tianzun, the Celestial Worthy of Primordial Beginning, existed before heaven and earth. In each cosmic cycle he reveals the sacred scriptures, written in self-generated celestial script, to the lesser gods, who pass them down to humanity.

Lingbao Tianzun, the Celestial Worthy of the Numinous Treasure, is the second of the Three Pure Ones. He holds the cosmic balance of yin and yang and keeps the sacred scriptures and talismans, mediating them from the primordial to the created world.

primary_sources: Yuan drama of the Eight Immortals
deities.summary: Lü Dongbin is the best loved of the Eight Immortals, a scholar who failed the examinations, woke from the Yellow Millet Dream and learned inner alchemy from Zhongli Quan. With his demon-slaying sword he roams the world healing, testing and teaching, and he still descends in spirit-writing to instruct his followers.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming period (16th c. CE; Zhao Gongming in the Fengshen yanyi)
primary_sources: Lunar New Year popular prints and liturgies
deities.summary: Caishen, the God of Wealth, is welcomed into every home on the fifth day of the New Year. As the martial Zhao Gongming riding a black tiger he guards and gathers riches; as the civil Bigan or Fan Li he bestows prosperity on the upright.

deities.earliest_attestation: by 6th c. CE; state cult codified 1369 CE (Ming Hongwu)
deities.etymology: 城隍 "wall and dry moat".
deities.summary: Chenghuang, the God of Walls and Moats, is the magistrate of the unseen world for each city. Usually a just official of the past appointed by Heaven, he keeps the registers of the living and dead, arrests wandering ghosts and reports to the courts of the underworld, mirroring the human magistrate who governs by day.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song period (10th–11th c. CE; Guankou cult in Sichuan)
deities.summary: Erlang Shen, the Second Son, is the god with a third eye in his forehead and the Howling Celestial Dog at his side. At Guankou he tamed the floods of the Min River; in heaven he is the warrior who matched Sun Wukong transformation for transformation and captured him.

alternate_names: Dragon Kings of the Four Seas
deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (7th–9th c. CE); imperial titles under the Song
deities.summary: The Dragon Kings rule the Four Seas and every river, lake and well. They bring the rain at Heaven's command, and villagers pray at their temples in drought. Ao Guang of the Eastern Sea, Ao Qin, Ao Run and Ao Shun keep crystal palaces beneath the waves.

deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (1st–2nd c. CE; bronze mirrors and tomb reliefs)
deities.summary: Dongwanggong, King Father of the East, is the yang partner of the Queen Mother of the West. He keeps the registers of the male immortals in the east as she keeps the female immortals in the west; together they balance the cosmos.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 16th c. CE (baojuan "precious scrolls" of Luo Qing's sect, 1509)
primary_sources: Baojuan (precious scrolls) of the Luo and later sectarian traditions
deities.summary: The Eternal Venerable Mother is the unborn source of all souls. Her children fell into the world of dust and forgot their true home; she weeps for them and sends Maitreya and her messengers so that all may return to the True Emptiness Native Land at the end of the age.

primary_sources: Shiji (Basic Annals of the Five Emperors)
deities.summary: Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, is the ancestor of the Chinese people and first of the Five Emperors. He defeated Chiyou at Zhuolu, gave the arts of medicine, the calendar, writing and silk through his ministers and consort, and at the end ascended to heaven on a dragon.

deities.earliest_attestation: Warring States period (4th c. BCE; Mencius)
primary_sources: Shennong bencao jing (Divine Farmer's Materia Medica)
deities.summary: Shennong, the Divine Farmer, taught humanity to plough and sow the five grains. He tasted a hundred herbs in one day, poisoning himself seventy times, to discover which plants heal; his materia medica is the root of Chinese medicine.

Zhurong is the god of fire and of the south, who rides two dragons. At the command of heaven he defeated the water god Gonggong, and in some accounts he separated heaven and earth by cutting the link between gods and mortals.

deities.earliest_attestation: Warring States period (Chuci Tianwen, Zuozhuan, Guoyu); fuller myth in Huainanzi (c. 139 BCE) and Liezi
deities.summary: Gonggong, the red-haired serpent-bodied water god, lost his war with Zhurong and in his fury rammed Mount Buzhou, the pillar of heaven. The sky tilted to the northwest and the earth sank to the southeast, which is why the stars move west and the rivers run east; Nüwa had to mend the broken sky.

Chiyou, horned and bronze-headed, with eighty-one brothers, invented metal weapons and waged war against the Yellow Emperor. At Zhuolu he summoned fog and storms until Huangdi's south-pointing chariot and the drought-goddess Ba defeated him. He was later worshipped as a war god and is honored as an ancestor by the Hmong.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming–Qing period popular scripture and belief
deities.summary: Meng Po waits at the Bridge of Forgetfulness at the end of the ten courts. Before any soul is reborn she gives it her soup of oblivion, so it forgets its past life and enters the next one clean.

alternate_names: Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak
deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (Mount Tai as abode of the dead); imperial title 1011 CE
deities.summary: The Great Emperor of the Eastern Peak lives in Mount Tai, where every soul returns at death. He holds the registers of life and death, oversees the seventy-two (or seventy-six) bureaus of the afterlife and sets the span of each human life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Song period (statue found on Mount Tai, 1008 CE)
deities.summary: Bixia Yuanjun, Sovereign of the Azure Clouds, is the mother goddess of Mount Tai. Women climb her mountain to pray for children and safe births; her attendants include Lady of Eyesight and the goddess who brings sons.

primary_sources: Book of Transformations of Wenchang (Wenchang huashu)
deities.summary: Wenchang, the Emperor-Lord of Literature, is the star-god of culture and examinations. Through seventy-three incarnations he lived as a righteous scholar and official; students pray to him before every examination, and he rewards virtue and learning.

deities.earliest_attestation: Han period (Black Warrior asterism); anthropomorphic Zhenwu from Song
deities.summary: Xuanwu, the Perfected Warrior, rules the north. Once a prince who left the palace to cultivate the Dao on Wudang Mountain, he was raised to heaven and subdued the demon tortoise and snake that now lie beneath his feet. He guards against demons, fire and flood.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tang period (Xu Youguai lu, 9th c. CE)
primary_sources: Xu Youguai lu (Sequel to Records of the Mysterious and Strange)
deities.summary: Yue Lao, the Old Man Under the Moon, binds the ankles of those destined to marry with an invisible red thread. Whatever distance or status separates them, the thread cannot be broken.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ming period as a triad; Shouxing (Canopus) worship from Zhou–Han
deities.summary: The Three Stars are Fu (blessing), Lu (rank and wealth) and Shou (longevity). Shouxing, the Old Man of the South Pole with his tall forehead, peach and staff, is the star Canopus and grants long life; the three stand together on every family altar.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Usa Shrine; Shoku Nihongi, 737 CE)
deities.summary: Hachiman is the kami of archery and war, protector of the nation and guardian of the warrior houses. He is the spirit of Emperor Ōjin, revered with his mother Empress Jingū; the Minamoto clan took him as their ancestral god, and in 781 the court named him a Great Bodhisattva who protects the Buddha's law.

alternate_names: Master of the August Center of Heaven
deities.summary: At the very beginning, when heaven and earth first parted, Ame-no-Minakanushi came into being alone in the Plain of High Heaven and hid his form. He is the first of the kami, the Lord of the Center of Heaven from whom the generative powers unfold.

Takamimusubi, the High Generative Force, is the second of the three primordial kami. With Amaterasu he directs the affairs of the High Plain of Heaven, sends envoys to pacify the land below and commands the descent of his grandson Ninigi.

Kamimusubi, the Divine Generative Force, is the third primordial kami. She revives Ōkuninushi when his brothers kill him, sends the tiny kami Sukunabikona as his partner, and gives the seeds that sprang from the slain food goddess to the world.

Ōkuninushi, Great Master of the Land, healed the White Hare of Inaba, survived death twice at his brothers' hands, endured Susanoo's trials in the underworld and won his daughter. With Sukunabikona he shaped and settled the land, then yielded it to the heavenly kami and withdrew to rule the hidden world from Izumo, where all the kami gather each tenth month to decide human bonds.

Sukunabikona, the tiny kami who came over the sea in a seed-pod boat, is the son of Kamimusubi. He helped Ōkuninushi build the land, taught medicine, hot springs, sake brewing and charms against pests, then left for the Eternal Land across the sea.

deities.earliest_attestation: Heian period (12th c. CE) as a named cult; Hiruko in Kojiki 712
deities.summary: Ebisu, the smiling fisherman with a sea bream under his arm, is the god of fishing, commerce and luck, and the only one of the Seven Lucky Gods native to Japan. At Nishinomiya he is Hiruko, the first child of Izanagi and Izanami, set adrift on the sea in a reed boat, who washed ashore and became the god of fortune.

When Amaterasu hid in the Rock Cave and the world went dark, Ame-no-Uzume danced on an upturned tub, baring herself, until the eight million kami roared with laughter. Curious, Amaterasu looked out, and light returned. Uzume is the ancestress of the shrine dancers and of kagura.

Sarutahiko, the long-nosed, shining kami, stood at the eight-way crossroads of heaven and earth to guide Ninigi down to the land. He is the god of roads, crossings and new beginnings, the leader who goes first, married to Ame-no-Uzume.

Takemikazuchi, the Brave Thunder kami born from the blood on Izanagi's sword, was sent down to demand that Ōkuninushi yield the land. Sitting cross-legged on the point of his sword planted in the waves, he defeated the strongest of Ōkuninushi's sons and secured the country for heaven. At Kashima he pins down the giant catfish that causes earthquakes.

Kagutsuchi, kami of fire, burned his mother Izanami as he was born, and she died of it. In grief and rage Izanagi cut his son apart; from his blood and body sprang thunder, mountain and sword kami. Fire is revered at Atago and Akiba shrines, where people pray for protection against blazes.

Ninigi, grandson of Amaterasu, descended from heaven to Mount Takachiho bearing the mirror, the sword and the jewel, and founded the line of the emperors. Choosing the beautiful Konohanasakuya-hime over her sister Iwanaga-hime, he made the lives of his descendants brief as blossoms.

Kinmamon is the highest god of the Ryukyu kingdom, who comes from Nirai Kanai beyond the sea and from the heavens. He descends at the sacred groves (utaki) to bless the king and the land, and speaks through the priestesses (noro and kikoe-ōgimi).

Shinerikyu is the male partner of Amamikyu. Sent down by the Lord of Heaven, the two built the islands of Ryukyu from stones, earth and plants, and from them came the first people, the ruling lines, the priestesses and the farmers.

Kamuy Fuchi, the Fire Grandmother, lives in every hearth and never leaves it. She is the first to receive every prayer, carries the family's words and offerings to the other kamuy, watches over the household and judges the conduct of its members.

Okikurmi, born of a kamuy and a human, came down to the Ainu homeland to teach people to hunt, fish, weave and pray properly. He defeated demons and monsters, and when the people became ungrateful he left for the land of the kamuy.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th c. CE (Asuka-period images; Hōryū-ji Guze Kannon)
deities.summary: Kannon is the bodhisattva who hears the cries of the world. In thirty-three forms, with eleven faces and a thousand arms, Kannon answers whoever calls the name, saving from fire, flood, bandits and the sorrows of birth and death. Pilgrims walk the thirty-three temples of the Saigoku route to meet each form.

Jizō, the monk-bodhisattva with staff and jewel, walks the six realms to save beings. He guards children, travellers and the dead; at the riverbank of Sai in the underworld he shelters children who died young from the demons and hides them in his sleeves.

Great King Enma judges the dead. Before his throne every soul's deeds are read from the scrolls and shown in the crystal mirror, and he assigns it to its realm of rebirth. In Japan he is the hidden face of Jizō: the stern judge and the compassionate saviour are one.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Konkōmyō-kyō / Golden Light Sutra transmission)
deities.summary: Benzaiten, goddess of flowing water, music, eloquence, wisdom and wealth, plays the biwa at Enoshima, Chikubushima and Itsukushima. She is the only goddess among the Seven Lucky Gods; as Uga-Benzaiten she wears a white serpent with an old man's head in her crown.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 9th c. CE (introduced with Tendai by Saichō)
primary_sources: Japanese Tendai and Shingon ritual manuals
deities.summary: Daikokuten stands on rice bales with his mallet of luck and his sack of treasures. Once the fierce black protector of the monastery kitchen, he became the smiling god of the harvest, wealth and the household, one of the Seven Lucky Gods; he is also honored as Ōkuninushi.

deities.earliest_attestation: 7th c. CE (Shitennō-ji, founded 593 CE; Hōryū-ji guardians)
deities.summary: Bishamonten, armored and holding a spear and a small pagoda, is the guardian king of the north and the most powerful of the Four Heavenly Kings. He protects the Dharma and the realm, gives victory to righteous warriors, and as one of the Seven Lucky Gods bestows wealth.

primary_sources: Āgama / Nikāya accounts of Brahmā's request (Japanese canon)
deities.summary: Bonten, lord of the Brahma heavens, is one of the twelve guardian devas. When the Buddha awoke and hesitated to teach, it was Bonten who descended and begged him to turn the wheel of the Dharma; he stands with Taishakuten as the Buddha's chief protector.

primary_sources: Japanese Buddhist canon (Śakra in the Āgamas and Jātakas)
deities.summary: Taishakuten rules the Heaven of the Thirty-Three on the summit of Mount Sumeru, holding the vajra. Lord of the devas and of the Four Heavenly Kings, he protects the Buddha and his followers and records the good and bad deeds of beings.

Tenjin is Sugawara no Michizane, the great scholar-statesman exiled to Dazaifu on false charges, where he died in 903. His angry spirit struck the capital with lightning, plague and death until the court restored his honors and enshrined him as a god. Now he is the patron of learning, calligraphy and examinations.
deities.tradition_claim: Enshrined at Kitano Tenman-gū and Dazaifu Tenman-gū; Tenjin worship spans Shinto and Buddhist practice.

deities.earliest_attestation: 10th c. CE (Chinese monk Budai, d. 916 CE); Japanese cult Muromachi period
primary_sources: Jingde Chuandeng lu (Transmission of the Lamp, 1004)
deities.summary: Hotei, the fat, laughing wandering monk with his cloth sack, was the Chinese monk Budai. At his death he revealed that he was Maitreya, the future Buddha, walking unrecognized among people. He brings contentment, abundance and the joy of children.

primary_sources: Shichifukujin popular prints and temple circuits
deities.summary: Fukurokuju, with his towering forehead, staff and scroll, embodies happiness, prosperity and long life together; his name joins the three. He is the Southern Star sage, accompanied by a crane or tortoise.

primary_sources: Shichifukujin popular prints and temple circuits
deities.summary: Jurōjin, the old man of longevity, walks with a staff hung with a scroll recording the lifespans of all beings and is followed by a deer. He grants long and healthy life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Muromachi–Edo period (15th–17th c. CE; group fixed by c. 17th c.)
deities.summary: The Seven Lucky Gods, Ebisu, Daikokuten, Bishamonten, Benzaiten, Fukurokuju, Jurōjin and Hotei, sail into port on the treasure ship (takarabune) at New Year. Gathered from Japan, India and China, together they bring every kind of good fortune.

deities.earliest_attestation: vernacular Korean term; written attestation 18th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Hananim, the Lord of Heaven, is the highest being in Korean belief, the one Heaven who sees everything, sends rain, rewards the good and decides fate. People turn to Haneullim when all lesser spirits fail.

Hwanin, the Lord of Heaven, saw that his son Hwanung longed for the world of humans. He gave him three heavenly seals and three thousand followers and sent him down to Mount Taebaek, where his grandson Dangun founded Gojoseon.

A bear and a tiger begged Hwanung to become human. He gave them mugwort and garlic and told them to stay out of the sun for a hundred days. The tiger fled; the bear endured and became a woman, Ungnyeo, who prayed for a child and bore Dangun, father of the Korean nation.

deities.earliest_attestation: Three Kingdoms period (mountain cults); Samguk yusa (1281)
deities.summary: Sanshin, the Mountain Spirit, is the lord of each mountain, usually an old sage with a white beard seated beside a tiger under a pine. Every Korean Buddhist temple has a shrine to him. He grants sons, long life and protection, and Dangun himself became the mountain god of Asadal.

deities.etymology: 竈王 (Jowang), the Korean reading of the Chinese Zaowang, "Kitchen King".
deities.summary: Jowangsin, the kitchen goddess, lives by the hearth, honored with a bowl of fresh water placed each morning. She guards the family's food and fire and its fortunes.

primary_sources: Barigongju muga (shaman song of the Jinogwi-gut)
deities.summary: Bari, the seventh daughter thrown away by her royal father for being another girl, was raised in the wild. When her parents fell mortally ill, only she would journey to the end of the world and the land of the dead to fetch the water of life. She served nine years, returned, revived them, and became the goddess who guides the dead and the ancestor of the shamans.
Seongju, the guardian of the house, lives in the main beam. He protects the household and its head; when a house is built or the family moves, the shaman performs the Seongju gut to install him.

primary_sources: Shaman songs of the afterlife journey
deities.summary: Yeomra Daewang, the great king of the underworld, judges the dead in the fifth of the ten courts. Shamans sing the soul's journey to his court, and the living make offerings so that he will judge kindly.
Seonangsin guards the village boundary and the mountain pass, honored at a cairn of stones and a sacred tree tied with cloth. Travellers add a stone and bow as they pass, asking for safe passage.

deities.earliest_attestation: 15th c. CE (Lĩnh Nam chích quái; Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, 1479)
primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
deities.summary: Lạc Long Quân, the Dragon Lord of Lạc, son of Kinh Dương Vương and a dragon princess of the sea, rid the land of monsters and taught the people to farm rice, cook and wear clothes. He married the mountain fairy Âu Cơ; their hundred sons are the ancestors of the Vietnamese, and the eldest became the first Hùng King.

primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
deities.summary: Âu Cơ, a fairy of the high mountains, married the Dragon Lord and laid a sac of a hundred eggs from which a hundred sons hatched. She led fifty of them into the mountains; she is the mother of the Vietnamese people, honored at the Hùng Temple festival.

deities.earliest_attestation: late 16th–17th c. CE cult; Vân Cát thần nữ truyện (18th c.)
primary_sources: Vân Cát thần nữ truyện (Đoàn Thị Điểm, 18th c.)
deities.summary: Liễu Hạnh, the second daughter of the Jade Emperor, broke a jade cup in heaven and was sent down to earth. She lived human lives, loved, wrote poetry, and returned again and again by her own will, until the court recognized her as a goddess. She is the foremost of the Four Immortals and the Holy Mother at the head of the Mother Goddess religion.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th–17th c. CE (Đạo Mẫu formation); recognized as UNESCO intangible heritage 2016
deities.summary: The Four Palaces are the realms of the Mother Goddess religion: Heaven (Thiên phủ, red), Mountains and Forests (Nhạc phủ, green), Waters (Thoải phủ, white) and Earth (Địa phủ, yellow). Each is ruled by a Holy Mother with her mandarins, ladies, princes and princesses, who descend in turn into the mediums during lên đồng.

alternate_names: Mother of the Mountains and Forests
deities.summary: Mẫu Thượng Ngàn rules the mountains and forests, dressed in green. She protects the hill peoples, the animals and the forest, and grants healing herbs and prosperity to those who serve her.
Mẫu Thoải, the white-robed Mother of the Water Palace, is the daughter of the Dragon King. She governs rivers, seas and rain and protects those who live by and travel on the water.

A boy of Phù Đổng who did not speak or walk for three years rose up when the Ân invaders came. He asked for an iron horse, iron armor and an iron staff, grew into a giant, drove out the enemy, and rode his horse up Sóc Sơn mountain into heaven.

deities.earliest_attestation: early 14th c. CE (d. 1300; Kiếp Bạc temple)
primary_sources: Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
Hịch tướng sĩ (Proclamation to the Officers, 1284)
deities.summary: Trần Hưng Đạo, the general who defeated the Mongol invasions three times, was deified after his death as Đức Thánh Trần. He commands the spirit armies against demons and disease; mediums and exorcists invoke him, and his seal drives out evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: folk practice; attested in Lê–Nguyễn period sources
primary_sources: Folk legend of the three Táo (two husbands, one wife)
deities.summary: The Táo Quân are three kitchen gods, two men and a woman, who live in the hearth. On the 23rd day of the twelfth month they ride a carp to heaven to report the family's deeds to the Jade Emperor, and the family sends them off with offerings and paper hats.

Sơn Tinh, the Spirit of Mount Tản Viên, won the hand of the Hùng King's daughter Mỵ Nương by arriving first with the bride-price. When the Water Spirit attacked in revenge, Sơn Tinh raised the mountains higher than the floods, and he defeats him every year. He is one of the Four Immortals.
Thủy Tinh, the Water Spirit, arrived too late to win Mỵ Nương. In rage he raised storms and floods against Sơn Tinh, and every year in the monsoon he attacks again and is beaten back.

deities.earliest_attestation: 17th–18th c. CE (Vietnamese adoption of the Po Nagar cult at Nha Trang)
primary_sources: Tháp Bà Po Nagar temple tradition
deities.summary: Thiên Y A Na, the Holy Mother of Heaven, came to the land as a girl on a floating log of agarwood, taught the people agriculture and weaving, and departed riding a crane. Her temple at Nha Trang draws pilgrims from all central Vietnam.

deities.earliest_attestation: Lê dynasty (15th c. CE) royal investiture of village gods
deities.etymology: Sino-Vietnamese reading of 城隍 (Chinese Chenghuang).
deities.summary: Every Vietnamese village has its Thành Hoàng, the guardian spirit enshrined in the communal house (đình). He may be a culture hero, a founding ancestor or a nature spirit, appointed by royal patent; he protects the village, and his festival is the high point of its year.

primary_sources: Juan de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)
Pedro Chirino, Relación de las Islas Filipinas (1604)
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit bhaṭṭāra / bhaṭṭāraka, "noble lord", via Malay/Old Javanese batara.
deities.summary: Bathala, the Maker of All (Maykapal), is the supreme god of the Tagalogs, creator of earth and of humankind, who governs all things from the sky. He is honored through the anito, the lesser spirits and ancestors who carry offerings and requests to him.

primary_sources: Juan de Plasencia, Customs of the Tagalogs (1589)
Pedro Chirino, Relación de las Islas Filipinas (1604)
San Buenaventura, Vocabulario de lengua tagala (1613)
deities.summary: Lakapati is the Tagalog deity of fertility and cultivated fields, invoked at planting with offerings so the land will bear and the people will not hunger. Lakapati joins male and female in one being.

Mayari, the moon goddess, daughter of Bathala, fought her brother Apolaki for rule of the world after their father's death. Apolaki struck out one of her eyes, which is why the moon is dimmer than the sun; reconciled, the two now share the sky, day and night.
Apolaki, the sun god and warrior, son of Bathala, is patron of war and of warriors. He fought his sister Mayari for the throne of heaven, then agreed to divide the sky with her.
Tala is the goddess of the stars and the morning and evening star, daughter of Bathala, who lights the way of travellers before the dawn.

Sitan is the guardian of Kasamaan, the realm of the dead and of misfortune. Four agents serve him, the Manggagaway who brings disease, the Manisilat who breaks families, the Mangkukulam who works fire-sorcery and the Hukloban who can kill with a gesture, leading people to ruin.

deities.earliest_attestation: 1582 CE (Miguel de Loarca, Relación de las Islas Filipinas)
deities.summary: Kaptan is the high god of the sky in the Visayan account of origins. His quarrel with Maguayen, lord of the sea, set sky and sea against each other, and the islands appeared between them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Spanish-era Visayan accounts (17th c.); living oral tradition
deities.summary: Bakunawa, the great sea serpent, rises from the ocean to swallow the moon. In the beginning there were seven moons, and it swallowed six; when it tries to devour the last, people beat gongs and pots to make it spit the moon out. Its appearance marks eclipses.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese/Balinese term; formalized as supreme God from 1959 (Parisada Hindu Dharma)
primary_sources: Parisada Hindu Dharma Indonesia doctrinal texts
deities.summary: Sang Hyang Widhi Wasa, the Absolute Divine Order, is the one God of Balinese Hinduism, of whom all the gods are manifestations. As Acintya, the Unthinkable, he is depicted dancing in flames on the empty throne of the padmasana shrine, beyond all form.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 15th–16th c. CE (Tantu Panggelaran); earlier Old Javanese Shaiva texts
deities.summary: Batara Guru, Lord Shiva as the divine teacher, rules the heaven of Jonggringsaloka over all the gods of the wayang. He commanded that Java be fixed in place by moving the peak of Mount Mahameru onto it, and he decides the fate of gods and men.

deities.earliest_attestation: Majapahit-era temple reliefs (14th–15th c. CE); Javanese wayang
deities.summary: Semar is the squat, pot-bellied servant of the Pandawa heroes, comic and rude, yet he is the god Sang Hyang Ismaya, elder brother of Batara Guru, sent to earth in humble form to guard and guide the righteous. When the gods go wrong, Semar alone can rebuke them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Tantu Panggelaran and Javanese/Sundanese folk texts
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit Śrī, the goddess of fortune (Lakṣmī).
