deities.summary: Dewi Sri is the rice goddess of Java and Bali. In the Sundanese tale she was a divine child who died young, and from her buried body sprang rice, coconut and the other food plants. Every harvest begins and ends with offerings to her, and she guards the granary.

primary_sources: Yogyakarta and Surakarta court ritual (Bedhaya Ketawang)
deities.summary: Kanjeng Ratu Kidul, Queen of the Southern Ocean, rules the spirits beneath the waves of the Indian Ocean. She took Panembahan Senopati, founder of Mataram, as her consort and promised to protect his descendants; the sultans of Yogyakarta and Surakarta are her spiritual husbands. Swimmers on the south coast avoid wearing green, her color.

deities.earliest_attestation: Calon Arang text (16th c. CE lontar); Balinese ritual drama
deities.summary: Rangda, the widow-witch queen of the leyak, haunts the graveyard with long tongue, tusks and claws. In the ritual drama she battles the Barong, entrancing the kris dancers to turn their blades on themselves; the Barong's power makes them invulnerable. Rangda is feared and also worshipped as a protector, for her power repels lesser evils.

deities.earliest_attestation: Balinese ritual tradition (attested in colonial-era records; much older)
deities.summary: The Barong, a lion-like protector spirit animated by two dancers, is the king of the good spirits and guardian of the village. In the eternal battle with Rangda neither wins, for good and evil must stay in balance.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Javanese and Balinese wayang
deities.etymology: From Sanskrit Ananta-bhoga, "endless coils", the serpent Ananta.
deities.summary: Antaboga, the great world-serpent, lives in the deepest level of the underworld (Saptapratala) and supports the earth. In meditation he made the World Turtle Bedawang, on whom the world rests, and in one Javanese telling his tears became the jewel from which Dewi Sri was born.

deities.earliest_attestation: Old Javanese period; Murwakala ruwatan texts
primary_sources: Javanese and Balinese temple gate reliefs (kala heads)
deities.summary: Batara Kala, the giant born from Batara Guru's spilled seed in the sea, is time the devourer. Batara Guru granted him the right to eat certain people, the sukerta, born in unlucky circumstances; in the ruwatan ceremony the puppeteer recites the sacred words that free them from his hunger. His fanged face guards temple gateways.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ngaju oral chants; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
deities.summary: Ranying Hatalla Langit, the supreme god of the Upperworld, is the hornbill whose union and battle with the Watersnake Jata created the cosmos and humanity. He is the source of life and order, the god to whom Kaharingan prayer ultimately goes.

deities.earliest_attestation: Ngaju oral chants; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
deities.summary: Jata, the Watersnake of the Underworld, is the female counterpart of Mahatala. The two are one divine totality divided into above and below; from their cosmic encounter came the world, and every ritual reunites them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Batak oral tradition and pustaha; recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: Mulajadi na Bolon, the Great Origin, is the supreme creator of the Batak. He dwells in the highest upperworld and created the three gods Batara Guru, Soripada and Mangalabulan, who rule the world; his daughter Si Boru Deak Parujar descended and formed the middle world on which humans live.

primary_sources: Penang and Malacca keramat shrine traditions
deities.summary: A Datuk Keramat is a holy guardian spirit, often a Muslim saint, a pious ancestor or the spirit of a place, who dwells at a tree, rock or tomb and protects the land around it. Malays and Chinese alike leave offerings of flowers, fruit and betel at his small shrine; he never accepts pork.

primary_sources: Burmese royal chronicles (Maha Yazawin; Hmannan Yazawin)
deities.summary: Thagyamin, King of the Nats, rules the Tavatimsa heaven and heads the official pantheon of the Thirty-Seven Nats. Each Thingyan (New Year) water festival marks his descent to earth for three days, when he records the good and bad deeds of people in golden and dog-skin books.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (official list traditionally fixed under King Anawrahta)
primary_sources: Burmese royal chronicles (Maha Yazawin; Hmannan Yazawin)
Taungbyone and Mount Popa festival traditions
deities.summary: The Thirty-Seven Nats are the official spirits of the Burmese realm, most of them humans who died violent, untimely deaths, wronged by kings, and became powerful spirits. King Anawrahta set them under Thagyamin to serve the Buddha's religion; spirit mediums (nat kadaw) dance them into presence at the great festivals.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th c. CE (Thirty-Seven Nats list); legend set in Tagaung period
deities.summary: Min Mahagiri, the Lord of the Great Mountain, was the blacksmith Maung Tint De, so strong that the king of Tagaung feared him. The king lured him with a promise to his sister and burned him alive beneath a saga tree; his sister leapt into the flames. Brother and sister became nats, enshrined at Mount Popa, and every Burmese household keeps a coconut for Mahagiri, guardian of the home.

deities.earliest_attestation: Pagan period legend (11th c. CE setting); chronicles
deities.summary: Me Wunna, a flower-eating ogress of Mount Popa, loved Byatta, King Anawrahta's flower-gatherer, and bore him the two Taungbyone brothers. After Byatta was executed, she died of grief and became Popa Medaw, Mother of Popa, the great nat of the mountain.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th–15th c. CE (mainland Southeast Asian Buddhist art; Pathamasambodhi)
primary_sources: Pathamasambodhi (Southeast Asian life of the Buddha)
iconography: kneeling woman wringing her long hair
deities.summary: When Mara challenged the Buddha-to-be beneath the Bodhi tree, he touched the earth to call a witness. Mae Thorani rose and wrung from her long hair the waters of all the merit he had poured out over countless lives; the flood swept Mara's army away. She is the goddess of the earth and of water offerings.

deities.earliest_attestation: late 13th c. CE (Ram Khamhaeng inscription, 1292: Phra Khaphung Phi)
primary_sources: Tai and Lao household and village ritual
deities.summary: Phi are the spirits that live in the land, the house, the village, the forest and the sky. The guardian of the land (chao thi) lives in the spirit house set before every home and building, receiving daily food, flowers and incense; village and ancestor phi protect the community, while wandering phi of the bad dead must be kept away.

deities.earliest_attestation: Tai/Lao folk ritual; recorded in Thai literary and court rites
primary_sources: Thai and Lao rice-planting and harvest rites
deities.summary: Mae Phosop, the Rice Mother, lives in the rice plant and its grain and holds its khwan (soul). Farmers make offerings to her when the rice is pregnant with grain and at harvest, and call back her soul so that the rice will return the next year.

deities.earliest_attestation: Lao/Thai oral tradition; Buddhist naga lore
primary_sources: Naga fireball (Bang Fai Phaya Nak) festival tradition
deities.summary: Phaya Nak, the naga king, lives in the Mekong and rules its waters. He protects the Buddha's relics and the river people; at the end of Buddhist Lent, fireballs rise from the Mekong where the nagas celebrate the Buddha's return from heaven.

deities.earliest_attestation: Khmer oral and shrine tradition (pre-Angkorian roots)
primary_sources: Khmer village shrine (khtom neak ta) traditions
deities.summary: Neak Ta are the ancestral guardian spirits of the Khmer land, each attached to a place, a stone, a tree, a termite mound or a village. They are the true owners of the ground, honored at small shrines and consulted through mediums before planting, building or traveling.

deities.earliest_attestation: 8th c. CE (Po Nagar temple inscriptions, Nha Trang)
primary_sources: Cham and Sanskrit inscriptions of the Po Nagar temple
deities.summary: Po Nagar, Mother of the Kingdom, created the land of Champa, its eaglewood and rice. The Sanskrit inscriptions of her tower-temple at Nha Trang honor her as Bhagavatī, the Goddess, a form of Shiva's consort; she is still worshipped by the Cham as the mother of their people.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Tangaroa, son of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, is the atua of the sea and of all that lives in it. When Tāne separated their parents, Tangaroa's children fled; the fish went to the sea with him and the reptiles to the forest with Tāne, and ever since sea and land have fought. Fishermen return the first catch to Tangaroa.

primary_sources: Māori whare wānanga traditions as published in the 19th–early 20th c.
deities.summary: Whiro, lord of darkness, opposed Tāne at every step. Defeated when Tāne ascended to the uppermost heaven to bring down the baskets of knowledge, Whiro withdrew to the underworld, from where he sends disease and death to consume the bodies of humans.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Tāwhirimātea, atua of winds and storms, alone opposed the separation of Earth and Sky. In rage he followed his father Ranginui into the sky and sent his children, the winds and clouds, to tear down Tāne's forests and whip up Tangaroa's seas. He still makes war on his brothers.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Haumia-tiketike is the atua of wild food plants, especially the bracken fern root (aruhe). He hid in his mother's body from Tāwhirimātea's storm, but his hair showed above the ground and Tū found him and made his children food.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Rūaumoko, the youngest child of Ranginui and Papatūānuku, was still unborn at the separation. When the brothers turned their mother face-down so she would not grieve to see her husband, Rūaumoko was left at her breast within the earth for warmth; his stirring makes the earthquakes and volcanic fire.

primary_sources: George Grey (ed.), Ko nga Mahinga a nga Tupuna Maori (1854)
deities.summary: Mahuika, the fire goddess who keeps fire in her fingernails, lives in the underworld. When Māui put out all the fires of the world and came to her, she gave him nail after nail until, angry at his trickery, she set the world ablaze. Before the last flame died she threw her final nail into the trees, which is why fire can be drawn from wood.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Kanaloa, god of the ocean depths, of voyaging and of healing, travels with Kāne; together they open springs of fresh water by striking the earth with a staff and drink ʻawa wherever they go. Kahoʻolawe is his island, and the octopus is one of his bodies.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Haumea, goddess of birth and fertility, is the mother of Pele, Hiʻiaka and many gods. She taught women to give birth through the body, possesses the magic stick Makalei that draws fish, and renews herself by returning as a young woman generation after generation.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Milu rules Lua-o-Milu, the underworld beneath the earth, entered through openings at the edges of the islands such as Waipiʻo. Souls who have no ʻaumakua to guide them to the realm of their ancestors fall into his domain.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Wākea, the Sky Father, mated with Papahānaumoku, Earth Mother, and from them came the islands of Hawaiʻi. From Wākea and Hoʻohōkūkalani came the taro plant Hāloa and the first chief, ancestor of the Hawaiian people; the ali'i trace their genealogy to him.

primary_sources: Samuel M. Kamakau, Ka Poʻe Kahiko
deities.summary: Papahānaumoku, Papa who gives birth to islands, is the Earth Mother. From her union with Wākea she bore the islands of Hawaiʻi; she is the foundation on which all life stands.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Kamapuaʻa, the pig-man god of rain, fertile wetlands and sexual vigor, is a shape-changer who can be a man, a pig, a fish or a plant. He courted Pele and fought her, rain against fire, until the land was divided between them: the wet windward side his, the dry volcanic lands hers.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Poliʻahu, goddess of snow, lives on the summit of Mauna Kea in her white mantle. She defeated Pele in a contest at the hōlua sledding race; when Pele sent fire, Poliʻahu covered the mountain in snow and froze the lava.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded 19th c. CE (Hawaiian-language newspapers)
deities.summary: Hiʻiaka, youngest and favorite sister of Pele, carried as an egg in Pele's bosom, is goddess of the hula, of healing and of the ʻōhiʻa forests. Sent by Pele to fetch her lover Lohiʻau, she journeyed through all the islands, slaying moʻo monsters and reviving Lohiʻau from death.

primary_sources: Fornander Collection of Hawaiian Antiquities and Folk-Lore
deities.summary: Kamohoaliʻi, elder brother of Pele and king of the sharks, guided Pele's canoe to Hawaiʻi. He protects fishermen and voyagers and can take human or shark form; families who have the shark as ʻaumakua are under his care.

primary_sources: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)
deities.summary: Hikuleʻo rules Pulotu, the paradise and underworld of the Tongan chiefs. When the souls of the high-born arrive, Hikuleʻo receives them. In the Tongan division of the cosmos, Tangaloa holds the sky, Maui the earth and Hikuleʻo the realm below.

primary_sources: George Turner, Samoa a Hundred Years Ago and Long Before (1884)
deities.summary: Saveasiʻuleo, with the upper body of a man and the tail of an eel or fish, rules Pulotu, the Samoan realm of the dead beneath the sea. He is the father of the war goddess Nafanua.

Nafanua, war goddess and daughter of Saveasiʻuleo, rose from Pulotu to free her people of Falealupo from oppression. Covering her breasts with leaves so she would be taken for a man, she won the war and became the supreme authority in Samoa, granting the four paramount titles; she foretold that a new rule would come from the sky.

primary_sources: E. W. Gifford, Tongan Myths and Tales (1924)
deities.summary: Tangaloa ʻEitumatupuʻa came down from the sky by a great ironwood tree and fathered with a mortal woman ʻAhoʻeitu, the first Tuʻi Tonga, sacred king of Tonga. Tangaloa Tufunga, the carpenter, cast down chips from his workshop in the sky that became islands.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded late 18th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Taʻaroa existed alone in his shell (Rumia) in the endless darkness. He broke out, made the shell the dome of the sky and the earth, and from his own body made the world: his spine the mountains, his flesh the soil, his guts the clouds, his blood the red of sunsets. He created the gods and all things; Taʻaroa is the ancestor of all.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Taputapuātea marae at Raʻiātea (pre-contact); recorded late 18th c. CE
deities.summary: ʻOro, son of Taʻaroa, is god of war, whose cult spread from the great marae Taputapuātea on Raʻiātea across the Society Islands. Human sacrifices were offered to him in war; in peace he is ʻOro of the laid-down spear, and his worship founded the ʻArioi society of performers and priests.

deities.earliest_attestation: Rapa Nui oral tradition; petroglyphs at ʻOrongo; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
primary_sources: Katherine Routledge, The Mystery of Easter Island (1919)
deities.summary: Makemake, creator of humanity and god of fertility, is patron of the Tangata Manu (Birdman) cult at ʻOrongo. Each year he brought the sooty terns to the islet of Motu Nui; the man whose servant first returned with an egg became the sacred Birdman for the year.

primary_sources: E. S. C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (1930)
deities.summary: Tanaoa is primordial darkness and the lord of the sea. In the beginning there was only Tanaoa and his companion Mutu-hei, silence; then Atea, light, rose up and drove out Tanaoa, and Ono, sound, broke the silence. Tanaoa remains god of the ocean and the winds.

primary_sources: E. S. C. Handy, Marquesan Legends (1930)
deities.summary: Atea is light, who rose against primordial darkness and became the sky. With his wife Atanua, the dawn, he fathered the gods and the first people of the Marquesas.

primary_sources: W. W. Gill, Myths and Songs from the South Pacific (1876)
deities.summary: Vari-ma-te-takere, the Very Beginning, lives at the bottom of the coconut-shell universe in a space so narrow her knees touch her chin. From her own body she plucked her children, Vatea and the other gods, who rose to fill the levels above.

primary_sources: Ulithi and central Carolinian oral tradition
deities.summary: Lugeilan, son of the sky god Anulap, is the sky god of knowledge. He came down to earth, took a mortal wife and fathered the trickster Olifat.

primary_sources: Ulithi and central Carolinian oral tradition
William Lessa, Tales from Ulithi Atoll (1961)
deities.summary: Olifat, son of Lugeilan and a mortal woman, is the trickster of the Carolines. He climbed to heaven on a column of smoke to find his father, survived every attempt of the gods to kill him, gave sharks their teeth and stingrays their stings, and brought fire to humanity by sending a bird to carry it.

deities.earliest_attestation: Chamorro oral tradition; recorded 17th c. CE (Spanish mission accounts)
primary_sources: Spanish mission accounts of the Mariana Islands (17th c.)
deities.summary: Puntan, the first being, before he died asked his sister Fuʻuna to make the world from his body. His eyes became the sun and moon, his eyebrows the rainbows, his breast the sky and his back the earth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Chamorro oral tradition; recorded 17th c. CE (Spanish mission accounts)
primary_sources: Spanish mission accounts of the Mariana Islands (17th c.)
deities.summary: Fuʻuna, sister of Puntan, made the world from her brother's body as he asked. Then she turned herself into the rock at Laso Fuʻa in Humåtak, Guam, from which the first human beings came.

primary_sources: Thomas Williams, Fiji and the Fijians (1858)
deities.summary: Degei, the great serpent god of Fiji, lives in a cave in the Nakauvadra range. He hatched the first humans from eggs laid by a hawk and taught them to grow food. When he turns over, the earth quakes; the souls of the dead pass before him on their way to the afterlife, and he decides their fate.

Dakuwaqa, the shark god, guards the reefs and the fishermen of Fiji. He fought every guardian god of the islands until the guardian of Kadavu, a giant octopus, defeated him; he promised in return to protect the people of Kadavu from sharks forever.

Marawa, the spider-friend of Qat in the Banks Islands, also carved people from wood. When he buried his figures and dug them up, they had rotted; so Marawa brought death into the world, while Qat's people lived.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded early 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Tolai (Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain) oral tradition as recorded by missionaries (early 20th c.)
deities.summary: To Kabinana and his foolish brother To Purgo were made by their father drawing two figures on the ground. Everything To Kabinana does is clever and good: he made the useful things, the good fish and the fertile land.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; recorded early 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Tolai (Gazelle Peninsula, New Britain) oral tradition as recorded by missionaries (early 20th c.)
deities.summary: To Purgo (also called To Karvuvu) is the foolish twin who gets everything wrong. Trying to imitate his brother he made the shark, which devours fish and people, and his mistakes brought death, hardship and darkness into the world.

primary_sources: A. W. Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
deities.summary: Daramulan, a sky being of the Yuin and neighboring peoples, presides over the initiation of young men. His voice is the sound of the bullroarer; in some southeastern accounts he is the son or the one-legged companion of Baiame, and he watches from the sky to see that the law is kept.

primary_sources: A. W. Howitt, The Native Tribes of South-East Australia (1904)
deities.summary: Waa the Crow is one of the two great moiety ancestors of the Kulin nations, counterpart of Bunjil the Eaglehawk. Clever and cunning, Waa obtained fire for the people from the women who kept it hidden.

Ngurunderi, the great ancestor of the Ngarrindjeri, chased the giant Murray cod Ponde down the river, and the fish's thrashing carved the Murray's course. Pursuing his runaway wives, he shaped the lakes and coast of the Coorong, then crossed to Kangaroo Island and went up into the sky, where he can be seen in the Milky Way.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 19th–20th c. CE
primary_sources: Worrorra, Ngarinyin and Wunambal rock-shelter paintings
iconography: white face with eyes and nose, no mouth
deities.summary: The Wandjina are the creator beings of the cloud and rain who came from the sea and sky in the Lalai (creation time), shaped the land, gave the law and finally lay down in rock shelters, where they left their images. They have no mouths; their power is expressed directly. When the paintings are refreshed, the rains and the increase of life continue.

primary_sources: W. Lloyd Warner, A Black Civilization (1937)
deities.summary: Yurlunggur (Wititj), the great Olive Python of the Yolngu, lives in the sacred waterhole Mirrarrmina. When the Wawilak Sisters camped there, he rose, brought the monsoon storm and flood, and swallowed them; his rising and falling is the coming of the wet season.

primary_sources: W. Lloyd Warner, A Black Civilization (1937)
deities.summary: The two Wawilak Sisters journeyed north across Arnhem Land, naming the plants, animals and places. At the waterhole of the great python they were swallowed in the monsoon storm and later regurgitated; their journey founded important ceremonies and the order of the seasons.

alternate_names: Rainbow Serpent of West Arnhem Land
deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 20th c. CE
primary_sources: Kunwinjku rock art and bark painting
deities.summary: Ngalyod, the Rainbow Serpent of the Kunwinjku, is a creator being who shaped the land and its waterholes in the creation time. She lives in deep pools; she punishes those who break the law by flood or by swallowing them, and she brings the rains and fertility.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity; recorded 20th c. CE
iconography: band of lightning arcing around the body
stone axes on head, elbows and knees
deities.summary: Namarrkon, the Lightning Man, brings the storms of the wet season. Stone axes on his head, elbows and knees strike the clouds to make thunder and lightning; his children are the bright orange-and-blue Leichhardt's grasshoppers that appear before the storms.

The Waagal is the serpent creator of the Noongar people, whose winding path across the land made the rivers, lakes and hills of the southwest, among them the Swan River (Derbarl Yerrigan). The Waagal remains in the deep waters and springs and protects them.

deities.earliest_attestation: rock art of considerable antiquity (Arnhem Land paintings); term coined 1926
primary_sources: Arnhem Land and Kimberley rock art
A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, "The Rainbow-Serpent Myth of Australia" (Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, 1926)
deities.summary: Across Australia, great serpent beings associated with water, rain and the rainbow shaped the land in the creation period and still live in deep waterholes. They give fertility and rain, and they punish those who break the law. Each Country knows its own serpent by its own name: Wunggurr, Ngalyod, Yurlunggur, Waagal and many more.

primary_sources: T. G. H. Strehlow, Aranda Traditions (1947)
deities.summary: Karora, the great bandicoot ancestor, lay asleep beneath the soil at Ilbalintja in the Dreaming. From his navel a sacred pole rose to the sky; from his armpit bandicoots emerged, and later his sons came from his body. When his work was done he returned to rest beneath the waters of the soak.

primary_sources: Charles P. Mountford, The Tiwi: Their Art, Myth and Ceremony (1958)
deities.summary: Purukupali's infant son Jinani died while his mother Bima neglected him for Japara, the moon man. In grief and anger Purukupali refused Japara's offer to revive the child, declaring that from then on all must die and never return. He walked into the sea with his son's body, and the first pukumani mortuary ceremony was held.

primary_sources: Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. 6 (1908)
deities.summary: Bomai came to Mer (Murray Island) from the west in the form of an octopus and other beings, and became known as Malo. Malo brought the law of the Meriam: respect for others' land and gardens, care for the people. "Malo's law" governs land tenure on Mer to this day and was cited in the Mabo case.

deities.etymology: Sumerian; Suen is the older form that became Akkadian Sîn
deities.summary: The Moon god of Ur, firstborn of Enlil and Ninlil, conceived in the netherworld and raised to the sky. He sails the heavens in his crescent boat, measures the months, and brings the herds and the rising waters. His daughter Inanna and son Utu are the Evening Star and the Sun; his high priestess at Ur was Enheduanna.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2500 BCE (Early Dynastic king list as antediluvian king)
deities.etymology: Sumerian dumu-zid, 'faithful/true son'
deities.summary: The shepherd who became Inanna's bridegroom and king. When Inanna returned from the Great Below she gave him to the demons as her substitute; his sister Geshtinanna shares his fate so that each spends half the year below. The land mourns him in the dry season and rejoices at his return.

Lady Wind, wife of Enlil and queen of Nippur. Pursued by Enlil and following him into exile below, she bore Nanna and three underworld gods; she sits beside him in the Ekur deciding the fates of the land.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2400 BCE (Gudea of Lagash's personal god)
iconography: entwined serpents on staff (Gudea libation vase)
deities.summary: Serpent-lord of the underworld and personal god of Gudea of Lagash. With Dumuzi he guards the gate of heaven, and below he is throne-bearer of the netherworld and keeper of the roots of trees.
The primeval sea, 'the mother who gave birth to heaven and earth' and to all the gods. At her urging Enki shaped humankind from the clay above the Abzu so that the gods could rest.

deities.etymology: Akkadian Sîn from Sumerian Suen
deities.summary: The Moon god of Ur and Harran, wise lord who determines the months and reveals omens. Nabonidus raised him above all gods; at Harran his cult endured into the Islamic era.

Tiamat's consort and general, to whom she gave the Tablet of Destinies. After Marduk's victory Kingu was judged guilty of the rebellion and slain; from his blood Ea fashioned humankind to bear the toil of the gods.

primary_sources: Puduhepa's prayer to the Sun Goddess of Arinna/Hebat
iconography: standing on a lion or panther
deities.summary: The Hurrian Queen of Heaven, consort of Teshub, standing on a lion at the head of the goddesses at Yazılıkaya. Queen Puduhepa declared her one with the Sun Goddess of Arinna.

deities.etymology: Anatolian *tarḫu- 'to conquer, overcome'
deities.summary: The Storm God of Hatti, king of heaven and husband of the Sun Goddess of Arinna. He drives a chariot drawn by the bulls Sherri and Hurri, wields the thunderbolt, defeats the serpent Illuyanka, and guarantees the treaties of the Hittite kings.

alternate_names: Queen of the Land of Hatti
deities.summary: The supreme goddess of the Hittite state, Queen of Hatti, wife of the Storm God and mother of the weather gods of Nerik and Zippalanda. The Hittite king and queen are her priests; she gives them the kingship.

The farming god, son of the Storm God, who in anger put his shoes on the wrong feet and vanished. With him fertility left the land: the hearth went cold, ewes rejected their lambs, grain did not grow, and the gods starved. A bee sent by Hannahanna stung him awake, and Kamrusepa's rites calmed his rage so that he came home.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1400 BCE (Hurrian Kumarbi cycle in Hittite translation)
primary_sources: Song of Kumarbi / Kingship in Heaven (CTH 344)
deities.summary: The first king in heaven, who ruled nine years until his cupbearer Anu overthrew him and he fled down to the dark earth. His descendant Kumarbi later avenged him on Anu.

The diorite giant begotten by Kumarbi on a great rock to overthrow Teshub. Set on the shoulder of Upelluri, who carries heaven and earth, he grew from the sea until he reached the sky; Ea cut him from his base with the ancient copper knife that once separated heaven from earth.

The serpent who defeated the Storm God. In one telling the goddess Inara feasted him until he could not return to his hole and the mortal Hupasiya bound him; in another he took the Storm God's heart and eyes until the god's son recovered them. Told at the spring purulli festival.

Sister of Teshub, goddess of love, war and healing magic, standing among both the gods and the goddesses at Yazılıkaya. She tried to seduce Ullikummi with music and beauty, and was patron of Hattusili III.
Ruler of the netherworld, to whom the Hittite kings made offerings for health and long life; associated with the Sun Goddess of the Earth who opens the gates of the dead.

primary_sources: Chogha Zanbil temple inscriptions of Untash-Napirisha
deities.etymology: Sumerian nin-šušinak, 'lord of Susa'
deities.summary: Lord of Susa and judge of the dead. He receives souls in the netherworld and weighs their deeds with his assistants Ishmekarab and Lagamal; on earth he is protector of the city and of oaths.
The great god of Elam, lord of heaven and protector of the king, whose name forms the throne names of many Elamite rulers. With Kiririsha and Inshushinak he heads the pantheon.

deities.etymology: Elamite, probably 'great goddess'
deities.summary: The Great Goddess of Elam, 'mother of the gods', worshipped at Liyan on the Gulf coast and in the sacred precinct of Chogha Zanbil.

primary_sources: Musasir temple accounts in Sargon II's Eighth Campaign letter
deities.summary: The supreme god of Urartu, whose temple at Musasir held the kingdom's treasures. The kings of Urartu marched 'by the might of Haldi' and attributed all their victories to him.
The Urartian storm and war god, second of the state triad, after whom the fortress-city Teishebaini was named.
The Urartian Sun god, third of the state triad, depicted as a winged sun disc held aloft.

deities.etymology: West Semitic ʿṯtrt, feminine of ʿAthtar (the Venus-star god)
deities.summary: The great goddess of Sidon and Tyre, warrior and lover, 'name of Baal'. Kings of Sidon were her priests; sailors carried her across the Mediterranean to Kition, Carthage, Eryx and Pyrgi.

The healing god of Sidon, whose spring-fed temple at Bustan esh-Sheikh drew the sick for centuries. A youth who castrated himself to escape a goddess's desire and was restored to life by her, he became lord of healing.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 9th c. BCE (Zincirli); prominent at Carthage 5th c. BCE
deities.etymology: Possibly 'lord of the incense altar (ḥmn)' or 'lord of Amanus'
deities.summary: The chief god of Carthage, enthroned between sphinxes, consort of Tanit 'Face of Baal'. Vows to him and Tanit were paid at the tophet; in Roman Africa he lived on as Saturn, lord of the harvest.

iconography: smiting god with mace and shield
deities.summary: The archer god of plague and war, gatekeeper of the underworld at Ugarit. Egyptian pharaohs adopted him as a smiting war god; on Cyprus he was hailed as Apollo.
'Skilful and Wise', the craftsman of the gods, whose home is Kaphtor and Memphis. He forged the clubs Yagrush and Ayamur with which Baal defeated Yam, built Baal's palace, and made Aqhat's bow.

The Sun goddess of Ugarit, 'torch of the gods', who travels by day over the earth and by night through the underworld. She helped Anat carry the dead Baal home and found him again, and rebuked Mot at El's command.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2500 BCE (Malik at Ebla); 7th c. BCE (biblical polemic)
deities.etymology: From Semitic mlk 'king', vocalised in the Hebrew Bible with the vowels of boshet 'shame'
deities.summary: A god of the underworld and the royal dead to whom children were 'passed through the fire' in the valley of Hinnom, according to Israelite prophets who condemned the rite.
The national god of Moab. In Mesha's words, Chemosh was angry with his land and let Israel oppress it, then restored it to Moab and drove Israel out before the king.
The national god of the Ammonites at Rabbah, whose name means 'the king'.

deities.etymology: Aramaic ʿAtarʿateh, combining ʿAthtar/Astarte with ʿAttah/Anat
deities.summary: The great goddess of Hierapolis-Bambyke, mother and protectress of the city and of fish and doves. Her temple housed the throne between lions, and her galli priests served her in ecstatic rites.
Lord of Heaven, the high god of the Aramaeans and Phoenicians, who answered King Zakkur and of whom Philo of Byblos says the Phoenicians held the sun to be him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Nabataean inscription at Hegra (1st c. CE); Meccan cult to 630 CE
deities.summary: The great god of the Kaaba at Mecca, an image of red carnelian with a golden right hand, before whom divining arrows were cast to decide marriages, journeys and disputes.

deities.etymology: Arabic al-ilāt, 'the goddess', feminine of al-ilāh
deities.summary: 'The Goddess', worshipped as a square white stone at Ta'if and across North Arabia and Palmyra. One of the three daughters the Meccans named beside Allah.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (Dedan inscriptions, debated); Nabataean 1st c. BCE
deities.summary: 'The Mightiest', goddess of the sacred acacias at Nakhla near Mecca, most beloved of the Quraysh, associated with the morning star.

deities.etymology: Semitic mny 'to apportion, count'
deities.summary: Goddess of fate and allotted portion, worshipped as a black stone at Qudayd on the Red Sea road, especially by the Aws and Khazraj of Yathrib.

deities.etymology: Semitic wdd 'to love'
deities.summary: The god of love and friendship, national god of the Minaeans, and among the Kalb at Dumat al-Jandal worshipped as a giant armed man. The Quran names him first among the gods of Noah's people.

primary_sources: Nabataean inscriptions at Petra and Hegra
Epiphanius, Panarion 51 (Dusares born of the virgin Chaamou)
deities.etymology: Arabic dhū l-sharā, 'he of the Shara (mountains)'
deities.summary: The supreme god of the Nabataeans and of the royal house, worshipped as a black rectangular stone on a golden base at Petra. At Bostra his festival was the 'Actia Dusaria'.

primary_sources: Awwam (Mahram Bilqis) temple inscriptions at Marib
deities.summary: The national god of Saba, lord of the great Awwam temple at Marib, to whom the mukarribs of Saba dedicated the irrigation works and treaties of the realm. The Sabaeans called themselves 'the children of Almaqah'.

deities.etymology: Common Semitic ʿṯtr; masculine counterpart of Astarte
deities.summary: The highest god of the South Arabian pantheons, invoked first in Sabaean inscriptions, the Venus-star and giver of rain. At Ugarit the same god tried to sit on Baal's throne but his feet did not reach the footstool.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th–4th c. BCE (Artaxerxes II inscriptions); Avestan hymn older
primary_sources: Berossus via Clement of Alexandria, Protrepticus 5
deities.etymology: Avestan an-āhitā, 'unblemished, immaculate'
iconography: four-horse chariot of wind, rain, cloud, sleet
deities.summary: The Moist, Strong, Immaculate One: the heavenly river that flows from Mount Hukairya to the sea Vourukasha and purifies the seed of men and the wombs of women. Warriors and kings sacrifice to her for victory; Artaxerxes II invoked her beside Ahura Mazda and Mithra.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1380 BCE (Mitanni treaty, as Mitra); Avesta
deities.etymology: Indo-Iranian *mitra- 'contract, covenant'; cognate of Vedic Mitra
deities.summary: The yazata of the covenant, lord of wide pastures with a thousand ears and ten thousand eyes, who rises before the sun over Mount Hara and smites the contract-breaker with his mace. He is judge of souls with Sraosha and Rashnu at the Chinvat Bridge.
Best Truth, the Amesha Spenta who embodies cosmic order and presides over fire. Through Asha the sun keeps its path and the righteous act rightly; the lie (druj) is his enemy.
Holy Devotion, the Amesha Spenta who is the Earth and the daughter of Ahura Mazda; she rejoices when the earth is farmed and suffers when corpses are buried in her.
Desirable Dominion, the Amesha Spenta of righteous rule and of metals; the kingdom of Ahura Mazda that the faithful long for.
Wholeness and Immortality, the paired Amesha Spentas of waters and plants, who will be the food and drink of the blessed at the renovation of the world.

primary_sources: Nemrut Dağ inscription of Antiochus I (Artagnes-Herakles-Ares)
deities.etymology: Avestan vərəθraγna 'smiting of resistance'; cognate of Vedic vṛtrahan, Indra's epithet 'slayer of Vritra'
deities.summary: The yazata of victory who comes in ten forms — wind, bull, horse, camel, boar, youth, raven, ram, buck, and warrior with a golden blade — to give strength and triumph to the righteous.

deities.etymology: Avestan aži 'serpent' (cognate Vedic ahi)
deities.summary: The three-headed, six-eyed dragon created by Angra Mainyu to destroy the world of the living. Thraetaona (Fereydun) overcame him and bound him in Mount Damavand, where he waits to break free at the end of time.

deities.etymology: Indo-Iranian *Yama 'twin'; cognate of Vedic Yama
deities.summary: The radiant king of the golden age, under whom there was neither heat nor cold, old age nor death. He enlarged the earth three times and built the var, a walled enclosure, to preserve the best of creatures from the great winter; he lost his royal glory through a lie.

deities.etymology: Avestan gaya marətan 'mortal life'
deities.summary: The first human, shining like the sun, created by Ahura Mazda. Slain by Angra Mainyu's assault, his seed passed into the earth, and from it grew the rhubarb plant that became Mashya and Mashyana, the first couple.

alternate_names: King of the Paradise of Light
primary_sources: Theodore bar Konai, Liber Scholiorum XI
deities.summary: The God of the Realm of Light, dwelling with his five Shekhinas — Reason, Mind, Intelligence, Thought, Understanding — and his twelve aeons. He does not fight; when Darkness attacked he called forth emanations to go out in his stead.
deities.tradition_claim: The Manichaean scheme of two eternal principles, Light and Darkness

primary_sources: Theodore bar Konai, Liber Scholiorum XI
deities.summary: Lord of the Realm of Darkness, a composite monster with lion head, eagle wings, fish body and dragon feet, ruling five worlds of smoke, fire, wind, water and darkness. Desiring the Light he saw at the border, he invaded it and swallowed the Primal Man's sons, mixing light with matter.

The second emanation, who rescued the Primal Man from the abyss by calling to him, then built the cosmos from the flayed and slain archons: the heavens from their skins, the mountains from their bones, the earth from their flesh.

The emanation who set the sun and moon in motion as ships of light and appeared to the archons in beautiful male and female forms, so that in their lust they released the light they held; from what fell came plants and animals.

alternate_names: Ra-Horakhty who rejoices in the horizon in his name Shu who is in the Aten
deities.earliest_attestation: c. 1900 BCE (as solar disc); exclusive cult under Akhenaten c. 1350 BCE
primary_sources: Great Hymn to the Aten (tomb of Ay, Amarna)
Middle Kingdom Story of Sinuhe (Aten as sun disc)
iconography: solar disc with rays ending in hands
deities.summary: The living sun disc, sole god of Akhenaten's revelation. His rays end in hands that hold the ankh to the nostrils of the king and queen; he alone made the earth according to his desire, and every land and creature lives when he rises.

alternate_names: Father of the Gods (as primeval water)
iconography: bearded man raising the solar barque
deities.summary: The limitless dark water that existed before creation and still surrounds the ordered world. From Nun rose the primeval mound on which Atum came into being; the sun is reborn from him each dawn.
The goddess of Sais, archer and weaver, who at Esna rose from the primeval waters, created the world by speaking seven words, and bore Ra. She is called father of fathers and mother of mothers.
The air and light between heaven and earth, first son of Atum, sneezed or spat out with his sister Tefnut. He holds his daughter Nut aloft above Geb and gives breath to every living thing.
Moisture, daughter of Atum and twin of Shu, mother of Geb and Nut. As the Eye of Ra she once withdrew in anger to Nubia and had to be coaxed home by Thoth and Shu, bringing back the inundation.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 2000 BCE (Middle Kingdom apotropaia); popular to Roman period
iconography: frontal dwarf with lion mane and tongue out
deities.summary: The dwarf lion-faced protector of households, mothers and newborns, who dances, plays the tambourine and sticks out his tongue to frighten snakes and demons away.

iconography: black bull with white triangle on brow
deities.summary: The living sacred bull of Memphis, herald and soul of Ptah, recognised by his markings. At death he became Osiris-Apis and was buried in the Serapeum; from him the Ptolemies shaped Serapis.

primary_sources: Book of the Dead, Spell 125 (Papyrus of Ani, Papyrus of Hunefer)
deities.summary: The Devourer who waits beside the scales in the Hall of Two Truths. If a heart is heavier than the feather of Ma'at, she eats it and the soul dies a second death.

deities.etymology: Greek khaos 'gap, chasm', from khainō 'to gape'
deities.summary: First of all things came to be the Chasm. From Chaos were born Erebus and black Night, and from Night Aether and Day.
Primordial Darkness, born from Chaos with Night. By Night he fathered Aether and Day; his name also marks the dark region through which the dead pass to Hades.
The misty pit as far below Hades as heaven is above the earth, walled in bronze, where the Titans are imprisoned. As a primordial god he fathered Typhon on Gaia.
The Titaness of divine law and right order, second wife of Zeus, mother of the Seasons and the Fates; she convenes the assemblies of the gods and once held the oracle at Delphi.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (Derveni Papyrus refers to Protogonos); Orphic Rhapsodies
deities.etymology: Greek phainō 'to bring to light, shine'
deities.summary: The shining first-born, double-sexed and golden-winged, who burst from the cosmic egg laid by Chronos in the Aether. He revealed all things and was the first king; Zeus later swallowed him and so contained the whole cosmos within himself.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 6th c. BCE (Pherecydes of Syros); Orphic Rhapsodies
deities.summary: Ageless Time, a winged serpent with the heads of a bull, a lion and a god, who with Ananke encircles the cosmos. He produced Aether and Chaos and laid the egg from which Phanes was born.
The queen of the Etruscan gods, consort of Tinia and member of the Capitoline triad with Menrva. At Pyrgi, Thefarie Velianas dedicated a temple to her, which the Phoenician text renders as Astarte.
Goddess of wisdom, war, crafts and health, born armed from Tinia's head and wielder of a thunderbolt; third of the Etruscan triad that passed to the Roman Capitol.

deities.etymology: Probably Etruscan turan 'lady, mistress'
deities.summary: The winged goddess of love and vitality, attended by Lasa spirits; patron of Velch (Vulci).
Messenger of the gods and guide of souls; as Turms Aitas he leads the dead to the underworld.
The winged female underworld spirit who attends the dying and guides the soul on its journey, holding a torch to light the way and a scroll recording the person's fate.
God of wine, vegetation and joyful growth, son of Semla, patron of Pupluna (Populonia).
The youthful armed war god of the Etruscans, lover of Turan.
King of the underworld, enthroned with his queen Phersipnai (Persephone), wearing a wolf-skin cap.

deities.earliest_attestation: Roman-era accounts of Etruscan tradition (Cicero, 1st c. BCE)
primary_sources: Libri Tagetici (lost, cited by Roman authors)
deities.summary: The child-prophet with the wisdom of an old man who rose from a furrow at Tarquinia as the ploughman Tarchon cut it, and dictated the Etrusca disciplina — the art of reading livers and lightning — to the assembled lucumones before vanishing.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. BCE (tradition); attested 3rd c. BCE
deities.etymology: Latin, possibly from favere 'to be favourable'
deities.summary: The horned god of the woods and fields, early king of Latium, who speaks oracles to those who sleep in his groves. The Lupercalia was held in his honour.

deities.earliest_attestation: 296 BCE (temple vowed by Appius Claudius Caecus)
deities.summary: The war goddess of Rome. Before her temple stood the column from which the fetial priest hurled a spear to declare war, and there the Senate received envoys and victorious generals.
Goddess of luck and fate, with her great oracle at Praeneste where children drew the oak lots. She holds the rudder that steers and the cornucopia that gives, and stands on the wheel that turns.
The punisher of broken oaths and god of the dead, who drags the dying away; in folk speech his name lived on as the ogre.

The god of the Getae, to whom every fifth year a messenger was sent by being thrown onto spears. He taught that neither he nor his guests would die but would go to a place where they would live forever; he withdrew into an underground chamber for three years and reappeared.
deities.tradition_claim: Herodotus records the Greek counter-claim that Zalmoxis was a former slave of Pythagoras; the Getae revered him as a god.

deities.summary: The Thracian huntress and moon goddess whose cult Athens admitted at Piraeus; her festival the Bendideia featured a torch race on horseback.

iconography: votive bronze hand in benediction gesture
deities.summary: The horseman and sky-father of the Thracians and Phrygians, worshipped with nocturnal mysteries in which a snake was drawn through the initiate's robe. His votive hands, raised in blessing and covered with symbols, were dedicated across the empire.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 4th c. BCE; thousands of reliefs 2nd–3rd c. CE
primary_sources: Votive reliefs from Bulgaria, Romania and northern Greece
Greek and Latin dedications (Heroi, Deo Heroni)
deities.summary: The divine rider shown galloping toward an altar or tree around which a serpent coils, spearing a boar or other beast. He protects the living, heals, and guides the dead.

primary_sources: CIL VIII 2581 (Lambaesis dedication by a legate from Risinium)
deities.summary: The protector-god of Risinium (Risan, Montenegro), described in a Latin verse dedication as a lofty rider with a lance.

primary_sources: Votive altars from the Privilica spring near Bihać (Iapodes)
deities.summary: God of springs and waters among the Iapodes, honoured with altars at a sacred spring and equated by the Romans with Neptune.

deities.earliest_attestation: Roman era (sanctuary at São Miguel da Mota, Alandroal)
primary_sources: Over 80 votive inscriptions from São Miguel da Mota (Portugal)
deities.summary: The god of the hill-sanctuary of São Miguel da Mota, invoked for health and protection and consulted through incubation; worship of him continued among Romanised Lusitanians as 'most present and powerful god'.

primary_sources: Votive inscriptions from Turobriga and Mérida (Emerita Augusta)
deities.etymology: Celtic *ate-gena 'reborn' (proposed)
deities.summary: The goddess of Turobriga, of rebirth and spring, identified with Proserpina; curse tablets asked her to punish thieves.

primary_sources: Votive inscriptions and paterae from Lusitania and Gallaecia
deities.etymology: Possibly from Indo-European *bhendh- 'to bind'
deities.summary: A protector god of communities and warriors, worshipped under many local epithets as guardian of a settlement or group.
Goddess of rivers, springs and valleys in Gallaecia and northern Lusitania, honoured at the Fonte do Ídolo in Braga.

primary_sources: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum I.52
deities.summary: The Black God of the Baltic Slavs, to whom curses were spoken at feasts as the cup was passed: all misfortune comes from him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Inferred from Helmold (12th c.); name attested only later
primary_sources: Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum I.52 (implied good god)
deities.summary: The White God, giver of good fortune, the bright counterpart of Chernobog.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 980 CE (Vladimir's pantheon in the Primary Chronicle)
primary_sources: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), entry for 980
deities.summary: One of the gods whose idols Vladimir set on the hill at Kiev. The winds are called his grandchildren, blowing arrows from the sea.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 11th–12th c. CE (Old Russian anti-pagan sermons)
primary_sources: Slovo nekoego khristolyubtsa (Word of a Christ-lover)
deities.summary: The god of kin and birth, to whom bread, cheese and honey were set out with the Rozhanitsy, the birth-fate maidens; he breathes life into the newborn and destines it.

The four-headed god of Arkona on Rügen, holding a horn of wine from which the priest read the coming year's harvest, and owning a white horse whose steps through rows of spears foretold war. His temple fell to the Danes in 1168.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE (Jan Łasicki, De diis Samagitarum)
deities.summary: The Earth goddess who brings forth all life, greeted with a kiss by those who rise in the morning, and given the first drops of beer and bread at every meal. The dead return to her.

deities.earliest_attestation: 16th c. CE (Christian sources as devil); older folk tradition
primary_sources: Lithuanian and Latvian folk tales and dainas
deities.etymology: Baltic *vel- 'dead' (cf. Lithuanian vėlės 'souls of the dead')
deities.summary: Lord of the dead and of the underworld, cunning shape-shifter and owner of wealth, eternally pursued by Perkūnas who strikes him with thunder. Under Christianity he became the devil, often outwitted by a clever peasant.
The Moon, husband of Saulė the Sun. When he fell in love with Aušrinė the Morning Star, Perkūnas cut him in pieces, which is why the moon waxes and wanes; the stars are the children of Sun and Moon.

primary_sources: Karelian creation runes collected by Elias Lönnrot
deities.summary: The virgin daughter of the air who descended to the sea and floated for seven hundred years. A teal laid its eggs on her knee; when they broke, the lower halves became the earth, the upper the sky, the yolk the sun, the white the moon. She shaped the shores and bore Väinämöinen.
Lord of Tuonela, the land of the dead beyond the black river where the swan swims. With his wife Tuonetar and their daughters he keeps the dead; Väinämöinen barely escaped his nets.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: The king of the sea and the waters, with his wife Vellamo. Agricola wrote that Ahti brought fish from the water; fishermen asked his favour.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: The bearded king of the forest, with his wife Mielikki ruling Tapiola. Hunters prayed to him to open his storehouses of game.

The reckless, handsome hero who, sent to shoot the swan of Tuonela, was killed and his body cut to pieces in the river of the dead. His mother raked his pieces from the water with a copper rake, joined them, and a bee brought balm from heaven to restore him to life.

deities.earliest_attestation: Folk runes; 1551 CE (Agricola: Ilmarinen gives calm and storm)
primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.etymology: Finnish ilma 'air, sky, weather'
deities.summary: The eternal smith who hammered the vault of the sky so skilfully that no seam shows, and forged the Sampo, the mill of plenty, as the bride-price for the Maiden of Pohjola.

primary_sources: Mikael Agricola, preface to the Psalter (1551)
deities.summary: Once the sacred grove where the dead were honoured, Hiisi became a forest demon and giant who sends sickness and evil; his elk is chased by Lemminkäinen.

deities.etymology: From Norse Þórr karl, 'Old Man Thor'
iconography: wooden image with nail and flint in the head
deities.summary: The thunder god who drives away trolls and evil spirits with his two hammers, and who also governs rain and the sea. His wooden image was raised with hammers at sacred sites.
The ruling father, highest of the gods, who is mostly at rest and acts through his son Rádienbárdni. He gives souls to Máttaráhkká to be carried into the world.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who receives the child's body into the mother and helps women in labour; she lived under the hearth, and porridge was offered to her after a birth.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who can turn an unborn girl into a boy and who watches over children and hunters; a small bow was set in the porridge in her honour.
Daughter of Máttaráhkká who lives under the threshold of the goahti, guarding those who go in and out and the newborn in its first steps.
The old woman who rules Jábmiidáibmu, the realm of the dead beneath the earth. Black animals were buried alive to her to ransom the sick.
The great god of the Oeselians, born, they said, on a wooded hill in Vironia and flown from there to Saaremaa; his grove was felled by the crusaders.

primary_sources: Estonian folk tales (Kaval-Ants and Vanapagan cycle)
Friedrich Reinhold Kreutzwald, Eesti rahva ennemuistsed jutud (1866)
deities.summary: The Old Heathen, a giant farmer of the other world, strong and dim, forever cheated by his clever farmhand Kaval-Ants. The church made him the devil.

deities.earliest_attestation: Medieval Hungarian texts; folk legends recorded 19th–20th c.
deities.summary: In Hungarian folk creation tales, Isten sends Ördög down to the bottom of the primeval sea to bring up sand; Ördög hides some in his mouth, and it swells into the mountains. He is Isten's companion-adversary in the making of the world.
deities.tradition_claim: The dualist earth-diver legend is shared across Eastern European folk Christianity.

primary_sources: Basque legends collected by José Miguel de Barandiarán
deities.summary: The hairy giant lord of the woods who guards the flocks, warns shepherds of storms with his cry, and once held the secrets of sowing grain and forging, until San Martin Txiki tricked them from him.

primary_sources: Basque folk prayers and customs collected by José Miguel de Barandiarán
deities.summary: Grandmother Sun, daughter of Ama Lurra (Mother Earth), to whom she returns each night. She was created to drive away the night spirits, and the eguzkilore (sun-thistle) on doors stands for her.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 3rd c. BCE (by chronicle tradition, King Pharnavaz); recorded in medieval chronicles
primary_sources: Life of St Nino (Conversion of Kartli)
deities.etymology: Often derived from Ahura Mazda (via Armenian Aramazd), though a local origin is also proposed
deities.summary: The chief idol and god of Kartli, set up by King Pharnavaz on the mountain above Mtskheta: a man of copper in golden armour with emerald and beryl eyes and a turning sword. St Nino's prayer brought down hail that shattered him.

deities.earliest_attestation: Nart sagas and dzuar cult, recorded 19th c.
deities.etymology: Ossetian, from 'saint George' (Uas- 'holy')
deities.summary: The protector of men, warriors and travellers, the most honoured of the dzuars. Riding a white horse with three legs he appears among the Narts; women may not speak his name.

The greatest Nart hero, born from a swelling on his father's back and tempered steel-hard in the forge of Kurdalægon. He fought the heavenly spirits themselves; dying, he demanded his sword be thrown into the sea, and when it was, the sea turned blood-red and boiled.
Lord of thunder and of the wheat, who protects the harvest and strikes with lightning. Those killed by lightning are his, buried where they fell, and a ram is sacrificed to him.

primary_sources: Ossetian Nart sagas (Soslan in the Land of the Dead)
deities.summary: Ruler of the land of the dead, who decides where each soul will go, to paradise or hell, and receives the dead at the gate of his realm.
The smith of heaven who forges weapons for the Narts, mends Batradz's body and tempers him in his forge, and gives iron lips to the dead.
The one great god of the Adyghe, creator of all, above the other powers; prayers begin and end with his name.
The god of thunder and lightning; a person or animal struck by lightning was considered chosen and was honoured with dances and songs.
The smith of the Narts and god of the forge, who made the first iron tools and weapons, forged the sickle for the harvest, and sought the end of the world.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 5th c. CE recording (Movses Khorenatsi, Agathangelos) of older tradition
primary_sources: Movses Khorenatsi, History of Armenia I.31
Agathangelos, History of the Armenians (temple of Ashtishat)
deities.etymology: Middle Iranian Varhagn, from Avestan Verethragna
deities.summary: The fiery god born when heaven, earth and the purple sea were in labour: from a reed came smoke, then flame, and from the flame a youth with hair and beard of fire and eyes like suns. He fought and reaped the dragons and stole straw from Barsham, scattering it across the sky as the Milky Way.

deities.etymology: Armenian 'little star'
deities.summary: Goddess of love, beauty and water, beloved of Vahagn, worshipped with him at Ashtishat. At the summer festival of Vardavar people splash one another with water in her honour.

primary_sources: Agathangelos, History of the Armenians (temple of Tir near Artashat)
deities.etymology: Iranian Tīr (Tishtrya / Mercury-planet)
deities.summary: The scribe of Aramazd, god of writing, learning and dream-interpretation, who records the fate of each person; his temple stood near Artashat.

primary_sources: Eznik of Kolb, Against the Sects
deities.etymology: From Avestan Spenta Armaiti
deities.summary: The Earth and the underworld below it, realm of the dead; in the Armenian translation of 2 Maccabees her name renders that of Dionysus.
The sky and the god who dwells in it; the word for God in Albanian, which in folk use also names the heavens and the thunder that falls from them.

deities.earliest_attestation: Calendar name (e enjte, Thursday) and folk tradition
deities.summary: The fire god honoured in the hearth, whose day is Thursday; fire is sworn by and never spat into.
A semi-divine winged hero, born with a caul and small wings under his arms, who fights the kulshedra with lightning, thrown boulders and uprooted trees to release the waters.

deities.etymology: From Latin chersydrus, 'water-snake'
deities.summary: The many-headed female dragon who withholds the waters, causing drought, or spews fire and floods; she grows from the bolla serpent that has gone unseen for years. The drangue is her eternal foe.

deities.etymology: Celtic *Lugus, possibly 'oath' or 'light' (disputed)
deities.summary: The god of the Gauls whom Caesar called Mercury, inventor of all the arts, guide on roads and journeys, and the greatest power over trade. Lugdunum, 'fort of Lugus', was his city, and the assembly of the Gauls met there in August.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 60 CE (Lucan); Pillar of the Boatmen (14–37 CE)
deities.summary: One of the three gods to whom Lucan says the Gauls gave cruel offerings. On the Pillar of the Boatmen he hews a tree in which a bull and three cranes stand; the Berne scholiast says his victims were hung from trees.
The bright healing god, patron of Aquileia and Noricum, whose priests served him at Bayeux; the Romans called him Apollo.

The Gauls' Herakles: an old man, bald and sun-browned, with club and bow, who leads a crowd of men by thin chains of gold and amber running from his tongue to their ears — eloquence that binds stronger than force.

primary_sources: Gallo-Roman dedications pairing her with Mercury
Gloucester relief of Mercury and Rosmerta
deities.etymology: Celtic *ro-smert- 'great provider'
deities.summary: The Great Provider, goddess of abundance, paired with Mercury across Gaul and the Rhineland.

primary_sources: Math fab Mathonwy (Fourth Branch of the Mabinogi)
deities.summary: Son of Arianrhod, who laid three curses on him — no name, no arms, no human wife — which Gwydion broke by trickery. Struck by Gronw's spear in a posture neither indoors nor out, he flew up as an eagle, rotting in an oak, until Gwydion sang him down and restored him.

primary_sources: Branwen ferch Llŷr (Second Branch of the Mabinogi)
deities.summary: The giant king of the Island of the Mighty who waded the sea to Ireland and lay as a bridge for his army. Wounded by a poisoned spear, he bade his men cut off his head, which spoke and feasted with them for eighty years and was buried at the White Mount in London to guard Britain from invasion.

deities.earliest_attestation: Culhwch and Olwen (c. 1100); Maponos inscriptions 2nd–3rd c. CE
primary_sources: Romano-British inscriptions to (Apollo) Maponus at Hadrian's Wall (RIB)
deities.etymology: Celtic *Maponos 'divine son'
deities.summary: The Great Son of the Great Mother, stolen from his mother when three nights old and imprisoned in Caer Loyw until Arthur's men, guided by the oldest animals, freed him to hunt the boar Twrch Trwyth.

deities.earliest_attestation: Culhwch and Olwen; Welsh Triads; Matrona inscriptions
deities.etymology: Celtic *Mātronā 'great mother'
deities.summary: The Great Mother, mother of Mabon, remembered in the Triads as the mother of Owain and Morfudd by Urien.

deities.etymology: Possibly Celtic 'sun' or 'eye'
deities.summary: The goddess of the hot springs at Bath, where an undying fire burned on her altar. Those wronged threw lead curse tablets into her spring, asking her to punish thieves.

deities.etymology: Celtic *noudont- 'catcher, acquirer'; cognate of Irish Nuadu
deities.summary: God of the great healing sanctuary at Lydney above the Severn, with its dormitory for incubation and votive dogs; one man cursed the thief of his ring in his name.
The Sun, invoked in the Merseburg charm with her sister Sinthgunt to heal the foal of Balder; in Norse tradition she drives the sun's chariot chased by the wolf Sköll.
The goddess of the Marsi whose much-frequented temple Germanicus razed during an autumn festival.

deities.etymology: Probably Germanic *badwō 'battle'
deities.summary: The Frisian goddess whose sacred grove was the place where nine hundred Roman soldiers were cut down during the revolt of 28 CE.

iconography: iron staff topped with a bird
deities.summary: Lord of leaves and of every healing plant. No medicine works, no rite is complete, without his herbs; the saying goes "kosi ewe, kosi orisa" — without leaves there is no orisha. He is one-legged, one-eyed, and speaks in a high voice through his bird.
The divine hunter and tracker, whose arrow never misses its mark. He is the orisha of the forest, of pursuit and of justice, and companion of Ogun and Eshu among the warrior orisha.

iconography: layered cloth masquerade costume covering the whole body
deities.summary: The collective ancestors returning to the living in masquerade. When the Egungun dance in their layered cloth, the dead of the lineage walk in the town again, bless their descendants and enforce the moral order.
Owner of the deep ocean, beyond Yemoja's shallows. Olokun holds the unfathomed depths, their wealth and their terror; once Olokun rose to flood the earth and was chained at the sea's bottom.

iconography: pair of carved ere ibeji figures
deities.summary: The divine twins, born as Taiwo (the first to taste the world) and Kehinde (the one who came behind and is the elder). Twins carry great power; when a twin dies an ere ibeji figure is carved and cared for as the living child.
Orisha of the farm, the harvest and the fertile earth. He judges disputes among the orisha and guards against witchcraft; the yam harvest is his.

Progenitor of the Yoruba kings, who descended from heaven at Ile-Ife with a chain, a handful of earth and a five-toed hen and made dry land where there was only water. All crowned Yoruba kings trace their lineage to his sons.

iconography: ibori (beaded cowrie shrine of the head)
deities.summary: The divine head: each person's personal destiny-deity, chosen in heaven before birth. Ifá teaches that no orisha can bless a person without the consent of their Ori; Ori alone follows a person all the way to the end.
Death personified, one of the ajogun (warrior-forces against humanity). Iku comes when the days written in a person's Ori run out, and Orunmila's sacrifices can turn him away before his time.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; royal Dahomey cult 17th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: Lord of the earth and of smallpox. Sakpata punishes with disease those who wrong the earth and heals those who honor him; the kings of Dahomey feared his priests and at times banished his cult.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; royal Dahomey cult 17th–19th c. CE
deities.summary: The thunder vodun, head of the sky pantheon. His thunderbolt strikes liars and thieves; the ram and the double axe are his.

iconography: human figure with a blade for a head
deities.summary: Vodun of iron, war and tools; the sword Mawu-Lisa used to shape the world. Gu was sent to earth to clear the bush and teach humans to work metal.

The cosmic serpent, coiled under and around the earth, who carried Mawu-Lisa in his mouth as the world was made and holds it together. The rainbow is his body; motion, wealth and life-force flow through him.
Master of the sea, chief of the water vodun (Hu), who sends rain and the fish.
The divine voice of destiny read through divination. Fa is the "word of Mawu", each person's fate written before birth and disclosed by the bokonon (diviner).
The great abosom (god) of the Tano River, war and thunder, eldest son of Nyame among the river gods. He is invoked by Asante and Bono for strength in battle.
Eldest son of Nyame, god of the Bia River and of the bush, who lost his inheritance of the fertile lands to his younger brother Tano by trickery.
The hook-footed monster of the deep forest, who dangles his legs from the high branches to snatch travelers; ally of witches (abayifo).
The trickster-spirit of war, chaos and bargains, who drives warriors to fury and is called on for victory. Igbo tradition knows him as a dangerous but necessary force, not an absolute evil.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; carved figures from 19th c. CE
iconography: horned seated figure holding a knife and a tusk or head
deities.summary: The horned personal god of the right hand: a man's strength, will and achievement. A man consecrates his Ikenga and offers to it before an undertaking, and it is split and buried with him at death.
The spirit of divination, healing and creative madness. Agwu calls the dibia (diviner-healer) to his work, and those he chooses but who refuse him are troubled until they accept.
The sun, eye of Chukwu, giver of light, knowledge and perfection; Igbo prayers turn to the rising sun.
The personal guardian spirit and destiny given to each person by Chukwu. "Onye kwe, chi ya ekwe" — when a person says yes, his chi says yes too.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: The supreme creator of the Edo, who sent his sons to found the world; the youngest took a snail shell of earth and so became owner of the land.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: Son of Osanobua and king of the waters, source of wealth, children and beauty. Women keep his white altars; the Oba of Benin is his earthly counterpart.

primary_sources: Benin court ritual and brass plaques
deities.summary: The king of death, who rules the dead and claims the blood offered to him.

deities.etymology: Shared with Maasai Enkai/Ngai; commonly taken as a loan from Maa.
deities.summary: The one creator and giver of all things, who lives in the sky and comes to rest on Kirinyaga (Mount Kenya). People pray facing the mountain; he is approached through elders and sacrifice under the sacred mugumo fig tree.
The first man and woman, placed by Ngai at Mukurwe wa Nyagathanga; their nine daughters became the mothers of the nine Kikuyu clans.

alternate_names: Nhialic (Divinity, the one in the sky)
deities.summary: Divinity, the creator in the sky. Once heaven was close and joined to earth by a rope, until the first woman struck it with her hoe; Nhialic withdrew, and death and toil entered the world.
The great free-divinity of rain, lightning and fertility, the most powerful of the powers between Nhialic and people.
The first woman, patron of women and gardens, whose hoe struck the sky and caused Divinity to withdraw. Her emblem is the little snake.
The first man, a free-divinity associated with the sun, fire and illness.
Spirit, the creator who is like wind and air, everywhere present yet in the sky. He is the father of all, who gives and takes life, and to whom the Nuer submit in all misfortune.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Portuguese records from 16th c. CE
primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
deities.summary: The supreme creator, Nzambi the all-powerful, who made the world and stands above all spirits; he is not given shrines but is the source of all power the minkisi carry.

primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
iconography: mirror-sealed medicine pack in the belly
deities.summary: Spirit-powers held in consecrated containers and carved figures. Each nkisi is a spirit from the land of the dead bound into an object by the nganga (ritual expert); the nkondi, studded with nails, hunts down oath-breakers and witches.

primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
iconography: the Kongo cosmogram (dikenga) with its horizontal line
deities.summary: The great water that divides the land of the living from the land of the dead. The sun crosses it daily; the soul crosses it at death and is reborn on the far side; the Kongo cosmogram marks it as the horizontal line.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Capuchin records 17th c. CE
primary_sources: Portuguese and Capuchin records, 16th–17th c. CE
deities.summary: Spirits of water and stone, bound to particular springs, pools and rocks, who protect the land and its people and can make places fertile or dangerous.
The red, cruel first king, identified with the rainbow serpent, who ruled without manners or law until he was overthrown by his nephew Kalala Ilunga.
The refined hunter-prince from the east who brought good manners and sacred kingship; father of Kalala Ilunga by Nkongolo's sister.
Hero-son of Mbidi Kiluwe, who defeated Nkongolo and founded the second Luba empire and its sacred kingship.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; Matopo shrine cult from at least 17th c. CE
deities.summary: The high God of rain and fertility, who speaks as a voice from the caves of the Matopo Hills. Mwari is both male and female, sky and pool, and is approached through the oracle and through the mhondoro spirits.

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; spirit medium attested 1890s CE
deities.summary: A great mhondoro (royal ancestral lion-spirit) who speaks through female mediums. Through the medium Charwe she led resistance in the 1896–97 rising and prophesied, "my bones will rise again."

deities.earliest_attestation: oral tradition; medium attested 19th c. CE
deities.summary: A powerful mhondoro and prophet-spirit, guardian of the Shona, remembered for prophesying the coming of foreigners.

The first-appearing one, God of the sky, thunder and earthquakes, who existed before all things. Where uNkulunkulu is the first ancestor who brought people out of the reeds, uMvelinqangi is the one who was first of all.
The Princess of Heaven, daughter of God, maiden of rain, rainbow and the growing crops. In spring girls honor her with songs and gardens so she will bless the harvest.
The ancestral spirits of the lineage, who watch over their descendants, speak through dreams and the izangoma diviners, and are fed with beer and cattle.
A small, malicious water-sprite sent by witches to cause illness and harm, against which people raise their beds on bricks.

The supreme creator of the Xhosa. When he made the world the sea-dragon tried to destroy it, and his mother Djobela, the earth, raised the four giants to hold the world's corners as mountains. He is invoked with a stone thrown on the cairn.
deities.tradition_claim: Later Xhosa Christianity used uThixo, a word drawn from the Khoikhoi divine name, for God.

alternate_names: Gauwa (as high god, in some reports)
deities.summary: The great god of the Ju|'hoan, who made the earth, the animals and people and lives in the eastern sky. In the old stories he was a trickster who behaved outrageously; now he is the giver of life and death.
The lesser god of the west and the spirits of the dead (ǁgauwasi), who shoots invisible arrows of sickness and death and plays tricks on people; in the healing dance the healers fight him off.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.etymology: Often rendered "wounded knee"; later Xhosa uThixo is widely traced to this name.
deities.summary: The rain-giver and great chief of the Khoikhoi, who lives in the red sky of dawn, sends the thunderclouds and fought ǁGaunab, the lord of the dark sky. He was killed and rose again, stronger with each wound.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The lord of darkness, death and the black sky, enemy of Tsui-ǁGoab, who brings sickness and lives among the dead in the west.

primary_sources: Nama and Korana prayers recorded 19th c. CE
deities.summary: The great hunter, magician and culture hero, born of a cow that ate grass, who died many times and rose again; his many graves are the stone cairns where travelers add a stone for luck.
The oldest ancestor, who died and was reborn as a serpent; he carries the life-force of the earth and the growth of the fields, and his priest the Hogon is fed by him at night.
The androgynous spirit of the river Niger, of water, speech and order, who reorganized the world after Pemba's disorder, gave the seasons and taught people speech and law.

The first creative being, who came from the primal vibration as a seed and made the earth, then sought to dominate creation through his acacia tree and the women he made; his rule brought disorder until Faro intervened.
The first woman, Pemba's companion, who rebelled and ran through the world spreading impurity, sorcery and disorder, yet also brought agriculture.
The supreme deity of the Serer, both near and far, male and female, to whom the saltigue (seer-priests) turn in the yearly Xooy divination for the rains.
The ancestral and saintly spirits, often in serpent form, who mediate between Roog and the living and are honored at shrines and sacred trees.
The creator and father of the gods, who made all things and stands above the lubaale (national gods).
Benevolent lubaale of Lake Victoria, giver of fish, children, health and plenty; his chief shrine was on the Ssese Islands.
The war god of Buganda, brother of Mukasa, who fought for the kingdom from the clouds and was mortally wounded by a captive woman who learned his secret.
Death, brother of Nambi, who followed her and Kintu to earth when she turned back for millet; ever since he kills people and hides in the earth.
The first man and first king of Buganda, who passed the tests of Gulu, the sky-king, to win his daughter Nambi.

primary_sources: Oromo oral tradition and women's Ateetee ritual
deities.summary: The Oromo goddess of fertility and motherhood, honored by women with songs and offerings to bring childbirth and protect families.

The creator, the "Fragrant Lord" in the sky. In one tale the god of the sky and the god of the earth both made people — the earth-god shaped the bodies and the sky-god gave the breath — so at death the body returns to earth and the breath to heaven.
The ancestors, closest powers to the living, honored in the famadihana (turning of the bones), when the dead are rewrapped in new shrouds and danced with.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 3rd c. BCE (Musawwarat es-Sufra Lion Temple)
primary_sources: Lion Temple inscriptions at Musawwarat es-Sufra (hymn to Apedemak)
iconography: lion head on a man's body
lion-headed serpent rising from a lotus
deities.summary: The lion-headed war god of Meroë, "Lion of the South, strong of arm," who goes before the king in battle and grants victory, abundance and the king's rule. At Naqa he appears as a lion-headed serpent rising from a lotus.

deities.earliest_attestation: c. 15th c. BCE (Egyptian temple); Kushite royal cult from 8th c. BCE
iconography: Jebel Barkal pinnacle (seen as a uraeus)
deities.summary: Amun who dwells in the Pure Mountain of Jebel Barkal and chooses the kings of Kush. By his oracle the Napatan kings were crowned, and Piye marched north in his name to conquer Egypt.

primary_sources: Musawwarat es-Sufra temple statues and inscriptions
deities.summary: Meroitic god of procreation and creation, guardian of temple doorways together with Arensnuphis.

primary_sources: Musawwarat es-Sufra and Philae temple inscriptions
deities.summary: Kushite god, "the good companion," hunter and guardian, later honored at Philae alongside Egyptian gods and equated with Shu and Onuris.
The ram-horned god of the oracle in the Siwa oasis, known throughout the Libyan desert and the Greek world. Alexander crossed the sand to consult him and was hailed as his son.
The bull-horned war god of the Laguatan Libyans, born of Ammon and a cow, whose image was carried into battle before the warriors.

primary_sources: Amazigh folk ritual of Taslit n Unzar (Bride of Anzar)
deities.summary: The rain god of Amazigh folk tradition, who loved a maiden and withheld the rain until she gave herself to him; in drought villages carry a doll, the Bride of Anzar, in procession to bring the rain.

Virgin martyr shut in a tower by her pagan father, who beheaded her for her faith and was struck dead by lightning. She is patron of artillerymen, miners and all in danger of sudden death, and is invoked against thunder and fire.
