facets.scholarly_note: The blurred line between YHWH and his angel is a classic problem; see Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (2015), on the "two powers" reading.

facets.facet_name: The Sea Dragon Crushed by God
facets.core_claim: God broke the heads of Leviathan in the primordial battle and will slay him at the end of days; he embodies the hostile sea that only God can master.

facets.facet_name: The Creature God Made to Play
facets.core_claim: In Psalm 104 and Job 41 Leviathan is no rival but a creature: magnificent, untameable by man, yet God's plaything.

facets.facet_name: Food of the Righteous at the End
facets.core_claim: In the age to come Leviathan and Behemoth will be served as food to the righteous.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Beast of the Land
facets.core_claim: Behemoth is the land counterpart to Leviathan: a mighty creature of the first days, mastered only by God and destined to be eaten at the end.

facets.facet_name: Cut in Pieces at Creation
facets.core_claim: By his power God stilled the sea and by his understanding struck down Rahab; the victory over her is the victory that founds the world.

facets.facet_name: The Star Who Would Be Most High
facets.core_claim: The Day Star sought to raise his throne above El's stars on the divine mountain and was cast down to the Pit: the archetype of hubris against the Most High.
facets.scholarly_note: In context a taunt-song against a Babylonian king that appears to reuse a Canaanite myth of a morning-star deity's failed ascent; see Mark S. Smith, The Origins of Biblical Monotheism (2001).

facets.facet_name: The Seven-Headed Twisting Serpent
facets.core_claim: Litan belongs to the host of Yam, the hostile sea, and is slain by Baal and Anat so that the storm-king may rule.

facets.facet_name: Oracle God of Ekron
facets.core_claim: Kings sent to the god of Ekron to learn whether they would recover; he is a Baal who speaks through his oracle.
facets.scholarly_note: "Lord of the Flies" may be a deliberate Hebrew deformation of zbl bʿl, "Baal the Prince", a title of Baal Hadad at Ugarit; the Gospels' Beelzeboul preserves the -l ending.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Topheth Fire
facets.core_claim: At the Topheth outside Jerusalem the faithless offered their children by fire to the King; the Torah condemns the rite as the defilement of God's name.
facets.scholarly_note: Whether mlk names a god or a type of sacrifice (Punic molk, attested in Carthaginian tophet inscriptions) is debated; Milton later made Moloch a fallen angel.

facets.facet_name: The Dawn, Twin of Dusk
facets.core_claim: Shahar is the morning: born of El, twin to the evening god Shalim, the bringer of the new day.

facets.facet_name: The Pretender Who Could Not Fill the Throne
facets.core_claim: Athtar ascends the divine mountain to take the vacant throne, proves too small for it, and descends to rule the earth: a would-be king of heaven brought low.
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate with Akkadian Ishtar and South Arabian ʿAthtar, where the deity is the Venus-star; many scholars see the Isaiah 14 Day Star myth behind this episode (Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God).

facets.facet_name: Commander of the Sons of Darkness
facets.core_claim: Belial rules the dominion of wickedness for an appointed time; all who walk in darkness belong to his lot until the final war.

facets.facet_name: Snarer with Three Nets
facets.core_claim: Belial catches Israel in three nets dressed up as righteousness: fornication, wealth and defilement of the temple.

facets.facet_name: Chief of the Remaining Spirits
facets.core_claim: God leaves one tenth of the evil spirits under Mastema's command, so that humans may be tested and punished.

facets.facet_name: Instigator of the Akedah
facets.core_claim: It is Prince Mastema who challenges God to test Abraham's faithfulness by commanding the sacrifice of Isaac, as the satan challenges God over Job.

facets.facet_name: The Angel Who Heals
facets.core_claim: Raphael heals the blind, drives out demons, and heals the earth itself after the corruption of the Watchers.

facets.facet_name: Binder of Demons
facets.core_claim: Raphael binds Azazel in Dudael and pursues Asmodeus to Upper Egypt where he binds him.

facets.facet_name: Leader of the Heavenly Lights
facets.core_claim: Uriel reveals the true courses of the sun and moon so that the righteous may keep the correct calendar.

facets.facet_name: Warden over Tartarus
facets.core_claim: Uriel is "over the world and over Tartarus", the angel who shows Enoch the prison of the stars that transgressed.

facets.facet_name: The Jealous Demon of the Bridal Chamber
facets.core_claim: Asmodeus slays the bridegroom out of desire for the bride and is put to flight only by the remedy God reveals through his angel.

facets.facet_name: King of Demons
facets.core_claim: In rabbinic legend Ashmedai rules the demons, knows the secret of the shamir, and briefly usurps Solomon's throne.

facets.facet_name: The Wicked One, Chief of the Satans
facets.core_claim: Samael heads the satans; he rode the serpent into Eden and works to bring accusations against Israel before God.

facets.facet_name: The Angel of Death
facets.core_claim: Samael is the angel of death who comes for each soul, filled with eyes, with a drawn sword dripping gall.
facets.scholarly_note: The Talmud (Bava Batra 16a) records Resh Lakish: "Satan, the evil inclination and the angel of death are one."

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Sitra Achra
facets.core_claim: In Kabbalah Samael and Lilith rule the Other Side, the husks (qelippot) that mirror the holy emanations.
facets.scholarly_note: Developed in 13th-c. Castilian Kabbalah; see Gershom Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (1941).

facets.facet_name: Weaver of Crowns from Prayer
facets.core_claim: Sandalphon gathers the prayers of the faithful and binds them as crowns for God; he spans earth and the highest heaven.
facets.scholarly_note: Later Kabbalah identifies Sandalphon with the transfigured Elijah, as Metatron is the transfigured Enoch.

facets.facet_name: The Tempter and Accuser
facets.core_claim: Satan tempts humanity to sin as he tempted Christ, and accuses the brethren before God day and night until he is thrown down.

facets.facet_name: The Angel Who Fell
facets.core_claim: Satan was created good, rebelled out of pride, and was cast out of heaven with the angels who followed him; in the Life of Adam and Eve he falls because he refuses to worship the image of God in Adam.

facets.facet_name: Prince of This World
facets.core_claim: For a time Satan holds sway as ruler of this world and prince of the power of the air, blinding unbelievers — until his judgment at the end of the age.

facets.facet_name: The Brightest Angel Cast Down for Pride
facets.core_claim: Lucifer, first among the angels, sought to set his throne above the stars of God; for that pride he fell from light into darkness and became Satan.
facets.scholarly_note: The Vulgate also uses lucifer for the morning star that rises in believers' hearts (2 Peter 1:19), and the Exsultet calls Christ the true Lucifer; the word only gradually became a proper name of the Devil.

facets.facet_name: Prince of Demons
facets.core_claim: Beelzebul commands the demons that possess and afflict people; Christ's exorcisms show that his house has been entered and his goods plundered.

facets.facet_name: Lord and Giver of Life
facets.core_claim: The Spirit is fully God, co-eternal with the Father and the Son, the breath of life by whom all things are given life and sanctified.
facets.scholarly_note: East and West divide over whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father "and the Son" (filioque, added in the West from the 6th c.).

facets.facet_name: The Paraclete Who Abides
facets.core_claim: Christ promises another Advocate, the Spirit of Truth, who will remain with the disciples, teach them all things and remind them of all he said.

facets.facet_name: Captain of the Hosts Who Casts Down the Dragon
facets.core_claim: When war broke out in heaven, Michael and his angels fought the dragon and threw him down; he is the champion of God against Satan.

facets.facet_name: Weigher and Guide of Souls
facets.core_claim: Michael receives the souls of the dying, weighs them, and defends them against the Accuser at the hour of death.

facets.facet_name: Angel of the Annunciation
facets.core_claim: Gabriel brings God's decisive announcements, above all the Incarnation of the Word in Mary's womb.

facets.facet_name: The Counterfeit Christ of the End
facets.core_claim: The Antichrist imitates Christ — a death-wound healed, worship demanded, signs performed — in order to lead the world astray before the Second Coming.

facets.facet_name: King of the Abyss
facets.core_claim: Abaddon rules the locust-host of the abyss and is destruction itself, released for an appointed time at the end.
facets.scholarly_note: In the Hebrew Bible ʾăbaddôn is a place — "Destruction", paired with Sheol and Death; Revelation personifies it.

facets.facet_name: Ruler of the 365 Heavens
facets.core_claim: Abrasax presides over the full round of heavens, his name containing the number of the year; through it the cosmos is ordered and the initiate gains protection.
facets.scholarly_note: On magical gems he appears as the "anguipede": cock-headed, armoured, with serpent legs. Sethian texts make Abrasax a positive luminary servant rather than an archon.

facets.facet_name: Bearer of Revelation
facets.core_claim: Every revelation to every prophet came through Jibrīl; he carried the Qurʾān from God to Muḥammad over twenty-three years.

facets.facet_name: Angel of Rain and Provision
facets.core_claim: Mīkāʾīl directs the rain, plants and provision by which God sustains His creatures.

facets.facet_name: Sounder of the Last Trumpet
facets.core_claim: When God commands, Isrāfīl will blow the Trumpet that ends the world and then the blast that raises the dead.
facets.scholarly_note: The Qurʾān mentions the Trumpet but does not name its angel; the name comes from ḥadīth and later tradition.

facets.facet_name: The Angel of Death
facets.core_claim: ʿAzrāʾīl gathers the souls of the dying at their decreed moment and delivers them to the angels of mercy or of punishment.
facets.scholarly_note: The name ʿAzrāʾīl is not Qurʾānic; it appears in later tradition.

facets.facet_name: Spirits Created from Smokeless Fire
facets.core_claim: The jinn are a hidden creation parallel to humanity — believers and unbelievers, righteous and wicked — able to see us where we cannot see them.

facets.facet_name: The Seal of the Prophets
facets.core_claim: Muḥammad completes the chain of prophets from Adam through Abraham, Moses and Jesus; with him revelation is sealed.

facets.facet_name: The Intercessor on the Day of Judgment
facets.core_claim: When all others hold back, the Prophet will prostrate beneath the Throne and be granted intercession for his community.

facets.facet_name: The Muḥammadan Light (Nūr Muḥammadī)
facets.core_claim: In Sufi teaching the Reality of Muḥammad (al-ḥaqīqa al-muḥammadiyya) is the first thing God brought forth, the prototype of creation and of the Perfect Human.
facets.scholarly_note: Sufi doctrine (islam-sufi), not shared by all Sunni scholars; the Prophet remains fully human and a creature.

facets.facet_name: The Angels Who Taught Sorcery at Babylon
facets.core_claim: They taught the magic that separates husband from wife as a test; in the exegetical story their descent and fall become a warning about angelic pride.

facets.facet_name: Warden of the Fire
facets.core_claim: Mālik guards Hell and its nineteen keepers, carrying out God's justice on the condemned without mercy or disobedience.

facets.facet_name: The Great Life
facets.core_claim: Life itself, the infinite Light, is the source from which the worlds of light emanate; it is untouched by matter and darkness.

facets.facet_name: The Descending Saviour of Knowledge
facets.core_claim: Manda d-Hayyi comes down from the Light to awaken souls imprisoned in the body and lead them back to the Life.

facets.facet_name: Fashioner of the Material World
facets.core_claim: Ptahil builds the earth and the human body but cannot give them life; his work is real yet flawed, and he must await forgiveness.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the Planets and Lady of Darkness
facets.core_claim: Ruha gives birth to the planetary rulers and labours to hold humanity in the world below the Light.

facets.facet_name: The Weigher of Souls
facets.core_claim: At Abathur's scales the soul is weighed; only the pure pass on to the Life.

facets.facet_name: Descent into the Underworld
facets.core_claim: Hibil Ziwa goes down into the depths, binds the powers of darkness and returns in triumph to the World of Light.

facets.facet_name: The Dragon King of Darkness
facets.core_claim: Ur is the monster of the dark waters whose rage threatens the Light; he is bound but not destroyed until the end.

facets.facet_name: The Great Baptiser
facets.core_claim: Yahya baptised thousands in living water and taught the way of the Life; Mandaeans repeat his baptism weekly.

facets.facet_name: The Creator Who Entrusted the World to His Angels
facets.core_claim: God made the world and delegated its governance to the Seven Angels, chief of whom is Tawûsî Melek.

facets.facet_name: Chief of the Seven Angels, Ruler of the World
facets.core_claim: God set Tawûsî Melek over the world; he governs it and mediates between God and humankind.

facets.facet_name: The Angel Who Bowed Only to God
facets.core_claim: His refusal to bow to Adam was not rebellion but loyalty to the one God, and it was vindicated.
facets.scholarly_note: Neighbouring Muslims and Christians identified him with Iblīs/Satan because of this motif; Yazidis reject the identification, which has fuelled persecution.

facets.facet_name: Saint of Lalish, Manifestation of the Peacock Angel
facets.core_claim: Sheikh ʿAdī is the holy reformer through whom Tawûsî Melek appeared on earth; to visit his tomb is to come to the centre of the world.
facets.scholarly_note: Historically a Sufi of Umayyad descent from the Beqaa valley; his order later developed into the Yazidi religion.

facets.facet_name: The Seven Who Govern Creation
facets.core_claim: The world is ruled by seven angels emanated from God's light, each with his human manifestation.
facets.scholarly_note: Some published lists (from the disputed "Black Book") give them names of the Islamic archangels — Jibrāʾīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, ʿAzrāʾīl, Dardāʾīl, Shamnāʾīl, Nūrāʾīl.

facets.facet_name: The Final Locus of the Divine Unity
facets.core_claim: The unknowable One showed himself in human form through al-Ḥākim, as an image in a mirror shows the face without containing it.

facets.facet_name: The Withdrawn Lord Who Will Return
facets.core_claim: Al-Ḥākim did not die but went into concealment; his return will mark the triumph of the Unitarians.

facets.facet_name: The Universal Intellect
facets.core_claim: From the One proceeds the Universal Intellect, and Ḥamza is its human manifestation, chief of the five cosmic ministers.

facets.facet_name: The Unknowable Essence
facets.core_claim: No one can know God's essence; humanity knows him only through his Manifestations and his attributes reflected in creation.

facets.facet_name: The Manifestation of God for This Age
facets.core_claim: Bahá'u'lláh is a perfect mirror of God's attributes, the latest in the line of Manifestations, bringing laws for a united world.

facets.facet_name: The Promised One of All Ages
facets.core_claim: He fulfils the expectations of every faith: the return of Christ in the glory of the Father, the Shah Bahram of the Zoroastrians, the Lord of Hosts, the Maitreya of the Buddhists.

facets.facet_name: The Gate and Herald
facets.core_claim: The Báb is both an independent Manifestation and the forerunner of Bahá'u'lláh, opening a new cycle of revelation.

facets.facet_name: Centre of the Covenant and Perfect Exemplar
facets.core_claim: Through ʿAbdu'l-Bahá the community remained united after Bahá'u'lláh, and in him believers see the teachings lived.

facets.facet_name: The One God Who Chose Mount Gerizim
facets.core_claim: God gave the Torah through Moses and chose Gerizim — not Jerusalem — as the place of his worship.

facets.facet_name: The Restorer of the Era of Favour
facets.core_claim: The Taheb will bring back the age of divine favour and reveal the hidden Tabernacle vessels on Gerizim.

facets.facet_name: The Unique Prophet
facets.core_claim: No prophet arose like Moses; through him alone the Law was given, and belief in him is an article of faith.

facets.facet_name: The Living Most High, Present in I and I
facets.core_claim: Jah is God in heaven and within each person, the one whose name the Psalms proclaim.

facets.facet_name: The Returned Messiah and King of Kings
facets.core_claim: In Haile Selassie the promised Christ returned in kingly character, the Lion of Judah who opens the seals.
facets.scholarly_note: Haile Selassie himself was a devout Ethiopian Orthodox Christian and did not claim divinity; Rastafari reject reports of his death in 1975.

facets.facet_name: Prophet of Repatriation
facets.core_claim: Garvey, like Moses, called a scattered people to return to the promised land of Africa.
facets.scholarly_note: The famous prophecy "Look to Africa, when a black king shall be crowned" is attributed to him by Rastafari; it is not found in his published writings.

facets.facet_name: Satan as Symbol of the Carnal Self
facets.core_claim: Satan stands for everything that is natural in humanity — pride, desire, rational self-interest — and for opposition to the spiritual tyranny of the herd.

facets.facet_name: The Four Crown Princes of Hell
facets.core_claim: In Satanic ritual the four quarters are given to the Crown Princes of Hell: Satan (south, fire), Lucifer (east, air), Belial (north, earth) and Leviathan (west, water).

facets.facet_name: Satan as Real Patron and Liberator
facets.core_claim: The Adversary of the Bible is a real and benevolent power whose rebellion against the tyrant-god opened the way to knowledge and freedom.

facets.facet_name: The Light-Bringer of Self-Illumination
facets.core_claim: Lucifer is the principle of illumination: the will to know, to question and to become one's own light.

facets.facet_name: The Prince of Darkness, Giver of the Black Flame
facets.core_claim: Set is the principle of isolate consciousness; his gift of the Black Flame lets the individual stand apart from nature and create itself.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Xeper (Becoming)
facets.core_claim: Set's word is Xeper: the Setian's endless self-creation and self-development.

facets.facet_name: The Eternal Rebel Against Arbitrary Authority
facets.core_claim: Satan embodies the refusal to bow to unjust power and the insistence on reason and conscience.

facets.facet_name: Emblem of Reconciled Opposites and Pluralism
facets.core_claim: Baphomet stands for the balance of opposites and the right of every conscience to stand in the public square.

facets.facet_name: Hieroglyph of the Astral Light
facets.core_claim: Baphomet is not the Devil but the image of the universal agent through which all magic works: solve et coagula, the balance of opposites.
facets.scholarly_note: The name appears first in 14th-c. accusations that the Templars worshipped an idol; it is most likely a garbling of "Mahomet". Lévi's 1856 drawing created the now-standard image.

facets.facet_name: Infinite Space and the Stars
facets.core_claim: Nuit is the totality of possibility, infinitely extended; every star — every individual — is a point within her body.

facets.facet_name: The Point at the Core of Every Star
facets.core_claim: Hadit is the core of each individual, the secret self who experiences Nuit's infinity; their union is the source of all.

facets.facet_name: Crowned and Conquering Child, Lord of the Aeon
facets.core_claim: Ra-Hoor-Khuit is the active, solar Horus enthroned over the new age; his law is Thelema, will.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Silence
facets.core_claim: Hoor-paar-kraat is the inward, silent aspect of the god of the Aeon, the stillness from which will acts.

facets.facet_name: The Scarlet Woman and Holy Grail
facets.core_claim: Babalon is the sacred harlot of the Aeon, the cup of total surrender through which the initiate dissolves the ego and crosses the Abyss.

facets.facet_name: The Angel Who Dictated the Law
facets.core_claim: Through Aiwass the new Law was delivered word for word; he is the messenger of the gods of the Aeon.

facets.facet_name: The Beast, Prophet of the New Aeon
facets.core_claim: The Beast is the prophet through whom the Word of the Aeon, Thelema, is uttered.

facets.facet_name: The Great Mother of Many Names
facets.core_claim: All goddesses are one Goddess, mother of nature and of all living souls, worshipped at the full moon.

facets.facet_name: Maiden, Mother and Crone
facets.core_claim: The Goddess shows three faces as the moon waxes, is full and wanes: youth, motherhood and wisdom.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Beasts and the Hunt
facets.core_claim: The Horned God is the vital power of animal life and the green world, the hunter and the hunted.

facets.facet_name: The God Who Dies and Is Reborn
facets.core_claim: Through the year the God is born, weds, dies and returns, guiding the dead to rest and rebirth.

facets.facet_name: The Supreme Intelligence and First Cause
facets.core_claim: God is the first cause; every effect has a cause, and the intelligence behind the universe is God, who leads all spirits to perfection.

facets.facet_name: The Promised Consoler
facets.core_claim: The Spirit of Truth fulfils Christ's promise by revealing the immortality of the soul, reincarnation and the law of love.

facets.facet_name: Infinite Mind, All-in-All
facets.core_claim: God is the only Mind and the only reality; whatever is unlike God is illusion, dispelled by spiritual understanding.

facets.facet_name: The Comforter as Divine Science
facets.core_claim: The Comforter promised by Christ is Divine Science, the spiritual law that heals as Jesus healed.

facets.facet_name: Christ as the Divine Idea
facets.core_claim: The Christ is the spiritual idea of God that came to the flesh to destroy incarnate error; Jesus demonstrated it.

facets.facet_name: The Universal Sovereign Whose Name Must Be Sanctified
facets.core_claim: Jehovah alone is Almighty; history is the vindication of his rightful sovereignty.

facets.facet_name: Holy Spirit as God's Active Force
facets.core_claim: The holy spirit is not a person but Jehovah's active force, by which he creates and empowers his servants.

facets.facet_name: The Firstborn Son, Michael the Archangel
facets.core_claim: Before coming to earth Jesus was Michael, the chief of the angels; he is God's son and agent, but not God Almighty.

facets.facet_name: The One God, Not Three
facets.core_claim: Scripture and reason show one God, the Father; the doctrine of the Trinity is a later human invention.

facets.facet_name: The Covenant of Mercy
facets.core_claim: Through the covenant Christ gave her, Mary intercedes and obtains mercy for all who invoke her.

facets.facet_name: The Shining Sky-Father
facets.core_claim: Dyaus is the bright sky itself and its fatherhood: 'Heaven is my father, my begetter' (RV 1.164.33). Paired with Earth he engenders the world and the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Dyaus Pitā is the closest linguistic survival of PIE *Dyēus ph2tēr (Greek Zeus Patēr, Latin Iuppiter). His cult in the Rigveda is already faded, an instance of the 'deus otiosus' pattern.

facets.facet_name: Broad Mother Earth
facets.core_claim: 'Earth is my mother, I am her son' (Atharvaveda 12.1.12). She bears all creatures, holds the herbs and waters, and is the firm ground of dharma.
facets.scholarly_note: In Puranic Hinduism she becomes Bhūdevī, consort of Viṣṇu (rescued by Varāha) — continuity of the Vedic figure into Vaiṣṇava theology.

facets.facet_name: The Golden Impeller
facets.core_claim: Savitṛ, golden-handed and golden-eyed, raises his arms and sets the world in motion and in rest; even the waters and winds keep his ordinances.
facets.scholarly_note: Often distinguished from Sūrya as the sun's animating power rather than its disk; the distinction blurs in later Vedic texts.

facets.facet_name: Guide of Roads and of the Dead
facets.core_claim: Pūṣan knows every road; he protects herds, brings back what is lost, conducts brides to their new home and leads the departed safely to the fathers (RV 10.17).

facets.facet_name: Guardian of Hospitality and Marriage
facets.core_claim: Aryaman keeps the customs that bind the people: guest-friendship, the marriage alliance and the safety of roads; he leads the ancestors.
facets.scholarly_note: Dumézil's Mitra-Varuna places Aryaman as a minor sovereign alongside Mitra (contract) and Varuṇa (binding power); an Avestan cognate Airyaman exists.

facets.facet_name: Apportioner of Fortune
facets.core_claim: Bhaga deals out to each his lot of wealth and luck; 'even the strong man says: may I share in Bhaga' (RV 7.41.2).
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate with Avestan baga and Old Persian baga 'god', and Slavic bogŭ 'god' (via Iranian); the word for 'god' in several languages derives from the same 'allotter' root.

facets.facet_name: The Thundering Rain-Bull
facets.core_claim: Parjanya roars like a lion, strikes down the trees and the wicked, and pours the waters that make the whole earth fruitful (RV 5.83).
facets.scholarly_note: A connection to PIE *Perkʷunos (Lithuanian Perkūnas, Slavic Perun) has been proposed but is phonologically contested.

facets.facet_name: Creator Who Is the Sacrifice
facets.core_claim: Prajāpati emits the creatures from his own body and is emptied by it; the sacrificer rebuilds him in the agnicayana altar, renewing the cosmos (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa).
facets.scholarly_note: Brāhmaṇa theology; Prajāpati's role passes to Brahmā in classical Hinduism. The question-verse refrain of RV 10.121 ('to which god shall we offer?') was later read as naming the god 'Ka'.

facets.facet_name: The Golden Embryo on the Waters
facets.core_claim: 'In the beginning arose the Golden Embryo; once born, he was the one lord of creation; he held the earth and this sky' (RV 10.121.1). From the egg the whole cosmos unfolds.

facets.facet_name: Slayer of the Three-Headed Monster
facets.core_claim: Trita, urged by Indra, kills the three-headed son of Tvaṣṭṛ and recovers the cows (RV 10.8.8). He bears the guilt of the slaying for the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate with Avestan Thrita / Thraētaona (slayer of three-headed Aži Dahāka) and the reconstructed PIE *Tritós who kills a three-headed serpent to regain cattle.

facets.facet_name: Fire Within the Waters
facets.core_claim: Apām Napāt blazes in the waters without kindling; the young waters circle and bathe him, and he gives the world its being (RV 2.35).
facets.scholarly_note: Shared Indo-Iranian deity (Avestan Apąm Napāt, guardian of the khvarenah in the sea Vourukasha). A cognate with Irish Nechtan and Roman Neptunus has been proposed and is debated.

facets.facet_name: The Rock Withholding the Cows of Light
facets.core_claim: Vala encloses the cows — the dawns and the light — in the mountain; the sacred song breaks him open and the day returns.
facets.scholarly_note: The Vala myth is a doublet of the Vṛtra myth: one withholds waters, the other light/cattle; both are opened by Indra.

facets.facet_name: The Howling Archer and Healer
facets.core_claim: Rudra the red, the wild archer whose arrows bring sickness to man and beast, is begged to turn his weapon away; the same Rudra holds a thousand remedies and is the best of physicians (RV 2.33).
facets.scholarly_note: Rudra is the Vedic precursor of Śiva, whose name 'auspicious' was first a euphemistic epithet of Rudra (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad).

facets.facet_name: Twin Horsemen and Physicians
facets.core_claim: The Aśvins drive their honey-chariot ahead of Dawn; they rescue the shipwrecked, restore sight and youth, and give a lost leg of iron to Viśpalā (RV 1.116–117).
facets.scholarly_note: The Aśvins, the Greek Dioskouroi and the Lithuanian Dievo sūneliai ('sons of god') are the standard PIE 'divine twins' set; Mitanni treaty names them as Nāsatya.

facets.facet_name: Storm-Troop of Rudra
facets.core_claim: The Maruts, sons of Rudra and Pṛśni, ride with spears of lightning and golden ornaments, shake mountains, and fight beside Indra against Vṛtra.

facets.facet_name: The All-Maker
facets.core_claim: Viśvakarman, with eyes, mouths, arms and feet on every side, welds heaven and earth together; he is the father who offered all worlds in sacrifice (RV 10.81–82). In the Purāṇas he builds the cities and weapons of the gods.
facets.scholarly_note: Vedic Viśvakarman is a cosmogonic creator; Puranic Viśvakarman is the divine architect, often merged with Tvaṣṭṛ.

facets.facet_name: Fashioner of Forms
facets.core_claim: Tvaṣṭṛ forges Indra's vajra, shapes every form in the womb and fashions the cup of the gods; his three-headed son Viśvarūpa and his creature Vṛtra oppose Indra.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Desire
facets.core_claim: Kāma, with his sugar-cane bow and flower arrows, pierces gods and men; when he shot Śiva the god's third eye burned him to ash, yet he lives on bodiless (Anaṅga) in every heart.
facets.scholarly_note: In RV 10.129 kāma (desire) is 'the first seed of mind' at the beginning — the cosmogonic root of the later deity.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Wealth and the Yakṣas
facets.core_claim: Kubera, king of the yakṣas, keeper of the treasures of the earth, rules Alakā on Kailāsa and guards the north.

facets.facet_name: Buffalo-Demon Usurper of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Proud of his boon, Mahiṣa seizes Indra's throne; only a woman — the Devī formed from all the gods' energies — can and does slay him.
facets.scholarly_note: Mysore (Mahishuru) claims him as its eponym; some Adivasi and Dalit communities (e.g. Asur people) honour Mahishasura as an ancestor king.

facets.facet_name: The Boon-Armoured Tyrant
facets.core_claim: Hiraṇyakaśipu declares himself the only god and demands his son worship him; his perfect boon is undone by a god who is neither man nor beast.

facets.facet_name: Drowner of the Earth
facets.core_claim: Hiraṇyākṣa hides the Earth under the waters of dissolution; Varāha kills him and raises her back to her place.

facets.facet_name: The Righteous Asura King
facets.core_claim: Mahābali's reign was a golden age; dethroned by Vāmana, he is honoured for keeping his promise and returns every Onam.
facets.scholarly_note: Kerala tradition portrays Mahabali as beloved; some political readings treat the Vamana story as Brahmanical displacement of a local king.

facets.facet_name: The Plough-Bearing Elder Brother
facets.core_claim: Balarāma bears the plough and pestle, drinks and fights with unmatched strength; at his death a white serpent leaves his mouth — he was Śeṣa all along.
facets.scholarly_note: One of the earliest attested Vaiṣṇava figures: depicted with plough on Indo-Greek coins of Agathocles beside Vāsudeva-Kṛṣṇa.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Universe at Puri
facets.core_claim: Jagannātha is Kṛṣṇa-Viṣṇu himself, present in the dāru-brahman (wooden absolute); his prasāda erases caste distinctions among those who share it.
facets.scholarly_note: Many scholars see a tribal (Sabara) origin for the wooden icons; the temple legend preserves this in the story of Viśvavasu the Sabara.

facets.facet_name: The God Who Waits on the Brick
facets.core_claim: Viṭṭhala waits on the brick for his devotees; he is mother and father to the poor saints of the Vārkarī path.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Seven Hills for the Kali Age
facets.core_claim: Veṅkaṭeśvara dwells on the Seven Hills to save humanity in the Kali Yuga; whoever surrenders at his feet is protected.

facets.facet_name: Celibate Lord of Sabarimala
facets.core_claim: Ayyappan unites Śiva and Viṣṇu in one son; whoever keeps the vow and calls 'Swamiye Saranam Ayyappa' becomes Ayyappa — devotee and deity share his name.
facets.scholarly_note: Ayyappan is widely linked with the older Sāstā / Ayyanār guardian cult of Tamil and Kerala villages.

facets.facet_name: Warrior Śiva of the Deccan
facets.core_claim: Khaṇḍobā rides out on his horse with sword and dog to destroy Maṇi and Malla and protect his devotees; he is the family god (kuladevata) of Maharashtrian households of every caste.
facets.scholarly_note: Likely a regional pastoral deity Sanskritized as a form of Śiva/Bhairava.

facets.facet_name: Sun-God in the Seven-Horse Chariot
facets.core_claim: Sūrya, soul of all that moves and stands (RV 1.115.1), sees all deeds, drives away darkness and disease, and is the visible form of Brahman.
facets.scholarly_note: Saura iconography (boots, tunic) and the Maga priests of the Sāmba Purāṇa reflect Iranian influence on North Indian sun worship.

facets.facet_name: The Waxing and Waning Moon
facets.core_claim: Candra is the cup of soma drunk by the gods each fortnight and refilled; he governs mind, plants and the lunar mansions.

facets.facet_name: Red Planet, Son of Earth
facets.core_claim: Maṅgala, the fiery son of Bhūmi, grants courage and land, and when ill-placed brings strife and accidents.

facets.facet_name: Preceptor of the Gods
facets.core_claim: Bṛhaspati is the power of prayer (brahman) itself, priest of the devas, whose song broke open the rock and freed the light.

facets.facet_name: Preceptor of the Asuras
facets.core_claim: Śukra, the one-eyed sage, alone knows the secret of raising the slain; he serves the asuras with perfect loyalty, warning Bali against Vāmana.

facets.facet_name: Slow Judge of Karma
facets.core_claim: Śani dispenses the fruit of one's deeds without favour; his affliction purifies, and those who endure it rise.
facets.scholarly_note: Indian astrology absorbed Hellenistic planetary lore (Yavanajātaka, 2nd–3rd c. CE); Śani's malefic character matches Hellenistic Saturn.

facets.facet_name: Eclipse-Swallowing Head
facets.core_claim: Rāhu the head, immortal but bodiless, chases the sun and moon; at every eclipse he devours them, and they slip out through his severed throat.

facets.facet_name: Headless Shadow-Planet
facets.core_claim: Ketu, the body without a head, cuts attachments and grants mokṣa-oriented insight, even as he brings sudden loss.

facets.facet_name: The Nine Seizers of Fate
facets.core_claim: The grahas take hold of every life according to karma; worship of all nine together averts their harm.

facets.facet_name: Purifying River Descended from Heaven
facets.core_claim: Gaṅgā flows from Viṣṇu's foot through Śiva's locks to earth and on to the underworld; she washes away sin and carries the dead to liberation.

facets.facet_name: World-Bearing Serpent of Eternity
facets.core_claim: Śeṣa remains when all else dissolves; on his coils Viṣṇu rests between creations, and his yawning shakes the earth.

facets.facet_name: Rope of the Churning of the Ocean
facets.core_claim: Vāsuki gives his body as the rope of the cosmic churning, enduring both sides' pulling so that the nectar of immortality appears.

facets.facet_name: Serpent Guardians of Waters and Treasure
facets.core_claim: The nāgas hold the rains and springs and the hidden jewels of the earth; honoured, they give fertility and offspring; offended, they bring drought and skin disease.

facets.facet_name: Eagle Who Stole the Nectar
facets.core_claim: Garuḍa, blazing like fire, defeats the gods, takes the amṛta yet does not drink it, and wins his mother's freedom; Viṣṇu makes him his vehicle and banner.
facets.scholarly_note: Garuda spread across Buddhist Asia (garuḍa/khyung, Indonesian national emblem, Thai royal insignia).

facets.facet_name: Earth-Born Queen
facets.core_claim: Sītā comes from the furrow and returns to the earth's embrace; her steadfastness is the measure of dharma.
facets.scholarly_note: The Vedic Sītā is the personified furrow (RV 4.57); the epic heroine preserves the agrarian origin.

facets.facet_name: Kṛṣṇa's Bliss-Energy
facets.core_claim: Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa are one soul in two bodies; she is the inner power of God's own joy, and pure love (prema) flows from her.

facets.facet_name: Wandering Messenger-Sage
facets.core_claim: Nārada moves freely among gods, demons and men, carrying news and kindling conflicts that bring the plan of Viṣṇu to fruition.

facets.facet_name: The Guru Who Is the Trinity
facets.core_claim: Dattātreya is the original guru, the three gods in one form, who teaches non-duality to all who seek, free of caste and rule.

facets.facet_name: Queen of Serpents Who Demands Worship
facets.core_claim: Manasā both sends and cures snakebite; those who refuse her suffer, those who honour her are protected and blessed with children.

facets.facet_name: Goddess Who Brings and Cools the Pox
facets.core_claim: Śītalā's visitation is the fever; her grace is its cooling. She sweeps disease away with her broom and sprinkles healing water.

facets.facet_name: Physician Bearing the Nectar
facets.core_claim: Dhanvantari came up from the milk ocean with the nectar of immortality and taught the science of life to humanity.

facets.facet_name: Skull-Bearing Guardian of the Sacred City
facets.core_claim: Bhairava punishes pride, guards every temple's boundary and the city of Kāśī; even death (Kāla) fears him.
facets.scholarly_note: Bhairava's skull-penance myth reflects Kāpālika ascetic practice; in Kashmir Śaivism Bhairava names the supreme consciousness itself.

facets.facet_name: Warrior Born of Śiva's Grief
facets.core_claim: Vīrabhadra is Śiva's grief turned to fury; he shatters the rite that excluded Śiva and restores the god's due.

facets.facet_name: Bull-Gatekeeper of Śiva
facets.core_claim: Nandī is the perfect devotee who forever gazes at Śiva; through him the worshipper approaches the Lord.

facets.facet_name: Battle-Mothers, Energies of the Gods
facets.core_claim: Each god's power takes female form and rides his mount into battle; together with Kālī they annihilate Raktabīja.
facets.scholarly_note: The epic Mothers of Skanda are dangerous child-seizing beings; the later Seven Mothers are protective goddesses — a transformation visible in iconography.

facets.facet_name: Ten Faces of the Goddess in Ten Directions
facets.core_claim: The Mahāvidyās are the full spectrum of the Goddess, from terrible to beautiful; each is a path of wisdom, and together they are the one Mahādevī.

facets.facet_name: Goddess Whose Body Became the Sacred Land
facets.core_claim: Satī's sacrifice consecrates the land: every Śakti Pīṭha holds a part of her body, and the Goddess is present in the earth itself.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of the Yoni Pīṭha
facets.core_claim: Kāmākhyā is the creative womb of the cosmos; her monthly cycle renews the fertility of the earth.

facets.facet_name: Night-Riding Guardian of the Village
facets.core_claim: Ayyanār circles the village boundary on horseback through the night; no evil spirit or thief passes him.
facets.scholarly_note: Identified with Ayyappan as Sāstā (Hariharaputra); worship is often vegetarian at his shrine while his attendants (e.g. Karuppasamy) receive animal sacrifice.

facets.facet_name: Mother of Rain and Pox
facets.core_claim: Māri is the heat that brings the pustules and the rain that cools them; her devotees honour her with neem leaves and cool offerings so that she may be gentle.
facets.scholarly_note: One Tamil origin legend identifies her with Renukā (Yellamma), whose head was joined to an outcaste woman's body.

facets.facet_name: The Beheaded and Restored Mother
facets.core_claim: Renukā was slain for a moment's doubt and raised again; she now mothers the poor and outcast who come to her hill.
facets.scholarly_note: The devadasi dedication once associated with her cult was outlawed by the Karnataka Devadasis (Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1982.

facets.facet_name: Fierce Guardian Muni
facets.core_claim: Munīśvaran drives off demons and malevolent ghosts; once satisfied he guards his people faithfully.

facets.facet_name: Black Guardian of Justice
facets.core_claim: Karuppu stands at the eighteen steps and judges disputes; a false oath sworn before his sickle brings ruin.

facets.facet_name: Final Avatar Who Ends the Kali Age
facets.core_claim: Nārāyaṇa came as Vaikuṇḍar to destroy the last fragment of Kroni and inaugurate the age of Dharma; all castes drink from one well before him.
facets.scholarly_note: Historically a 19th-c. social-religious reform movement against caste oppression in Travancore.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Evil Reborn in Every Age
facets.core_claim: Kroni was divided and each piece took birth to fight the avatāras; with the destruction of Kaliyan, evil ends forever.

facets.facet_name: Lord Worn on the Body
facets.core_claim: 'The rich will make temples for Śiva; what shall I, a poor man, do? My legs are pillars, the body the shrine, the head a cupola of gold' (Basava).

facets.facet_name: Founder-Saint of the Lingayat Path
facets.core_claim: Basava taught that work is worship (kāyakave kailāsa) and that every devotee of Śiva is equal; in him Nandī came to earth.
facets.scholarly_note: Venerated rather than worshipped in most Lingayat practice; included as the tradition's founding figure.

facets.facet_name: Formless Creator in the Void
facets.core_claim: In the beginning was only water and Phura; from his breath came the gods and from his will the world.

facets.facet_name: King of Heaven, Ancestor of Kings
facets.core_claim: Lengdon rules heaven and gave the Ahom their kings; the Swargadeo is heaven's descendant.
facets.scholarly_note: Assamese Hinduization identified Lengdon with Indra.

facets.facet_name: Divine Brothers Who Descended to Rule
facets.core_claim: The brothers came down the golden ladder with the sacred Somdeo image and taught the worship of ancestors.

facets.facet_name: Thunderbolt Guardian of the Buddha
facets.core_claim: Vajrapāṇi wields the vajra of indestructible wisdom; he protects the Buddha and the Dharma and is the power aspect of the enlightened mind, with Mañjuśrī (wisdom) and Avalokiteśvara (compassion).
facets.scholarly_note: In Gandharan art Vajrapāṇi is depicted with the iconography of Herakles (club-like vajra, lion skin) — a documented Greco-Buddhist adaptation.

facets.facet_name: Guardians of the Four Quarters
facets.core_claim: The Four Great Kings report to Śakra on the deeds of humans and protect all who uphold the Dharma; the Āṭānāṭiya protective verses are their gift.

facets.facet_name: Wealth-Giving King of the North
facets.core_claim: Vaiśravaṇa, who 'hears everything', guards the north, rules the yakṣas and grants prosperity to those who keep the precepts.

facets.facet_name: Devout King of the Thirty-Three
facets.core_claim: Sakka rules the Tāvatiṃsa heaven by seven vows of virtue; though king of gods, he is a disciple of the Buddha, still within saṃsāra.
facets.scholarly_note: A deliberate reframing of Vedic Indra: powerful but subordinate to the Buddha.

facets.facet_name: Brahmā Who Begged the Buddha to Teach
facets.core_claim: Sahampati kneels before the Buddha and requests the turning of the Wheel; the highest god of the world becomes the Dharma's first petitioner.
facets.scholarly_note: The Brahmajāla's deluded Brahmā, who mistakes being first-born for being creator, is a Buddhist critique of Brahmanical creator theology.

facets.facet_name: Child-Devourer Turned Protector of Children
facets.core_claim: Hārītī, once the terror of mothers, learned compassion through her own loss; now she guards children and grants offspring, and the monasteries feed her each day.
facets.scholarly_note: Often paired with the yakṣa Pāñcika; Gandharan Hārītī with cornucopia shares iconography with Kushan Ardochsho and Greek Tyche.

facets.facet_name: Tamer of the Spirits of Tibet
facets.core_claim: Guru Rinpoche, born in a lotus, subdued the gods and demons of the land and made them guardians of the Dharma; he will return to all who call him.
facets.scholarly_note: Historical role is uncertain; the Testament of Ba records an 8th-c. tantric master; the larger biography develops in terma literature.

facets.facet_name: Oath-Bound Protector Spirit
facets.core_claim: Pehar was once a wild king of spirits; bound by oath he now protects the Dharma and the Tibetan government and prophesies through his medium.

facets.facet_name: Heaven-Sent Demon-Subduing King
facets.core_claim: Gesar was a son of heaven born among men; he defeated the demons of north, south, east and west and will return to lead the armies of Shambhala.
facets.scholarly_note: In Buryat and Mongolian versions (Abai Geser) he is the son of Khormusta Tengri — a bridge between Tibetan and Mongol religion.

facets.facet_name: Healer of Lapis Light
facets.core_claim: Whoever hears the name of Bhaiṣajyaguru is freed from disease, misfortune and rebirth in the lower realms; his blue light heals all ills.

facets.facet_name: Wisdom That Gives Birth to Buddhas
facets.core_claim: 'The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Buddhas' (Aṣṭasāhasrikā): all awakened ones are born from the realization of emptiness she embodies.

facets.facet_name: Mandala of the Five Wisdoms
facets.core_claim: The five Jinas are the enlightened nature of the five aggregates; anger becomes mirror-wisdom, pride equality, desire discernment, envy accomplishment, ignorance the Dharmadhātu.
facets.scholarly_note: The Western term 'Dhyāni Buddha' was popularized by Brian Hodgson in the 19th c.; Sanskrit sources call them Jinas or Tathāgatas.

facets.facet_name: Serpent Who Sheltered the Buddha
facets.core_claim: Mucalinda shelters the Awakened One from cold and rain; the serpent power of the waters becomes the Dharma's protector.

facets.facet_name: First Ford-Maker and Teacher of Civilization
facets.core_claim: Ṛṣabha first gave humanity its arts and laws, then showed the path beyond them; he is the first of the twenty-four who cross and help others cross.
facets.scholarly_note: Also honoured in Hindu tradition as a partial avatāra of Viṣṇu (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5).

facets.facet_name: Serpent-Sheltered Ford-Maker
facets.core_claim: Pārśva remained unshaken under the storms of hatred; liberated on Sammeda Śikhara, he shows that equanimity conquers enmity across lifetimes.
facets.scholarly_note: Widely regarded as the earliest Jina with probable historicity.

facets.facet_name: Renouncer Moved by the Animals' Cries
facets.core_claim: Nemi turned back from his own wedding for the sake of animals; compassion for every living being is the door to liberation.

facets.facet_name: The Ford-Makers Across Saṃsāra
facets.core_claim: Each Tīrthaṅkara builds a ford across saṃsāra by founding the fourfold community; venerating them purifies the soul by contemplation, not by their intervention.

facets.facet_name: The Unmoving Standing Meditator
facets.core_claim: Victorious, Bāhubali saw the emptiness of victory; standing immovable in kāyotsarga, he conquered himself.

facets.facet_name: Serpent-Hooded Guardian Goddess
facets.core_claim: Padmāvatī guards the teaching of Pārśva and answers the prayers of the faithful who honour the Jina.
facets.scholarly_note: Jain doctrine holds that liberated Jinas do not respond to petitions; worldly requests go to guardian deities such as Padmāvatī.

facets.facet_name: Mother Under the Mango Tree
facets.core_claim: Ambikā protects children and the faithful of Nemi's teaching; her mango tree bears fruit for those who honour the Jina.

facets.facet_name: Grateful Serpent King Who Shielded the Jina
facets.core_claim: Saved by Pārśva in a previous life, Dharaṇendra repaid him by sheltering him in his supreme trial.

facets.facet_name: Enemy Across Lifetimes
facets.core_claim: Kamaṭha's hatred pursued Pārśva birth after birth, yet could not move him; at last the enemy bowed before the Jina.

facets.facet_name: Bearer of the Divine Light (Jot)
facets.core_claim: Through Nānak the Formless One spoke the Shabad; the same jot (light) passed through the ten Gurus as one flame lights another.
facets.scholarly_note: Sikhs do not regard the Gurus as God incarnate; the Guru is the vessel of the divine Word.

facets.facet_name: Creator of the Khalsa
facets.core_claim: The Guru called for heads and created the Pure Ones; the Khalsa is the Guru's own form, sovereign and fearless, protecting the oppressed.

facets.facet_name: Divine Power as the Sword
facets.core_claim: Bhagautī is Akāl's own might, the sword (kirpān) that upholds justice; to remember her is to remember the strength of God.
facets.scholarly_note: Sikh interpretation is contested: some read Bhagautī as the goddess Durgā, the Khalsa mainstream as an attribute of Akal Purakh.

facets.facet_name: All-Good Primordial Ground
facets.core_claim: Kuntu Zangpo is the pure, empty, luminous nature of mind; all beings are him who have not recognized themselves.

facets.facet_name: Great Mother of Wisdom
facets.core_claim: Satrig Ersang is the space of wisdom from which the enlightened arise; she loves all beings as a mother loves her only child.

facets.facet_name: White Light of Compassion
facets.core_claim: Shenlha Ökar radiates white light to all beings and is the intermediary between the primordial ground and the teacher in the world.

facets.facet_name: Fierce Queen of Existence
facets.core_claim: Sipe Gyalmo rules over all existence and guards the Bön teaching; she destroys its enemies and protects practitioners.

facets.facet_name: Adversary of the Teacher
facets.core_claim: Khyabpa Lagring set every obstacle before Shenrab, yet the Teacher's patience turned him; even the enemy found refuge.
facets.scholarly_note: Structural counterpart of Māra in the Buddha's life story.

facets.facet_name: Great Mountain Lord
facets.core_claim: Thanglha rules the snow peaks and the lake Namtso his consort; he protects the land and the lineages that honour him.

facets.facet_name: Distant Creator
facets.core_claim: Dezau made all things and stands above the gods who are worshipped at the shrines; the world rests on his creation.
facets.scholarly_note: Nuristani Imra is often derived from Yama-rājan, linking him to Vedic Yama; Kalasha usage of Khodai reflects Persian/Islamic influence.

facets.facet_name: Protector-Intercessor of the Valley
facets.core_claim: Mahandeo guards the valley's fields and flocks and carries the people's petitions to Dezau.
facets.scholarly_note: The name is cognate with Mahādeva (Śiva), but his cult is independent of Hindu Śaivism.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Family and Hearth
facets.core_claim: Jestak watches over households, marriages and children; her house is the heart of each lineage.

facets.facet_name: Solstice Visitor God
facets.core_claim: At Chaumos Balumain comes riding from the mythical homeland, blesses the purified people and departs bearing their wishes.

facets.facet_name: Living Embodiment of the Goddess
facets.core_claim: In the chosen Kumārī the goddess Taleju lives visibly; her tika and her gaze confer sovereignty and blessing.

facets.facet_name: Royal Tutelary Goddess
facets.core_claim: Taleju protects the kingdom and the king who honours her; when he failed her, she chose to live among the people in the Kumārī.

facets.facet_name: Compassionate Rain-Bringer
facets.core_claim: Bunga Dyah brings the monsoon to the valley; his chariot's journey ensures the rains and the rice harvest.

facets.facet_name: Patron of Merchants
facets.core_claim: Bhīmsen, strongest of men, guards the trader's road and the shopkeeper's scales.

facets.facet_name: Mother Protector of Birth and Children
facets.core_claim: Umay sits by the cradle and the birthing woman; she brings the child's soul and guards it while it is small.

facets.facet_name: Sacred Earth-and-Water of the Homeland
facets.core_claim: Tengri above and the holy Yer-Sub below gave the Turks their realm; to betray the land is to offend the sacred.

facets.facet_name: Mother Earth Beneath Eternal Heaven
facets.core_claim: Under Möngke Tengri, Etügen Eke nourishes grass, herds and children; she is honoured with milk sprinkled to the ground.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the Hearth Fire
facets.core_claim: The hearth fire is the lineage's life; Mother Fire purifies, protects and must never be insulted by water, blade or filth.

facets.facet_name: Chief of the Benevolent Tengri
facets.core_claim: Khormusta leads the western tengri against the dark eastern ones and sends his son Geser to earth to cleanse it of demons.
facets.scholarly_note: A rare documented chain: Avestan Ahura Mazdā → Sogdian Xurmazta → Uyghur/Mongolian Qormusta, with Buddhist identification as Indra.

facets.facet_name: Leader of the Dark Eastern Tengri
facets.core_claim: Ata Ulan and the eastern tengri send sickness and calamity; the shaman appeases them and Geser fights the demons they spawned.

facets.facet_name: Heavenly Bull Ancestor
facets.core_claim: Bukha Noyon came from heaven as a grey bull, defeated the rival bull and became father of the Buryat clans.

facets.facet_name: Demon of Childbed
facets.core_claim: Albasty lurks by the birthing woman to steal her lungs or liver and harm the child; she flees from iron and the name of God.
facets.scholarly_note: Cognate figures (Al, Ał) occur in Armenian and Persian folk belief.

facets.facet_name: Patron of Horses
facets.core_claim: Kambar-ata keeps the herds of horses; he is called on when mares foal and when the herd is lost in a storm.

facets.facet_name: Uniter of the Forty Tribes
facets.core_claim: Manas, born with blood clots in his hands, gathered the scattered Kyrgyz and guards them still; his spirit inspires the manaschi.

facets.facet_name: Sky-Father of the Scythians
facets.core_claim: Papaios, father of all, with Api the Earth begot the first Scythian; he is the sky over the steppe.
facets.scholarly_note: The name probably means 'Father' (cf. Greek pappas); Herodotus' equation with Zeus is interpretatio graeca.

facets.facet_name: Earth-Mother of the Scythians
facets.core_claim: Api, Earth and Waters, is the mother of the Scythian race and wife of the Sky.
facets.scholarly_note: Name often linked to Iranian *āp- 'water'; the snake-legged goddess of Herodotus 4.9 may be the same figure.

facets.facet_name: Solar Herd-God (Scythian Apollo)
facets.core_claim: Goitosyros brings the light and prosperity of the pastures.
facets.scholarly_note: Interpretation uncertain; known only from Herodotus.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Divination and Royal Investiture
facets.core_claim: Argimpasa grants sovereignty to the king who drinks from her cup and gives prophecy to her Enarees.

facets.facet_name: God of Waters and Horses
facets.core_claim: Thagimasadas rules the waters and the horses on which the Royal Scythians ride.

facets.facet_name: War-God as Iron Sword
facets.core_claim: The god lives in the akinakes sword on the brushwood mound; the blood of captives poured over it wins victory.

facets.facet_name: First Ancestor and the Golden Gifts
facets.core_claim: From Targitaos came the Scythians; the heaven-sent golden gifts chose his youngest son as king, and the kings guard them still.
facets.scholarly_note: Dumézil read the four golden objects as the Indo-European three functions (sovereignty/cult, war, production).

facets.facet_name: Wind of the Upper Region
facets.core_claim: Weshparkar is the wind that moves through heaven, mighty in battle and in the breath of life.

facets.facet_name: The Great God, King of Gods
facets.core_claim: Adbag is the great god who rules the gods of heaven.
facets.scholarly_note: The equation set Brahmā = Zurvan (Zrwa), Indra = Adbag, Mahādeva = Weshparkar is attested in Sogdian Buddhist texts.

facets.facet_name: Lion-Riding Lady of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Nana, the Lady, rides her lion holding sun and moon; she is the great goddess of the Sogdian cities and of the Kushan kings.
facets.scholarly_note: Descends from the Mesopotamian goddess Nanaya, identified with Inanna/Ishtar; worshipped from Bactria to Panjikent and named in the Rabatak inscription of Kanishka.

facets.facet_name: Wind-God in Śiva's Form
facets.core_claim: Oesho, mighty wind of heaven, bearer of trident and bull, protects the Kushan king who stamps his image on coin.
facets.scholarly_note: Whether Oesho is Śiva under a Bactrian name or Vayu in Śiva's iconography is debated; the Sogdian Weshparkar = Mahādeva equation supports a convergence.

facets.facet_name: Radiant Mithra of the Kushans
facets.core_claim: Miiro, radiant lord of the covenant, watches over oaths and kings.

facets.facet_name: God of Victory
facets.core_claim: Orlagno, Smiter of Resistance, brings victory to the righteous king and shatters his enemies.
facets.scholarly_note: Avestan Verethragna 'smiting of resistance/vṛtra' is cognate with Vedic vṛtrahan, Indra's chief epithet 'slayer of Vṛtra'.

facets.facet_name: Divine Royal Glory
facets.core_claim: Pharro is the shining glory that rests on the rightful king; without it no throne endures.

facets.facet_name: Lady of Abundance with the Cornucopia
facets.core_claim: Ardochsho pours out reward and plenty on the righteous and on the realm.

facets.facet_name: The Moon God
facets.core_claim: Mao measures the months and lights the night.
facets.scholarly_note: From Iranian Māh 'moon' (Avestan Māh), cognate with Sanskrit mās.

facets.facet_name: Sacred Fire
facets.core_claim: Athsho is the holy fire that purifies and carries worship upward.

facets.facet_name: White Creator of the Ninth Heaven
facets.core_claim: Ürüng Aiyy Toyon gives light, warmth and the human soul; at Yhyakh the people greet his sun with kumys.

facets.facet_name: Bringer of the Child's Soul
facets.core_claim: Aiyysyt descends to the birthing woman bearing the new soul from the upper world; she is thanked with a feast after the birth.

facets.facet_name: Terrible Lord of the Upper West
facets.core_claim: Ulu Toyon, quick to anger, sends disease and death but also gave humans their breath-soul and fire; the shaman must bargain with him.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Lower World
facets.core_claim: Arsan Duolai rules the dark lower world, feeding on souls; the heroes of the Middle World must defeat his sons.

facets.facet_name: Master of Game
facets.core_claim: Bayanay owns the beasts of the taiga; a hunter's luck is his gift, withdrawn from the greedy and the boastful.

facets.facet_name: Sky-Creator and Owner of Animals
facets.core_claim: Seveki shaped the earth on the waters and made people and reindeer; Khargi spoiled what he could, but Seveki's work stands.

facets.facet_name: Brother Who Marred Creation
facets.core_claim: Whatever Seveki made good, Khargi twisted; mosquitoes, disease and death are his share of creation.

facets.facet_name: Cosmic Hunter Who Recovers the Sun
facets.core_claim: When Kheglen the elk carried the sun into the forest, Mangi pursued it on skis and brought back the day; he watches the road of the dead.

facets.facet_name: Sky-Father of the Upper World
facets.core_claim: Num-Torum made the earth grow from the mud the loon brought up, lowered the first people, and sent his son to watch over them.

facets.facet_name: Mother Who Writes the Fate of the Newborn
facets.core_claim: Kaltash decides at birth how long each life will last, and protects the mother and child.

facets.facet_name: World-Watching Rider
facets.core_claim: Mir-Susne-Khum circles the earth on his winged white horse, seeing all; he intercedes for people and protects them from evil spirits.

facets.facet_name: Underworld Lord of Disease
facets.core_claim: Kul-Otyr rules the dark lower world in the north and sends the spirits of sickness; the dead go down to him.

facets.facet_name: Samoyed Sky-God
facets.core_claim: Num sees all from the upper sky, gives warmth and good weather, and made the earth from what the loon brought up.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Death Below
facets.core_claim: Nga, master of the lower world, claims the dead and tears at creation; shamans bargain with him for the sick.

facets.facet_name: Mother Earth of the Tundra
facets.core_claim: Ya-Nebya bears all that lives on the tundra and helps women in childbirth.

facets.facet_name: Raven Creator and Light-Bringer
facets.core_claim: Raven flew over the waters and made land, pecked open the dark to free the light, and taught people how to live.

facets.facet_name: Soul-Hunting Spirits
facets.core_claim: The kelet stalk people as prey; disease is their bite, and the shaman must drive them off.

facets.facet_name: Big Raven, First Ancestor
facets.core_claim: Kutkh made the land, gave the people fire and sea-creatures, and is their grandfather; his foolishness and cunning both shaped the world.

facets.facet_name: Revealer of the Eight Trigrams
facets.core_claim: Fuxi read the patterns of heaven and earth and drew the Eight Trigrams, the code of all change, giving humanity divination, writing's forerunner and the order of things.

facets.facet_name: Serpent-Bodied Primordial Pair with Nüwa
facets.core_claim: Fuxi and Nüwa, entwined at the tails and holding set-square and compass, are the first couple whose union re-peopled the world and who measure out the cosmos.
facets.scholarly_note: The brother–sister flood-survivor version is recorded in Tang-era and later sources and in southwest Chinese minority traditions; the Han reliefs show the entwined pair.

facets.facet_name: Judge of the Dead in the Fifth Court of Diyu
facets.core_claim: Yanluo reviews each soul's deeds in the mirror of retribution and sentences it within the ten-court bureaucracy of the underworld, under the authority of the Jade Emperor.

facets.facet_name: The Judge Demoted for Mercy
facets.core_claim: Yanluo first ruled the First Court, but he so often sent the wronged back to life that he was moved to the Fifth; his justice leans toward mercy.
facets.scholarly_note: The demotion tale is recorded in the late-imperial Jade Record (Yuli baochao).

facets.facet_name: The Lord on High of the Shang
facets.core_claim: Shangdi commands the weather, sends blessing or disaster on the realm, and receives the royal ancestors who mediate between him and the living king.

facets.facet_name: Shangdi as Huangtian, Sovereign Heaven
facets.core_claim: Shangdi and Tian are one: the moral Heaven that gives and withdraws the Mandate and receives the emperor's solstice sacrifice at the Altar of Heaven.

facets.facet_name: Mother of the Nine Dipper Stars
facets.core_claim: Doumu bore the stars of the Northern Dipper, the celestial office that records each person's lifespan; through her the registers of fate can be rewritten.
facets.scholarly_note: Her iconography and some titles are shared with the Buddhist goddess Mārīcī, with whom Chinese practice often identifies her.

facets.facet_name: Threefold Emanation of the Dao
facets.core_claim: The one primordial breath of the Dao divides into the three pure heavens and their three lords; they precede and outrank even the Jade Emperor.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Revealer of the Scriptures
facets.core_claim: Before all worlds, Yuanshi Tianzun was; at the start of each kalpa he opens the self-born celestial texts and transmits them downward through the heavens.
facets.scholarly_note: Some medieval Daoist texts identify him with Pangu, the primordial being.

facets.facet_name: Keeper of the Numinous Treasure
facets.core_claim: Lingbao Tianzun keeps the scriptures and talismans of the Numinous Treasure and balances yin and yang between the primordial heaven and the world.

facets.facet_name: Patriarch of Inner Alchemy
facets.core_claim: Lü Dongbin attained immortality through inner alchemy and returns among mortals to heal, test hearts and reveal the way by spirit-writing; Quanzhen honours him as a patriarch.

facets.facet_name: Bestower of Wealth and Prosperity
facets.core_claim: Caishen gathers and dispenses wealth; welcomed at New Year, he rewards diligence and honest dealing with abundance.

facets.facet_name: Magistrate of the Unseen City
facets.core_claim: Each city has its Chenghuang who governs its dead and spirits, records deeds, and escorts souls to the underworld courts, just as the earthly magistrate governs the living.

facets.facet_name: Tamer of Rivers at Guankou
facets.core_claim: Erlang (as the son of Li Bing) subdued the river dragon and the floods of the Min River, giving Sichuan the Dujiangyan waterworks and its fertile plain.

facets.facet_name: Three-Eyed Warrior of Heaven
facets.core_claim: With his third eye that sees through every disguise, his three-pointed blade and his celestial hound, Erlang defeats demons and even the Monkey King.

facets.facet_name: Rain-Giving Sovereigns of the Waters
facets.core_claim: The Dragon Kings govern seas, rivers and rain under the Jade Emperor; their favour ends drought and their anger floods the land.
facets.scholarly_note: The kingly, palace-dwelling form owes much to Indian naga-kings transmitted through Buddhism, joined to older Chinese rain-dragon cults.

facets.facet_name: Yang Counterpart of the Queen Mother
facets.core_claim: Ruling the eastern paradise and the registers of male immortals, Dongwanggong pairs with Xi Wangmu as yang to her yin.
facets.scholarly_note: Scholars generally regard him as a Han-era creation to give Xi Wangmu a cosmological counterpart.

facets.facet_name: Unborn Mother of All Souls
facets.core_claim: "True Emptiness Native Land, Eternal Venerable Mother": she is the uncreated mother to whom all her lost children will return.

facets.facet_name: Mother Calling Her Children Home
facets.core_claim: In the last kalpa the Mother sends Maitreya to gather the ninety-six myriad lost children back to her, ending the cycle of suffering.

facets.facet_name: Ancestral Sovereign and Civilizer
facets.core_claim: Huangdi founded civilized order: he defeated chaos at Zhuolu, established the arts of rule and medicine, and ascended to heaven on a dragon.

facets.facet_name: Yellow Thearch of the Center
facets.core_claim: In the Five Phases cosmology Huangdi is the deity of the center and of earth, around whom the four directional thearchs are ordered.

facets.facet_name: Divine Farmer Who Tasted the Hundred Herbs
facets.core_claim: Shennong gave the plough and the five grains, and by tasting every herb at the risk of his own life revealed the healing and poisonous plants.

facets.facet_name: Fire Lord of the South
facets.core_claim: Zhurong governs fire and the southern quarter and fought Gonggong to keep the waters from overwhelming the world.

facets.facet_name: Rebel Who Broke the Pillar of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Defeated in battle, Gonggong smashed Mount Buzhou, tearing a hole in heaven and tilting the world; floods poured out until the sky was repaired.

facets.facet_name: Rebel War God Defeated at Zhuolu
facets.core_claim: Chiyou forged the first weapons and challenged the Yellow Emperor's order with storm and fog; defeated, he became the patron of war.
facets.scholarly_note: Many Hmong communities regard Chiyou as a revered ancestor rather than a villain; the Han historiographic tradition casts him as rebel.

facets.facet_name: Server of the Soup of Oblivion
facets.core_claim: At the last threshold of the underworld Meng Po gives each soul the broth of forgetting, so that it carries no memory into its next birth.

facets.facet_name: Lord of Mount Tai, Keeper of Life and Death
facets.core_claim: From Mount Tai the Emperor of the Eastern Peak governs the bureaus of the dead and fixes each person's lifespan in his registers.

facets.facet_name: Mountain Mother Who Grants Children
facets.core_claim: From the summit of Mount Tai Bixia Yuanjun grants children, protects mothers in childbirth and heals the sight of the faithful.

facets.facet_name: Star-Lord of Literature and Examinations
facets.core_claim: Wenchang presides over literature, learning and the civil examinations, bestowing success on the diligent and virtuous.

facets.facet_name: Perfected Warrior of the North
facets.core_claim: Barefoot, sword in hand, standing on tortoise and snake, Zhenwu commands the northern heavens and quells demons; Wudang Mountain is his seat.

facets.facet_name: Binder of the Red Thread of Marriage
facets.core_claim: Yue Lao keeps the book of marriages and ties destined spouses together with a red cord that no circumstance can sever.

facets.facet_name: Star-Gods of Blessing, Rank and Longevity
facets.core_claim: Fu, Lu and Shou bring the three goods of life: happiness, success and long life. Shouxing, the South Pole star, decides each lifespan.

facets.facet_name: Protector of the Nation and the Warriors
facets.core_claim: Hachiman, the deified Emperor Ōjin, guards the nation and the warrior clans; samurai prayed to him before battle.

facets.facet_name: Hachiman Daibosatsu
facets.core_claim: Hachiman was the first kami to receive the title of bodhisattva; he protected the building of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji and unites kami worship and the Buddha way.

facets.facet_name: First Kami at the Center of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Ame-no-Minakanushi appeared first of all beings, alone and without a partner, and at once concealed himself; he is the still center from which creation proceeds.
facets.scholarly_note: Barely mentioned in the Kojiki; elevated to supreme creator by Edo-period Kokugaku theologian Hirata Atsutane and by several new religions; medieval practice linked him with the pole-star bodhisattva Myōken.

facets.facet_name: Primordial Generative Force (Musubi)
facets.core_claim: Musubi, the power that ties and generates, is embodied in Takamimusubi; with Amaterasu he governs heaven and orders the descent of the imperial grandson.

facets.facet_name: Generative Power Who Revives and Gives Seed
facets.core_claim: Kamimusubi restores the murdered Ōkuninushi to life and gathers the seeds of the five grains from the body of the food goddess; she is the life-giving musubi of the Izumo line.

facets.facet_name: Builder and Ruler of the Land
facets.core_claim: Killed and revived, tested in the underworld, Ōkuninushi built the country with Sukunabikona and taught medicine and agriculture before ceding rule to Amaterasu's line.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Hidden Realm and of Bonds (En-musubi)
facets.core_claim: After ceding the visible land, Ōkuninushi rules the hidden world (kakuriyo) from Izumo, where the gods assemble to tie the bonds of marriage and fate.

facets.facet_name: Tiny Healer Who Came Over the Sea
facets.core_claim: Small as a seed, Sukunabikona came from beyond the sea, gave medicine, brewing and healing springs, and returned to Tokoyo, the eternal land.

facets.facet_name: Smiling God of Fishing and Commerce
facets.core_claim: Ebisu brings the catch to fishermen and customers to merchants; luck, for him, arrives from beyond the sea.

facets.facet_name: The Rejected First Child Returned as Luck
facets.core_claim: Born boneless and cast away by his divine parents, Hiruko drifted across the ocean and came ashore as Ebisu; the rejected child becomes the bringer of fortune.
facets.scholarly_note: The Ebisu–Hiruko identification is medieval (Nishinomiya); Miho Shrine identifies Ebisu with Kotoshironushi instead.

facets.facet_name: Dancer Who Drew Out the Sun
facets.core_claim: Uzume's ecstatic, laughing dance before the cave drew Amaterasu out and restored light to the world; every kagura dance repeats it.

facets.facet_name: Guide at the Crossroads of Heaven and Earth
facets.core_claim: Sarutahiko waited at the crossroads of heaven to lead the heavenly grandson to earth; he opens every road and guards its crossings.

facets.facet_name: Thunder-Sword Who Subdued the Land
facets.core_claim: Takemikazuchi brought the land under heaven's rule by the power of thunder and sword and keeps the earthquake-catfish pinned beneath the keystone at Kashima.

facets.facet_name: Fire Whose Birth Brought Death
facets.core_claim: Kagutsuchi's birth killed Izanami and opened the way to Yomi; his slain body gave rise to many kami; fire both destroys and generates.

facets.facet_name: The Heavenly Grandson Who Descended with the Regalia
facets.core_claim: Sent down by Amaterasu and Takamimusubi with the three sacred treasures, Ninigi came to earth at Takachiho to rule the land; his great-grandson was the first emperor, Jimmu.

facets.facet_name: High God Who Comes from Beyond the Sea
facets.core_claim: Kinmamon arrives from Nirai Kanai and from heaven to the sacred groves, possesses the high priestesses and blesses the realm.

facets.facet_name: Male Creator of the Ryukyu Islands with Amamikyu
facets.core_claim: With Amamikyu, Shinerikyu raised the islands from the sea at heaven's command and became father of the first Ryukyuan peoples.

facets.facet_name: Hearth Grandmother Who Carries Prayers
facets.core_claim: Every Ainu prayer begins with Fire Grandmother in the hearth, who conveys words and offerings to the kamuy and testifies to the family's conduct.

facets.facet_name: Half-Divine Teacher of the Ainu
facets.core_claim: Okikurmi taught the Ainu the arts of life and the right ways of prayer, guarded them from evil, and withdrew when they grew disrespectful.

facets.facet_name: Bodhisattva Who Hears the Cries of the World
facets.core_claim: Whoever calls Kannon's name in danger is heard and saved; Kannon takes any form needed, monk, maiden, king or god, to reach each being.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of Children and the Dead
facets.core_claim: Jizō descends into every hell, protects the souls of children at the Sai riverbank, and guides travellers and the dead to safety.

facets.facet_name: Great King Who Judges the Dead
facets.core_claim: Enma reads each soul's record and its reflection in the mirror of deeds and pronounces its destination among the six realms.

facets.facet_name: Enma as a Manifestation of Jizō
facets.core_claim: The terrifying judge is Jizō in wrathful guise; judgment itself is an act of compassion.
facets.scholarly_note: The Enma–Jizō honji suijaku pairing is set out in the Jizō Jūō-kyō, a Japanese apocryphal sutra.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of Music, Eloquence and Flowing Water
facets.core_claim: Benzaiten gives eloquence, learning and music, protects the realm, and in her island shrines grants wealth that flows like water.

facets.facet_name: Smiling Lord of Rice and Wealth
facets.core_claim: Daikoku's magic mallet shakes out fortune and his sack never empties; he guards the kitchen and blesses the harvest.

facets.facet_name: The Great Black One, Protector of the Dharma
facets.core_claim: Daikokuten began as the wrathful black deva who protects monks and their food; his fierceness softened into abundance.

facets.facet_name: Guardian King of the North
facets.core_claim: Bishamonten guards the northern quarter of the world-mountain and those who hear the Dharma; warriors such as Uesugi Kenshin took him as patron.

facets.facet_name: Deva Who Asked the Buddha to Teach
facets.core_claim: Bonten, the highest of the world's gods, kneels before the Buddha and asks him to teach; even the creator serves the Dharma.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three
facets.core_claim: From his palace atop Sumeru, Taishakuten commands the devas and guardian kings and defends the Dharma against the asuras.

facets.facet_name: Vengeful Spirit Turned Patron of Learning
facets.core_claim: Wronged in life, Michizane's spirit raged as thunder over the capital; enshrined and pacified, he became Tenjin, who blesses students and scholars.

facets.facet_name: Maitreya Walking Unrecognized
facets.core_claim: Hotei's death verse revealed him as Maitreya in disguise; the future Buddha already walks among us, laughing, carrying the world's troubles in his sack.

facets.facet_name: Embodiment of Happiness, Wealth and Longevity
facets.core_claim: Fukurokuju carries in one person fuku (happiness), roku (wealth) and ju (longevity) and grants wisdom with long life.

facets.facet_name: Old Man of Longevity with the Scroll of Lifespans
facets.core_claim: Jurōjin keeps the scroll on which every life's length is written and grants years to the faithful.

facets.facet_name: Gods of Fortune on the Treasure Ship
facets.core_claim: At New Year the Seven arrive on the takarabune laden with treasure; placing their picture under the pillow brings a lucky first dream.
facets.scholarly_note: The membership varied before the Edo period (Kichijōten sometimes replaced Jurōjin).

facets.facet_name: The One Lord of Heaven
facets.core_claim: Above all spirits stands Hananim, Heaven itself as a personal lord, who watches over human conduct and governs destiny.

facets.facet_name: Hananim as the Name of God in Korean Christianity
facets.core_claim: Korean Christians call the one God Hananim (Protestant) or Haneunim, the Lord of Heaven Koreans already knew.
facets.scholarly_note: Adopted by Protestant translators from the 1880s; the Catholic Church in Korea historically used Cheonju (Lord of Heaven) and now also Haneunim.

facets.facet_name: Heavenly Father in the Dangun Myth
facets.core_claim: Hwanin rules heaven and sends his son Hwanung to earth with the three seals to benefit humankind broadly (hongik ingan).
facets.scholarly_note: The Samguk yusa glosses Hwanin as 帝釋 (Jeseok), i.e. the Buddhist Śakra/Indra. Daejonggyo (1909) treats Hwanin, Hwanung and Dangun as the triune Hanul.

facets.facet_name: Bear Who Became the Mother of the Nation
facets.core_claim: Through patient endurance in the dark cave the bear became a woman and mother of Dangun; she is the earthly mother of the Korean people.

facets.facet_name: Lord of the Mountain with His Tiger
facets.core_claim: Each mountain has its Sanshin who governs its land and creatures; with his tiger messenger he protects villages and grants offspring and longevity.

facets.facet_name: Goddess of the Hearth and Kitchen
facets.core_claim: Each morning the housewife sets clean water for Jowang, who protects the hearth, the family's food and its luck.

facets.facet_name: Abandoned Daughter Who Fetched the Water of Life
facets.core_claim: Bari crossed into the otherworld, served its guardian and returned with the water and flowers of life to raise her dead parents.

facets.facet_name: Guide of the Dead and First Shaman
facets.core_claim: Refusing worldly reward, Bari chose to become the deity who leads the souls of the dead to the other world; shamans sing her story in every funeral gut.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of the House-Beam
facets.core_claim: Seongju dwells in the ridge beam, the highest of the household gods, keeping the house and family whole.

facets.facet_name: Great King of the Underworld Court
facets.core_claim: Yeomra examines each soul's life and passes sentence; the jeoseung saja, his messengers, fetch the dead to his court.

facets.facet_name: Guardian of the Village and the Pass
facets.core_claim: At the seonangdang by the road, Seonangsin watches the village's boundary, keeping out disease and evil and protecting travellers.
facets.scholarly_note: The name derives from Chinese Chenghuang (城隍), the City God, merged with indigenous village-guardian cults.

facets.facet_name: Dragon Ancestor of the Vietnamese
facets.core_claim: From the sea came Lạc Long Quân, who slew the fish-demon, the fox-spirit and the tree-demon and civilized the people; all Vietnamese are "children of the dragon".

facets.facet_name: Dragon and Fairy Who Parted
facets.core_claim: Dragon and fairy could not dwell together; Lạc Long Quân led fifty sons to the sea while Âu Cơ led fifty to the mountains, dividing and peopling the land.

facets.facet_name: Mountain Fairy, Mother of the Hundred Sons
facets.core_claim: From Âu Cơ's hundred eggs came the hundred ancestors of the Viet; she is "Mẹ Âu Cơ", mother of the nation, who led half her children to the highlands.
